# OT1995 Current-Term Neutral Projection

## Scope, law and chronology

Current Court actions comprise 116 completed Court events and ten admitted noncase-law sources (126 canonical Records). Current Court-event cutoff: 1996-07-01. Chunk 10 completes seven Court events with no stopped matter. Colorado used the preserved pre-June26 baseline and Doe completion addendum, excluding its June26 peers. The four June28 matters used the complete earlier June26 law without treating one another as precedent; the two July1 matters used the complete earlier June28 law without same-day ordering. The bounded February8 Telecommunications Act sections504–506 and related Act section561 source insertion changes no completed adjudication; section505's amendment has its separate March9 effective date. Jones's financial-leave motion and petition, Wood's plenary grant, Maine No.35 and Louisiana No.121 implementation, the five inherited open matters, and Shieh's three separate certiorari petitions remain open. No transmission, service, expiration, execution or other unentered external event is presumed. Records control over these projections. Operator verification and commit remain pending; public rendering and term close are separate tasks.

**Historical progress entries:** Dated chunk-progress entries and per-chunk summaries below are snapshots as of the stage they describe. Source counts and "latest admitted source" dates stated in them (for example "eight" sources or "April 26") reflect that time. Current state: ten admitted noncase-law sources; the latest admitted-source effective date is April 29, 1996 (Utah H.B. 206). Utah H.B. 206 was admitted in chunk 8, and the Telecommunications Act cable provisions (§§504–506 with review under §561, and §551; effective February 8) in chunk 10.

OCC §7.4001(a)–(d) is additionally admitted at its April 1, 1996 effective date after the bounded insertion review found no material effect on the 17 completed April 1–May 20 Court events. This eighth source changes no completed Court Record or pending stage. February 9 publication is distinct from April 1 effectiveness; source admission itself adjudicated no special retroactivity or earlier-case application. Smiley subsequently supplies its own qualified judicial use of the interpretation for antecedent transactions without backdating the rule. The Richards/Whren/Degen/Exxon group was completed in chunk 7 on June 10; the earlier Romer/BMW/Henderson/Casarotto May 20 group retains its common May 13 entering law without a same-day peer dependency. [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_OCC_national_bank_interest_rule_7_4001_regulatory_effectiveness_1996-04-01.md).

The opening law is the [Holdings doctrinal volumes](../../../state/holdings/INDEX.md), [Standards and Tests](../../../state/STANDARDS_AND_TESTS.md) and [Standing State](../../../state/STANDING_STATE.md), through the complete June 29, 1995 group. The [Composition register](../../../foundation/COURT_COMPOSITION.md) supplies membership, seniority and the August 3, 1994 circuit allotments. Current decisions and statutes below apply from their own effective dates and within their stated limits.

The latest earlier endpoints are **Benten v. Kessler** (OT1991, July 17, 1992), **DeBoer v. DeBoer** (OT1992, July 26, 1993), and the full **June 30, 1994 OT1993 group**: Holder; De Grandy and companions; Bagwell; McFarland; Madsen; and Tuilaepa/Proctor. The full **June 29, 1995 OT1994 group** is Babbitt v. Sweet Home; Rosenberger; Miller/Abrams/United States v. Johnson; Pinette; and Chabad-Lubavitch of Georgia v. Miller. The established Pinette-to-Chabad sequence is already reflected in the opening law; the other same-day decisions remain uncoordinated peers. Neither group is truncated to a single last-listed case.

The opening noncase-law baseline includes OT1994's March 10 revised Vaccine Injury Table and April 4 Plant Variety Protection Act amendments within the trackers' operative and transition limits. No duplicate source event is created.

## Current law

The following summaries preserve current force and material limits. The linked public decisions supply their complete Holdings, Precedent Treatment and Law After Decision. Published separate grounds retain the noncontrolling status stated below.

| Effective date | Matter | Controlling law and limits | Authority |

| 1995-10-01 | North Carolina Session Law 1995-424; paternity amendment | The amendment permits a posthumous paternity judgment when the action began before the putative father's death; when it begins within one year after death and no estate-administration proceeding began within that year; or when an estate-administration proceeding began within that year and the action begins within the claims period specified by G.S. 28A-19-3(a). A judgment establishing paternity under this subsection must take effect as of the day before the father's death. In a contested paternity action brought more than three years after the child's birth or after the putative father's death, evidence from a blood or genetic marker test is required. The act applies only to actions commenced on or after October 1, 1995, but before October 1, 1998, without regard to the father's date of death, and expires October 1, 1998. No particular claimant's satisfaction of those requirements is established. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_North_Carolina_paternity_amendment_statutory_effectiveness_1995-10-01.md) |
| 1995-10-10 | Wood v. Bartholomew | Certiorari granted for plenary consideration on the unchanged Brady materiality question. No merits judgment or holding; existing Brady and Kyles law remains unchanged. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Wood_v_Bartholomew_certiorari_1995-10-10.md) |

Johnson excludes purely factual-sufficiency appeals. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Doe_v_Taylor_ISD_merits_1995-10-16.md) |

Netherland | Surviving nonweighing eligibility alone cannot dispose of an independent, properly available psychiatric-assistance claim or establish absence of an effect on sentence selection. Zant's narrower eligibility rule survives. The Court selects no collateral error-effect standard for this Ake category and finds neither a violation nor entitlement to relief. The category-specific Brecht and O'Neal holdings remain unchanged. The concurrence's proposed Chapman extension has no controlling force. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Tuggle_v_Netherland_summary_merits_1995-10-30.md) |

Strumpf, No. 94-1340 | A genuinely temporary payment refusal preserving a claimed offset for prompt judicial consideration is distinct from a completed setoff and, in this deposit-debt setting, does not violate the presented control or collection provisions. Section 553 creates no offset right, actual offset remains stayed without relief, and no general immunity for bank holds results. The sanctions judgment loses its stated foundation; separate statutory elements and unpresented claims remain unchanged. Section 363 cash-collateral and adequate-protection requirements remain separate. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Citizens_Bank_of_Maryland_v_Strumpf_merits_1995-10-31.md) |
| 1995-10-31 | Louisiana v. Mississippi et al., No. 121, Original | The island exception preserves the established side of a continuing island despite a navigation-channel shift, while permitting ordinary movement of the active boundary channel until cessation fixes it. The report's continuity and former-channel determinations control this sovereign dispute. No universal island definition, prescription holding, private-title judgment against absent owners or numerical boundary decree is added. The consistent implementing description was entered in the December 4 decree below; the retained jurisdiction and the doctrinal limits survive. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Louisiana_v_Mississippi_original_exceptions_1995-10-31.md) |
| 1995-11-07 | Libretti v. United States, No. 94-7427 | Former Rule 11(f) imposes no independent factual-basis inquiry into this criminal forfeiture sentence. Five Justices classify the particular property-extent determination as sentencing rather than a Sixth Amendment offense-element question and uphold the statutory special-verdict waiver on the affirmative agreement and courtroom assent. The constitutional reservation of four Justices does not displace that majority holding. A separate five-Justice ground rejects a wholesale new proceeding on the existing record while reserving the precise independent-duty question. Knowing waiver remains distinct from competence or silence, and consent cannot enlarge § 853. No general asset eligibility, pension-plan status or displacement of third-party relief is established. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Libretti_v_United_States_merits_1995-11-07.md) |
| 1995-11-13 | American Life League v. Reno | The challenged reproductive-service provisions survive the presented facial constitutional and categorical damages objections within their enacted definitions, motives, own-minor exception and protected-expression limits. Their commercial connection rests on direct interference with an actual medical-services market, not generalized social costs. Elected statutory damages remain possible for legally attributable, nonexcepted violations; the parent/guardian exception bars all FACE civil remedies, including injunctions, for qualifying exclusively own-minor conduct. No amount-specific award is adjudicated. The inclusive facility definition and separate ingress/egress/passage rules establish no geographic buffer or categorical outdoor immunity. Six Justices reject the broader constitutional exemption under Smith/Lukumi, while RFRA independently requires the five-Justice remand. The government must satisfy that statute for the identified person and application after a substantial burden is established; the Act's continued force does not establish every future enforcement as lawful. No new true-threat rule, worship holding, Fourteenth Amendment §5 power, automatic religious exemption or general damages-attribution theory is created. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_American_Life_League_v_Reno_merits_1995-11-13.md) |
| 1995-11-20 | A. St. P. C. v. B. C. | Due process requires clear and convincing proof that a parent sexually abused that parent's child before Section 9:364(D)'s complete ban on visitation and contact is triggered. The statute permits restoration only of supervised visitation after a contradictory (adversarial) hearing establishes both successful completion of a program designed for sexual abusers and the children's best interests. The separate state invalidation of mandatory extra weight for the qualified child's therapist remains undisturbed. Ordinary investigations, emergency protection and lesser custody or supervised-visitation measures retain their existing legal requirements; no abuse finding, unsafe-contact entitlement or new visitation schedule follows. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_A_St_P_C_v_B_C_merits_1995-11-20.md) |
| 1995-11-28 | Field v. Mans | For the actual-fraud claim presented under §523(a)(2)(A), creditors must prove actual and justifiable reliance under the recipient-specific standard, not universal objective prudence. The ordinary proof burden and obtained-by limitation remain. Subsection(A) excludes statements respecting the debtor's or an insider's financial condition; subsection(B) separately requires a materially false written statement of that kind, reasonable creditor reliance, and the debtor's causing it to be made or published with intent to deceive. Existing findings must be assessed under the correct rule; the Court does not declare the entire debt nondischargeable. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Field_v_Mans_merits_1995-11-28.md) |

Existing exclusions, actual control, qualifications, liability and individual remedy requirements continue to govern. | [Record](../entering-law/PUBLIC_NLRB_v_Town_and_Country_Electric_Inc_merits_1995-11-28.md) |

| 1996-02-05 | United States v. Bishop; United States v. Stokes; Third Circuit Nos. 94-5321 and 94-5387; 66 F.3d 569. | O'Connor's opinion has direct majorities for each portion. Eight Justices, all except Stone-Zsela, hold under Menna and Blackledge that Bishop's existing-record constitutional-power claim survives his plea; Broce still bars contradictory factual reopening, and not every objection survives. Stone-Zsela agrees only in reaching it. All nine apply Harris to the original §2119 economic vehicle-taking class within the interstate theft-prevention scheme, preserving the enacted vehicle-history element; remote movement alone, general crime costs and automatic instrumentality reasoning do not supply the ground. Lopez retains its limits. All nine separately sustain offense-date §924(c)'s express additional consecutive punishment and apply Hunter to this single prosecution even assuming Blockburger overlap. Use or carrying and the offense relationship remain independent requirements; Bailey's active employment, Smith's conduct/relation limits and Dixon/Grady's successive-prosecution rules are unchanged. All nine apply Manson and Biggers separately to station and in-court identifications: opportunity to observe, attention, prior-description accuracy, certainty and elapsed time are weighed against suggestion. Accepted independent recollection and supported perception and prompt separate viewings sustain admission; promptness, honest memory or independent guilt evidence alone cannot replace reliability. No mandatory five-label checklist results. O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer adopt Muniz's formerly four-Justice administrative rationale for a booking question reasonably related to necessary medical attention for an observed condition when content and setting support that function. Medical intent alone is insufficient; investigative demands and questions objectively reasonably likely to extract incriminating offense information remain outside it. The accident answer stays testimonial, and later usefulness alone does not defeat the bounded exception. Innis's express-questioning and objective limits remain. Those same seven sustain any recording's conveyance of that answer, without finding playback occurred. Eight, adding Stevens, hold that recording physical appearance or movement does not itself compel testimonial disclosure; ordinary evidence rules still apply and unlawful words do not automatically exclude separable physical observations. Those eight also sustain the separately reported video objection because it establishes no identified abuse or legal defect, without reconstructing an unreported relevance/prejudice analysis or declaring physical evidence categorically admissible. No emergency, waiver, additional content or fresh harmlessness finding is supplied. No precedent is overruled; the separate remands change neither Chapman nor ordinary evidentiary harmless-error rules. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Bishop_and_Stokes_merits_1996-02-05.md) |

| 1996-02-12 | United States v. Hale; Eighth Circuit No. 91-3830; 978 F.2d 1016; no Supreme Court docket supplied. | O'Connor's Part I, joined by all nine, sustains §922(o)'s possession prohibition as integral to direct control of machinegun transfers and available private stock, without an unwritten transaction-specific interstate element. Marketability, remote movement or general crime costs alone are insufficient; Lopez, Harris, American Life League and Bishop/Stokes retain their separate limits. The exceptions remain for transfers to or by, or possession by or under the authority of, the United States or its department or agency, or a State or its department, agency or political subdivision; and for lawful transfer or possession of a machinegun lawfully possessed before May 19, 1986. Manufacture before that date alone is insufficient, and no particular count is found within an exception. Part III-A, also joined by all nine, applies Love's personal-holder rule: no membership, current service or preparation for organized-militia activity is required. Actual weapon, conduct and restriction remain separate inquiries; military usefulness creates neither exclusion nor unrestricted immunity. Miller retains its weapon-and-record inquiry. In Part III-B, the eight Associate Justices vacate the thirteen-count appellate affirmance because its material affiliation premise fails and no adequate independent application supports it. Lower courts must use the actual objects, statutory branches and record as necessary, preserving established count-specific premises and ordinary procedural limits; no missing finding, new offense element, universal hearing, automatic-weapon classification, scrutiny tier or ultimate invalidity is declared. The same eight supply the separate Part II tax-administration and Part IV registration grounds sustaining all three §5861(d) convictions; Stone-Zsela agrees in those judgments only. Sonzinsky, Miller and Freed sustain genuine making/transfer-tax administration and registration, not every NFA application. Transfer tax is ordinarily $200 or $5 for an any-other-weapon transfer and payable by the transferor; making tax is $200 payable by the maker. Both taxes are subject to applicable exemptions; none is established here. The transferor registers to the transferee. Approval must precede transfer and must be denied if transfer, receipt or possession would put the transferee in violation of law; approval must precede making and must be denied if making or possession would put the maker in violation of law. No universal late-application duty results. No count establishes unavailable lawful approval or tax collection; that materially different application is reserved. Under Part V's eight-Justice rationale, these diligent-search/nonentry certificates on the accepted Rule 803(10) and 902(1) premises need no separate custodian-production or unavailability showing. Roberts, Inadi, White and Wright retain the exception-specific constitutional inquiry: authentication alone does not establish reliability, no affidavit-wide rule or infallibility presumption results, the Government keeps its proof burden, and competent rebuttal remains available. Scalia and Thomas retain their White reservation. Eight-Justice Parts VI-A and VI-B separately sustain the reported Senate offer's exclusion for failure to identify a passage, admissibility basis, foundation or demonstrated bearing establishing error, and reject judicial notice of disputed assertions merely because officially published. Properly founded rebuttal and older relevant criticism remain possible. Stone-Zsela adds no ground on certificate admission or either Senate judgment. Staples still requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant knew the characteristics making a rifle a whole-weapon machinegun, without requiring knowledge of illegality or nonregistration; no parts, preserved instruction or sufficiency claim is newly decided. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Hale_merits_1996-02-12.md) |
| 1996-02-12 | Sherman v. Community Consolidated School District 21 of Wheeling Township; Seventh Circuit No. 91-1684; 980 F.2d 437. No Supreme Court docket supplied. | The decision adds a bounded application permitting this civic Pledge program with effective freedom to abstain. Existing law continues to forbid official school worship, the substantial religious participation pressure identified in Lee, and compelled affirmation. The five-Justice contextual explanation controls at its stated scope; the three-Justice methodological reservation does not displace it. No rule about private religious access, public funding or every historical religious reference changes. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Sherman_v_Community_Consolidated_School_District_21_merits_1996-02-12.md) |
| 1996-02-21 | Behrens v. Pelletier; No. 94-1244. | The existing legal-immunity appeal category cannot be restricted by an automatic rule allowing only one pretrial appeal. A later order must receive the ordinary jurisdictional analysis, on properly assumed facts and without evidentiary reweighing. Surviving different claims neither destroy otherwise qualifying claim-specific review nor become reviewable through it. The final-judgment rule, independent collateral-order conditions, prior mandate and ordinary preservation limits remain in force. No new substantive immunity or general interlocutory-appeal entitlement results. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Behrens_v_Pelletier_merits_1996-02-21.md) |
| 1996-02-21 | Fulton Corp. v. Faulkner, No. 94-1239; 516 U.S. 325. | The compensatory-tax requirements now apply to North Carolina's issuer-based intangibles-tax preference: a resident investor's location does not shield discrimination directed at the interstate investment choice. Corporate income and share ownership have not been shown to be equivalent events, and general fiscal contribution does not establish the necessary actual offset. Darnell no longer authorizes the contrary Commerce Clause treatment. Ordinary nondiscriminatory corporate and property taxation remains available. Severability and tax relief remain governed by state law subject to federal nondiscrimination and due process; no universal refund formula or new tax is imposed. | [Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Fulton_Corp_v_Faulkner_merits_1996-02-21.md) |
| 1996-02-21 | Peacock v. Thomas, No. 94-1453; 516 U.S. 349 | Seven Justices hold that this later action alleges no underlying ERISA or plan violation supporting its asserted original jurisdiction; veil piercing supplies no independent violation and §502(a)(3) supplies no equitable relief at large. Eight Justices, including Stone-Zsela, hold that ancillary enforcement jurisdiction does not support a new independent action imposing the debtor’s entire obligation on another person. Kokkonen’s decree-effectuation branch remains distinct from factual interdependence; new facts, duties and defenses require independent authority. Rule 69 and §1367 do not supply original jurisdiction; the earlier suit predates §1367 and the later suit supplies no original claim. Traditional contempt, discovery, attachment, garnishment, debtor-property fraudulent-transfer proceedings and independently founded federal actions remain available. No separable restorative property award is affirmed. Particular property, recipients and values, personal jurisdiction and service, South Carolina enforcement law, federal displacement and later-conduct preclusion remain unresolved. The preserved service objection is not waived, and ancillary subject-matter authority alone supplies no nationwide service. Beecher is applied; Riggs and Labette County are distinguished by existing official duties. Mertens’s bounded equitable-category rule and antecedent-action reservation remain intact; O’Melveny and Travelers supply no general federal collection law. No general bar to alter-ego suits, third-person enforcement proceedings or equitable monetary relief, and no new ERISA collection cause, follows. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Peacock_v_Thomas_merits_1996-02-21.md) |
| 1996-02-26 | Jones v. ABC-TV, No. 95-7186; 516 U.S. 363 | All eight participating Justices leave financial eligibility reserved and decline Rule 39.8 denial on the present showing. Rule 39.1 requires the prescribed motion and notarized affidavit or §1746 declaration unless the qualifying appointed-counsel exception applies; none is established here. Benefit, borrowing and affidavit references establish neither the required particulars nor ability to pay, failure to file a document or falsity. Defects in the media and derivative §1986 claims do not dispose of the distinct paid-pro-se filing and requested-briefing objections. A supported Rule 39.8 denial remains permitted, not mandatory; ordinary pleading failure is not automatically frivolousness. Seven Justices apply the separate prospective-control requirement: support tied to this applicant, the filing category and inadequacy of individual treatment. Lower-court abuse findings and preservation of paid/criminal routes do not supply the missing showing. No categorical invalidation of prospective controls, universal warning requirement, numerical threshold or exhaustive lesser-measures requirement follows. Martin, Day, Sassower, Anderson and Attwood are applied; Zatko, McDonald and Sindram retain their bounded force. Financial eligibility, current-paper assessment, future controls and certiorari remain distinct; no merits ruling or acceptance of underlying access allegations follows. Stone-Zsela’s broader individual-consideration rule is noncontrolling. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Jones_v_ABC_TV_filing_order_1996-02-26.md) |
| 1996-02-26 | United States v. Maine et al. (Massachusetts Boundary Case), No. 35, Original; 516 U.S. 365 | The unsigned supplemental decree implements the surviving 1975 decree and 1986 Massachusetts determination. Vineyard Sound is state inland waters; Nantucket Sound is territorial seas and high seas except the interior indentations in decree paragraphs 2(c), (d) and (e). The five straight lines in the [operative schedule](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Maine_Massachusetts_Boundary_Case_supplemental_decree_1996-02-26.md#judgment--remedy) give the coastline geographic effect, with every endpoint approximate. The full five endpoint pairs and all three indentation exceptions are preserved in that schedule, which governs implementation. The classification is not reopened; no new historic-waters test, universal ancient-title burden, independent precise survey, new title, unrelated private ownership or another State’s boundary is adjudicated. Retained jurisdiction permits further proceedings, orders and writs necessary or advisable to effectuate and supplement the decree and the parties’ rights. | [Public decree](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Maine_Massachusetts_Boundary_Case_supplemental_decree_1996-02-26.md) |
| 1996-02-26 | Voting Rights Coalition v. Wilson; source petition No. 95-673; Ninth Circuit No. 95-15449 | All nine Justices sustain the NVRA’s actual federal-election registration duties. Article I, §4 supports congressional-election distribution, assistance, acceptance and transmittal at motor-vehicle, public-assistance and disability-service offices, including existing at-home disability services. Smiley and Siebold permit this shared registration administration despite real personnel, resource and accountability burdens; the commands need not be costless, trivial or voluntary. New York’s ordinary-commerce command prohibition survives; no general power to command state administration follows. Presidential coverage rests separately on Burroughs’s national protective principle and necessary-and-proper legislation for California’s chosen popular election, not Article I, §4 alone. The Act chooses neither the method of appointing electors nor their allocation. Eligibility statements, citizenship declarations and signed perjury attestations preserve state eligibility decisions; required form information and roll maintenance remain regulated. The federal mail form may not require notarization or other formal authentication. Article I, §2 and the Seventeenth Amendment retain their distinct qualification rules; Term Limits supplies only its bounded administration/qualification distinction. Section 11(a) independently authorizes the United States’ prospective enforcement of categorical noncompliance; private §11(b) notice conditions do not apply, and no finding establishes private compliance or general private-enforcement immunity. The Fourteenth/Fifteenth Amendment alternative is not reached. California’s reimbursement condition excuses no valid duty. Implementation must stay within the Act and avoid unauthorized impairment of retained state elections; no unauthorized command is established here. The federal-election scope and §4(b) exemptions retain their statutory dates: no-registration law continuously effective on and after March 11, 1993, or qualifying election-day registration continuously effective from that date or enacted by then to take effect with the NVRA and continuously maintained thereafter. They create no California opt-out. Under §5(a), license/renewal applications also register federal voters unless unsigned, and submitted registration updates prior registration; §5(d) address changes update registration unless the registrant states otherwise. Duplicate license information is forbidden except a second signature or information needed for the required eligibility statement/attestation; only minimum duplicate-prevention, eligibility and administrative information may be required. Section 7 covers all public-assistance and primarily disability-service offices and other designated offices; federal or nongovernmental offices require agreement. Distribution with service applications, renewals, recertifications and address changes may be omitted upon written declination; it is not mandatory omission. Assistance matches service-form assistance unless refused, and failure to mark either registration-choice box counts as declination for that assistance provision. Staff may neither influence or display political preference, discourage registration nor suggest that choice affects benefits; declination and source confidentiality remain. Sections 5(e) and 7(d) require transmittal within ten days of acceptance, reduced to five days when acceptance is within five days before the final registration day. These statutory periods do not restart the implementation-plan deadline. No identical state/federal rolls, particular plan, damages liability, new constitutional doctrine on every qualification dispute or later-practice determination follows. Concrete implementation challenges remain available; no prior holding is overruled. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Voting_Rights_Coalition_v_Wilson_merits_1996-02-26.md) |
| 1996-02-27 | Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Epstein, No. 94-1809;516 U.S. 367 | Part I, joined by all nine, applies §1738 to incorporated class-settlement judgments, starting with rendering-state effect despite class form, consent disposition or exclusive federal jurisdiction. Marrese’s competency limit for adjudicated claims does not automatically govern authorized releases. Individual settlement capacity and representative authority remain distinct; silence after notice is not individually negotiated assent, and broad language cannot cure constitutionally inadequate representation. Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer, establishes ordinary Delaware effect for this incorporated, affirmed judgment. Alleged state-law approval error supplies no collateral retrial; Nottingham’s identical-factual-predicate and representative limits and Prezant’s Rule 23/express-adequacy requirements remain intact, without a universal same-acquisition release rule or new constitutional findings. Part III, joined by all except Ginsburg, holds that §27 does not impliedly partially repeal §1738 for this judgment category: exclusive authority to adjudicate liability is consistent with an authorized representative release and assessment of federal claim value. Recognition neither removes federal jurisdiction nor validates direct coercive interference, injunctions or contempt; any independently preserved coercive-operation objection requires its own lawful treatment. Part IV-A, joined by all nine, requires constitutionally adequate representation independently of notice, objections or opt-outs; actual adequacy and binding remain undecided, precluding immediate dismissal. Part IV-B, joined by all except Stone-Zsela, reserves complete permissible collateral-review scope, including the asserted full-and-fair prior determination, for lawful consideration below. State findings, discovery and hearing remain material without answering every constitutional objection or authorizing unrestricted relitigation. Hansberry and Shutts preserve the representation prerequisite; Kremer preserves finality within actual due process and scope. Kokkonen’s incorporation distinction neither settles representative authority nor makes incorporation self-validating; Peacock’s new-debtor jurisdiction limit remains distinct. Central Bank’s confined affirmative-assistance action is unchanged and establishes no tender-rule private right or valuation. No securities liability, §§14(d)(6)–(7) private right, new federal class, unpresented count, damages or independent contractual-consent disposition is decided. Any applicable state-contract approach works through §1738 without fictitious negotiated assent. Valid opt-outs remain excluded; dismissal of covered claims is conditional on resolution of remaining legally available grounds. Stone-Zsela’s structural-failure collateral standard and the three-Justice fuller representation discussion are noncontrolling at their stated scope. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Matsushita_Electric_Industrial_Co_v_Epstein_merits_1996-02-27.md) |
| 1996-02-27 | Norfolk & Western Railway Co. v. Hiles, No. 95-6; 516 U.S. 400 | Thomas’s unanimous opinion extends the proper-setting qualification to ordinary nondefective drawbar alignment. Former 45 U.S.C. §2 absolutely requires automatic coupling by impact and uncoupling without going between car ends when equipment is properly set; ordinary alignment alone is no statutory breach. Affolder and Carter distinguish preparation from required performance; O’Donnell’s absolute engaged-coupler duty survives. The Act requires neither automatic realignment equipment nor prohibition of every preparatory task. Failure of required performance may be proved without negligence or an identified broken part. The railroad may show ordinary nondefective misalignment before proper setting, but cannot reclassify an actual malfunction or excuse a proven contributing violation by care, inspection, later successful operation, contributory negligence or assumption of risk. Violation and causal contribution remain distinct. Neither a futile or damaging impact nor any attempted impact is invariably prerequisite; an attempt alone would not establish directed liability here. The realignment injury and general need for lateral play establish neither breach nor this displacement’s ordinary/nondefective character. Excluded inspection/AAR affidavits are proffers, not findings; movement difficulty, uncoupling and curve evidence retain their proper role under Wagner and Parker. The per-se direction is reversed without final railroad judgment, a new negligence count, revived forfeited issue or guaranteed trial. The 1994 recodification changes no governing 1990 duty. Gottshall’s distinct negligent-emotional-injury rule is unchanged. No inspection safe harbor, general misalignment exemption, universal impact prerequisite, technology mandate or broader operating prohibition results. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Norfolk_and_Western_Railway_Co_v_Hiles_merits_1996-02-27.md) |
| 1996-02-27 | United States v. Chesapeake & Potomac Telephone Co.; NCTA v. Bell Atlantic Corp., Nos. 94-1893 and 94-1900; 516 U.S. 415 | The Court’s per curiam applies §2106 to the material repeal and unresolved surviving controversy, vacating the appellate judgment in both dockets and returning mootness for consideration before constitutional adjudication. It establishes neither final mootness nor automatic equitable vacatur. Church of Scientology requires meaningful remaining relief; Northeastern Florida distinguishes actual continued injury from a replacement ending it. Under §653(a)(1), local exchange carriers may offer cable service through a complying open video system; the separate permission for cable operators and others remains subject to permissible FCC regulations. Reduced regulatory burdens require subsection (b) compliance certification and Commission approval. Section 651(a)(3) applies ordinary Title VI to nonradio, non-common-carriage programming unless provided through an open-video system with approved certification. The FCC has six months for the specified rulemaking, including reconsideration, and must publish certification-receipt notice and approve or disapprove within ten days of receipt. Section 302(b)(3) protects continuation of previously approved video-dialtone systems. These rules establish neither a blanket six-month prohibition nor this proposed system’s compliance. Bancorp separates disposition authority from equitable entitlement, retaining the voluntary-settlement rule, exceptional-circumstances qualification and distinct involuntary-event treatment. Munsingwear supplies no missing antecedent mootness finding; Anderson v.Green’s contingent-program setting controls no present result. Lawrence preserves independently justified reconsideration without mechanical extension of its petition-stage rule. The Fourth Circuit may obtain further trial-court proceedings if needed; none is commanded. If no controversy survives it must direct appropriate dismissal and address remaining orders under applicable vacatur doctrine; otherwise proceedings stay confined to the surviving dispute. The trial judgment and injunction receive no present vacatur, extension or merits approval; former and successor constitutional merits, amendment entitlement and ultimate equitable relief remain open. No new speech tier or categorical rule for legislative-change vacatur results. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Chesapeake_and_Potomac_and_NCTA_v_Bell_Atlantic_statutory_change_disposition_1996-02-27.md) |
| 1996-03-04 | Hercules, Inc. v. United States, No. 94-818; 516 U.S. 417 | Souter’s Parts I–IV, joined throughout by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg, require an actual authorized express or implied-in-fact reimbursement undertaking under §1491(a)(1); the Tucker Act supplies jurisdiction, not a substantive promise or fairness-based obligation implied in law. Sutton’s authority limits apply equally to implied and express contracts, while Hatzlachh preserves genuine contract remedies independently of tort immunity. Uncertain possible breach damages do not invalidate an ordinary authorized warranty; no contract-specific appropriation, delegation or approval defect is found. Spearin’s ordinary specifications warranty assures prescribed procurement performance but alone does not cover these third-party tort settlements or associated defense expenses. The expenses receive a distinct disposition despite their possible existence after successful tort defense. Ryan and Weyerhaeuser preserve foreseeable third-party consequences of a proved service duty without a universal express-indemnity requirement; neither supplies the missing undertaking here. Kania’s nonprosecution/remote-expense language creates no categorical procurement bar, and damages do not universally end at delivery. The Federal Circuit’s tort-defense/settlement-causation equation is unnecessary and undecided; Boyle is unchanged. Thompson’s combined compulsion, specifications, alleged control/superior knowledge and statutory liability-protection circumstances do not establish the asserted indemnity. DPA §101 priority/compulsion authority and §707 protection against specified compliance damages/penalties do not themselves promise reimbursement; §707’s full immunity boundary remains reserved. Actual-authority and appropriation limits caution against an inferred open-ended commitment without proving that all indemnities are forbidden or a particular officer lacked delegation. Genuine authorized indemnities remain enforceable. Both preserved warranty claims and Thompson’s contextual theory are resolved; Hercules’s unpreserved separate indemnity and independent superior-knowledge, purchaser-use, good-faith or takings causes are not reopened. Knowledge, control and compulsion remain subsidiary arguments within preserved claims. No breach, specification defect, relative knowledge, veterans’ injury, damages reasonableness/allocation, contract-specific authorization or contract-litigation fee entitlement is found. The complete contracts, original specifications, production orders and delegations are not reproduced; no missing term or disclaimer is invented. X-Citement Video and Lebron permit defense of the favorable judgment on a supported alternative without new factual findings or unpresented causes. No earlier holding is overruled. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Hercules_Inc_v_United_States_merits_1996-03-04.md) |
| 1996-03-04 | Bennis v. Michigan, No. 94-8729; 516 U.S. 442 | Stone-Zsela’s Parts I–III, joined throughout by Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer, establish a qualified substantive due-process defense for the separately held interest in an ordinarily lawful automobile when the claimant proves nonparticipation, lack of knowledge and all reasonably expected prevention of another’s prohibited use. Calero-Toledo’s reservation is now adopted in this setting, not described as a prior holding; its actual entrustment holding and Goldsmith-Grant/Van Oster survive outside the protected category. Ordinary shared lawful use is not conclusive defeat; ignorance, marriage and joint title are not presumptions of success, and joint title does not prove an omitted precaution. Knowingly tolerated misuse, culpable entrustment and omitted reasonable precautions fall outside protection. Practical prevention requires neither constant supervision, omniscience nor every imaginable expenditure. Ordinary state factfinding applies with a meaningful opportunity to establish the defense; no numerical/heightened burden or universal State duty to disprove innocence is added. Actual transport and prohibited use permit forfeiture law’s invocation but do not settle each owner’s constitutional position. Austin’s punitive-forfeiture rule, Good’s process/movable-property limits and Buena Vista’s statutory claimant/qualified-relation-back rules remain distinct. No comprehensive instrumentality or property-nexus test, state-incorporation holding, independent Excessive Fines decision, contraband, materially different maritime, involuntary-possession or successive-culpable-owner-punishment ruling follows. A constitutionally/statutorily lawful forfeiture creates no automatic additional Takings payment; this premise cannot establish lawfulness before the defense is resolved. Five direct joins support Part II’s application; four dissenters independently accept only the valid-forfeiture compensation premise and do not join the Court. Fuller’s revocable-grazing-privilege valuation rule creates no general governmental compensation immunity. Tina must receive a meaningful opportunity to establish actual ownership, nonparticipation, lack of knowledge and reasonable prevention. The state lead opinion’s assumed ignorance/nonconsent and existing hearing resolve neither all predicates nor available omitted precautions. Existing usable evidence may be used; further proceedings are required as needed, without automatic complete rehearing. If protection is established, release, division, sale accounting or another lawful property remedy must preserve/restore her proven interest using actual ownership and value; equitable discretion implements and cannot replace required protection. Failure of proof leaves otherwise valid abatement available. No immediate return, half share, gross/net sum, mandatory sale, expense allocation or independent compensation is ordered; John’s conviction and lawful forfeiture of his interest remain intact and his interest is not transferred. No new state statutory construction results. Libretti’s authority/third-party boundaries remain distinct without importing federal forfeiture provisions. The state lead rationale had three votes and the fourth Justice concurred only in the result; no majority adoption of all lead reasoning, complete prevention findings, ownership fraction, valuation or argument concession is inferred. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Bennis_v_Michigan_merits_1996-03-04.md) |
| 1996-03-04 | Action for Children’s Television and Pacifica Foundation v. FCC; D.C. Circuit Nos. 93-1092 and 93-1100 | Ginsburg’s Part I, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas, treats nonobscene indecency as protected content-selected speech requiring careful tailoring to compelling interests and independent necessity/means review within actual broadcast characteristics. Child protection and parental supervision are compelling but do not establish this schedule’s necessity. Pacifica’s contextual holding and Red Lion’s distinct rule survive; Pacifica’s three-Justice speech-value discussion becomes no controlling hierarchy. Sable and Butler protect adult access while preserving media differences. Turner supplies deferential but independent review, not its content-neutral cable intermediate test or four-Justice record-insufficiency application; neither scientific certainty nor a specified legislative report is prerequisite. Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Kennedy and Thomas, finds the mandatory 6 a.m.–10 p.m. restriction insufficiently tailored on the actual record. Substantial child access, late audiences, rapid tuning and supervision difficulties do not adequately connect to sixteen-hour exclusion across media and contexts. Taping, paid alternatives and late access do not adequately answer practical free-broadcast adult access and parental choice. The FCC considered evidence and alternatives; their treatment and the rule’s sweep are insufficient, not wholly absent. Contextual definition, reasonable licensee judgment and clinical/bona-fide news applications supply no blanket news or serious-merit exemption. The tentative defense requires market-wide evidence of no appreciable child audience; ordinary program/station ratings remain inadequate until convincing evidence shows relevance despite grazing. No automatic low-rating defense follows. Receiver ownership, aggregate viewing, actual indecent-program exposure, radio quarter-hours and cumulative reach remain different measures; missing under-twelve radio evidence cannot be inferred, adult presence is not supervision, and small public-radio teen shares are not zero. The Court requires neither program-specific harm proof nor flawless alternatives and does not equate all media. Part III’s same five Justices finally require removal of the rule and prevention of §16(a)’s dependent command to impose it; Souter’s separate renewed-review vacatur is not a sixth invalidity vote and no Marks combination changes the remedy. All nine preserve the uniform 10 p.m.–6 a.m. harbor and rejection of favored-station treatment. The Government’s lack of a petition prevents harsher restoration under X-Citement Video. No replacement hour, revived all-day prohibition, unexamined severability substitute, new definition, automatic serious-merit exception, facial-vagueness ruling, individual sanction, damages, permission hearing or new multifactor test follows. Section 16(b)’s repeal, §1464, lawful contextual Pacifica authority and ordinary obscenity enforcement survive; the agency may not reproduce the invalid schedule under another label. Section 551 neither repeals §16, establishes mootness nor independently requires remand; Chesapeake’s actual-repeal disposition remains distinct. Its conditional statutory terms are retained below without a present operational or radio-equivalent factual premise. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Action_for_Childrens_Television_and_Pacifica_v_FCC_merits_1996-03-04.md) |
| 1996-03-11 | SSC Corp. v. Town of Smithtown; source petition 95-782 and cross-petition 95-1015 | Kennedy’s Parts I–III, joined throughout by all eight other Justices, separately sustain the purchased disposal term and invalidation of the compulsory ordinance. Smithtown pays for disposal as well as residential collection; performance remains incomplete at collection. White permits specifying that paid performance through contractors without rigid direct privity; separate suppliers, price items, volume savings/excess-volume risk and private facility ownership do not make actual purchased disposal unrelated downstream business. Contract form or participation elsewhere alone supplies no power over unrelated transactions. Reeves’s market-participant distinction applies within its scope. South-Central Timber’s four-Justice downstream analysis is distinguished for a completed sale followed by separate business, not promoted to a prior majority holding; its separate congressional-authorization holding supplies no permission for this ordinance. West Lynn requires substantive review of linked arrangements, which here reveals real purchasing despite the separate invalid ordinance. Boston Harbor remains a labor-preemption analogy, not an independent blanket Commerce exemption. No public ownership is inferred from financing, service guarantees or purchased capacity. Carbone invalidates the ordinance’s compulsory reservation of independently arranged private processing to the designated local private operator, including when other local processors are excluded too. Criminal enforcement identifies sovereign compulsion but is not the whole test; ordinary lawful health rules may also carry penalties. Exclusions for recyclables/unacceptable waste do not cure discrimination within covered demand. Financing and sanitation interests do not establish a legitimate local purpose that reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives cannot adequately serve; lawful purchasing, neutral health regulation and nondiscriminatory financing remain available on their terms. Oregon Waste’s distinction between discrimination and justification survives. No perfect-certainty requirement, duty to defeat every imaginable alternative or replacement program follows. State encouragement and contractual financial commitment are not congressional authorization. Pike remains for genuine evenhanded incidental burdens and supplies no replacement balancing here. O’Connor and Souter join this Carbone application/remedy while retaining their earlier classification objections; the original theory is neither reconsidered nor newly defended. No breach, diversion, debt, right to the more-than-$750,000 withheld sum, rescission, damages, automatic discovery/trial or new hearing is established. Only properly pending and legally available contract/payment proceedings remain. The decision supplies no antitrust immunity, actual CERCLA liability, general subcontract rule, natural-resource resolution, compensatory tax approval or rule for a materially different public waste system. Reported code/bid terms supply no unreported contract clause or added exception. No precedent is overruled. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_SSC_Corp_v_Town_of_Smithtown_merits_1996-03-11.md) |
| 1996-03-18 | Dalton v. Little Rock Family Planning Services, No. 95-1025 | All nine Justices join both parts of the per curiam on the second petition question only. Relief must protect the established Medicaid conflict without invalidating or suspending severable nonconflicting applications of Amendment 68. The July 25, 1994 whole-amendment injunction and distinct July 27, 1994 blanket declaration must both be conformed. The unreviewed lower funding construction is accepted for this remedial purpose, not adopted as a Supreme Court holding: otherwise-denied review of the first question decides neither Title XIX/Hyde construction nor a constitutional funding entitlement. Protection survives against using any amendment section or inconsistent state-plan provision to refuse medically necessary abortions for Medicaid-eligible rape/incest patients while Arkansas participates and controlling federal law requires coverage. The State need not continue participating, and no decree may reach nonconflicting applications merely because participation continues after a lawful change in the obligation. The FY1995 account conditions presently continue under Public Law 104-91’s precise rate, expenditure, effective-period and termination limits; no lapse, repeal or automatic dissolution is declared. A real lawful change may support appropriate modification. Confining relief leaves state text in place, creates no appropriation and inserts no exception; retained lawful §1 applications defeat the premise that §§2–3 must wholly fall. Genuinely remaining state severability issues remain for the proper court, but no section can evade surviving federal protection. Section 2’s policy and §3’s contraception exclusion/no-appropriation provision are not wholesale invalidated. NTEU permits broad relief for a proved indivisible defect while excluding unrelated claims; Madsen preserves lawful independent operation without extending its speech-specific test. No general ban on broad relief or new facial-review formula follows. Harris’s precise statutory funding reservation remains unresolved. Casey and Fargo’s complete access/proof/remedy rules survive without conversion to funding rights. The crime-victim example shows non-Medicaid operation without finding its funding source or constitutional validity. No separate Nebraska judgment, independent standing/enforcement/jurisdiction question from that case, direct-abortion-prohibition constitutionality or developed remaining-application challenge is decided. The Court awards no damages or past reimbursement, orders no payment for every abortion and requires no new hearing or trial. The merits correction is final and remand implements scope only; it does not reopen the unreviewed funding question. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Dalton_v_Little_Rock_Family_Planning_Services_summary_review_1996-03-18.md) |
| 1996-03-19 | Varity Corp. v. Howe, No. 94-1471; 516 U.S. 489 | Under ERISA §3(21)(A), fiduciary responsibility attaches to the particular exercise of discretionary plan administration, including plan information communicated in that capacity. Varity performed that function when it used its administrative authority, benefit comparisons and linked assurances of benefit security to induce the class's transfer; general employer status, corporate forecasting or participant perception alone would not establish it. An administrator violates §404(a)(1)'s loyalty duty when, acting in its fiduciary capacity, it knowingly and significantly misleads participants about benefit security to induce surrender of existing plan interests for the employer's benefit. Varity's found deception and the class's reliance satisfy that rule notwithstanding the reservation of lawful amendment or termination powers. Sections 409 and 502(a)(2) do not impose a categorical plan-only bar on §502(a)(3)'s express authorization of appropriate individual equitable relief for a §404 violation. Such relief must remain within traditionally equitable categories; where another ERISA provision supplies adequate relief for the injury, further equitable relief normally is unnecessary and therefore inappropriate, without an absolute rule governing every alternative pleading. The common categorical plan-only objection does not defeat the ten retirees' reviewed individual equitable recovery, while their distinct lower-court assignment-breach determination remains undisturbed because the petition did not sufficiently present a challenge to that ground. Affirmance preserves the clarified decree without deciding a new substantive assignment rule, the precise monetary classifications, or whether §502(a)(1)(B) is categorically unavailable to these retirees. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Varity_Corp_v_Howe_merits_1996-03-19.md) |
| 1996-03-19 | Meghrig v. KFC Western, Inc., No. 95-83; 516 U.S. 479 | Section 6972(a)(1)(B) requires waste that may present an imminent and substantial endangerment when suit begins. Past contribution may create a present threat, and the threat's physical effects may occur later; an allegation only of danger completely eliminated before filing does not satisfy the requirement. Section 6972(a)'s restraint and necessary-action powers authorize prohibitory and affirmative abatement relief, not a private reimbursement action for a past cleanup effort merely labeled damages or equitable restitution. Remaining endangerment when a proper action begins does not itself confer general authority to reimburse earlier expenses, including expenses labeled emergency cleanup; the following two categories remain unresolved. The enforcement arrangements address threats while abatement remains possible. Section 6972(b)(2) ordinarily requires ninety days after notice to EPA, the affected State and alleged contributors; an action respecting a subchapter-III violation may begin immediately after notification, without a general emergency waiver. Government-action bars require restraint or abatement of acts or conditions that may have contributed or are contributing to waste activities that may present the alleged endangerment. The federal bar requires a commenced and diligently prosecuted §6973 or CERCLA §106 action; actual §104 removal; costs to initiate a §104 remedial investigation and feasibility study plus diligent remedial action; or a court order, including a consent decree, or §106/§6973 administrative order under which a responsible party diligently performs removal, a remedial investigation and feasibility study or remedial action. The administrative-order bar lasts only within that order's scope and duration. The state bar requires a commenced and diligently prosecuted §6972(a)(1)(B) action, actual §104 removal, or costs incurred to initiate a §104 remedial investigation and feasibility study plus diligent CERCLA remedial action. These arrangements serve abatement, not an unrestricted later cost action. No bar is found satisfied here. The Court does not decide whether a private plaintiff may obtain an injunction requiring another party to pay cleanup costs arising after a citizen action has properly commenced, **or otherwise recover cleanup costs paid after invocation of RCRA's statutory process**. Neither category is affirmatively authorized. Statutory-process invocation is not equated with filing; classification of a particular notice-stage expense remains undecided. Remaining danger alone does not reserve every earlier emergency expense. EPA reimbursement under §6973 is not decided. Section 6972(f) preserves existing statutory and common-law rights without creating an alternative cause or guaranteeing recovery. Section 6972(e) permits litigation costs, including reasonable attorney and expert-witness fees, when appropriate in a final order for a prevailing or substantially prevailing party; it creates no cleanup-cost entitlement, and no fee award is made. CERCLA's petroleum exclusion is not imported into RCRA, and no universal petroleum-mixture classification is decided. The government's proposed Restatement restitution conditions are not adopted as new RCRA elements. Notice compliance supplies no alternative dismissal ground in this appeal. The state order and pending voluntary-dismissal request establish no new preclusion or mootness disposition. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Meghrig_v_KFC_Western_Inc_merits_1996-03-19.md) |
| 1996-03-20 | Wisconsin v. City of New York; Oklahoma v. City of New York; Department of Commerce v. City of New York, Nos. 94-1614, 94-1631 and 94-1985; 517 U.S. 1 | The identified California voter appellants have standing to pursue their own continuing representation injury where the challenged census determination has a concrete connection to the asserted loss of a California seat and authoritative review is substantially likely to provide redress through the statutory allocation process. Their claim does not depend on California's own appeal or require certainty that reconsideration will produce a chosen dataset or an injunction against the President. Franklin's rule that the Secretary's completed census determination is final agency action under §704 remains governing law despite later presidential transmission. Availability of that review does not reopen the district court's ordinary APA disposition in this constitutional appeal. The Court decides no new APA merits challenge and does not equate constitutional reasonableness with every requirement of APA review. The choice whether to supplement this nationwide enumeration with the proposed post-enumeration survey must bear a reasonable relationship to enumerating the population and securing population-based representation. Courts enforce that boundary while respecting the methodological judgment entrusted to the Secretary; a genuine enumeration effort and an explained choice addressing geographic accuracy and comparative uncertainty do not become unconstitutional merely because another method improves some accuracy measures. This nonadjustment decision satisfies that standard, and the panel's legitimate-objective-and-essentiality requirement is rejected. The Court creates no numerical tolerance, presumption of perfect accuracy or inevitable superiority of enumeration, automatic extension of intrastate burdens, or census exemption from judicial review. Proven discrimination, unauthorized methods and actual unsupported reasons remain subject to their governing legal requirements. The decision does not find actual PES manipulation, endorse every future-participation prediction, treat disruption as an independent cure for an unsupported count, or find a missed production deadline. Later statistical corrections bear on injury and relief, not on the information available in July 1991. Rejection of a constitutional duty to make this adjustment decides neither whether the Constitution prohibits this type of adjustment nor whether §195 categorically bars sampling for congressional apportionment. Reversal ends the panel's constitutional justification inquiry and requires implementation of judgment for petitioners on the reviewed challenge, without judicial selection of replacement numbers or disposition of unrelated matters. No adjustment, dataset, seat transfer, presidential injunction, funding redistribution or new redistricting is ordered. The separate tape-disclosure and protective-order ruling remains outside the judgment. No new merits hearing, renewed APA proceeding, special mandate date or continuing Supreme Court supervision is prescribed. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Wisconsin_v_City_of_New_York_merits_1996-03-20.md) |

| 1996-03-26 | Barnett Bank of Marion County, N.A. v. Nelson, No. 94-1837; 517 U.S. 25 | A congressional grant of national-bank power ordinarily protects its exercise against state laws that prevent or significantly interfere with that exercise. This protection includes lawfully conferred enumerated and incidental powers, whose existence and limits depend on the particular federal scheme, including any congressional incorporation of state restrictions. States retain authority under this ground where their laws do not prevent or significantly interfere with the federal power. Section 92 affirmatively authorizes the specified insurance-agency activity for a national banking association satisfying its conditions. Florida may not apply the challenged affiliation prohibition to prevent that association from exercising the authority §92 confers; the ability to comply with both laws by abandoning the federally authorized activity does not remove the conflict. Section 92 specifically relates to the business of insurance within 15 U.S.C. §1012(b). McCarran-Ferguson therefore does not preserve Florida's conflicting prohibition, even assuming it was enacted for the purpose of regulating that business. The federal exception removes the obstacle to ordinary preemption; the actual conflict established in Part I-B remains independently necessary. Florida's asserted concerns about coercion, concentration and insurer solvency are assumed in its favor without a final purpose classification. The Court finds neither protectionist purpose nor bank misconduct and imposes no least-restrictive-means test or requirement for a particular legislative record. McCarran-Ferguson's protection against federal enactments that do not specifically relate to insurance remains intact. Relief must prevent application of the conflicting affiliation prohibition to the bank's qualifying §92 activity, after resolution of the preserved association-location and customer-geography issues. A favorable preemption ruling does not itself establish this bank's eligibility, authorize unrestricted nationwide sales or dispense with the statute's conditions. Section 92 applies to an association located and doing business in a place with **no more than 5,000 inhabitants under the last preceding decennial census**. The insurer must be authorized by the authorities of the State where the bank is located to do business there, and the activity remains subject to the Comptroller's rules. The bank may solicit and sell insurance, collect premiums and receive agreed fees or commissions. It may neither assume nor guarantee payment of a premium on a policy issued through its agency, and may not guarantee the truth of an insured's application statements. Agency authority supplies no underwriting power or guarantee of insurer obligations. The independent-bank exclusion uses **less than 5,000 inhabitants under the last preceding census** and requires a bank that is not a holding-company subsidiary or affiliate; Barnett's affiliation defeats it. The financial-institution definition also excludes an institution with a Federal Reserve Board exemption under Bank Holding Company Act §4(d), and an institution that neither owns more than 10 percent of the capital stock nor exercises effective control of the specified bank, savings-and-loan or chapter 494 entity licensed or authorized in Florida. Neither other exclusion is found applicable. Credit life and credit disability are separately excluded from the restricted agency activities. Compatible state regulation survives. No complete invalidation of §626.988, independent agent-licensing disposition, damages, required new hearing, agency proceeding or special mandate date follows. No rule of deference to the Comptroller on preemption or McCarran-Ferguson is adopted. Other state requirements must be considered on their own terms and operation; no categorical immunity or safe harbor is supplied. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Barnett_Bank_of_Marion_County_v_Nelson_merits_1996-03-26.md) |
| 1996-03-27 | Morse v. Republican Party of Virginia, No. 94-203; 517 U.S. 186 | The end of the convention does not moot this statutory appeal where Morse seeks return of his identified $45 payment on a substantial statutory restoration theory that the judgment has not conclusively eliminated. That live personal controversy permits decision of the coverage and private-action questions without establishing repayment, the proper refund defendant or every plaintiff's prospective standing. On the accepted dismissal-stage allegations, a changed financial prerequisite to participation in this qualifying party's primary-like convention selecting its preferential general-ballot nominee is subject to §5. The combination of that electoral function, the pleaded participation practice and Virginia's statutory nomination relationship supplies coverage; the convention label creates no categorical exemption. The written delegate-selection, slating and instruction rules and the affidavit describing earlier fees remain for their proper treatment; the complaint's contrary allegations are not final findings. The controlling application does not establish an unprecleared switch from primary to convention. Different Senate seats, the unheld 1990 primary and disputed preservation prevent treating that additional theory as already proved or decided. No racial purpose, effect or substantive illegality is required merely to obtain this coverage determination or is found by it. Affected voters may pursue the asserted private action under §10 to enforce its voting protection against an alleged unlawful poll tax or qualifying substitute. Dismissal solely because §10 expressly directs the Attorney General to sue is erroneous. Recognition of this action does not decide that the convention charge is a prohibited poll tax, establish a refund remedy or create a general implied-action rule. RPV may maintain its argument that the charge is not a poll tax or substitute, but unresolved predicates on this dismissal record do not establish an alternative ground for affirmance. No refund, proper repayment defendant, racial discrimination or particular monetary entitlement is found. The effects of lawful §5 proceedings on further §10 relief remain for appropriate treatment rather than an automatic bar to recognizing the action. On remand the local court must enforce §5's submission requirement for a legally relevant, unprecleared fee change from the operative baseline, leaving preclearance purpose and effect to the designated D.D.C./Attorney General process. The private §10 claim proceeds under its statutory requirements and remaining defenses; neither reversal itself supplies substantive invalidity or a monetary award. Virginia's applicable baseline is **November 1, 1964**; the Act's other coverage dates do not replace it. Section 5 permits the prescribed D.D.C. declaration that the change lacks prohibited purpose and effect, or Attorney General submission followed by sixty-day nonobjection. Good cause permits expedited affirmative nonobjection within that period, with reserved reexamination upon additional information during the remaining sixty days. Neither nonobjection nor a declaratory judgment bars a later enforcement challenge. Coverage and approval are distinct from retrogression and substantive illegality. Section 10(b)'s voting-poll-tax language separately includes a substitute enacted after November 1, 1964; the statute's findings, constitutional declaration, official-enforcement direction and judicial procedures retain their distinct work. Former subsection (d)'s late-payment provision was repealed in 1975 and supplies no current exception. No unpresented §2 cause, §1983 action, classwide repayment, general damages rule or attorney-fee amount is decided. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Morse_v_Republican_Party_of_Virginia_merits_1996-03-27.md) |
| 1996-03-27 | Rutledge v. United States, No. 94-8769; 517 U.S. 292 | Section 848(c)'s requirement of action in concert with five or more other persons requires mutual agreement in a common criminal plan or enterprise. In the narcotics setting presented, §846 conspiracy is therefore a lesser included offense of CCE; the same agreement supports both challenged counts. Jeffers supplied the textual reasoning but assumed the included-offense conclusion. The Court now resolves it. The Government's unwitting-participant hypothetical does not give §846 an element absent from the statutory concert requirement. Here the same agreement supplied Count 2 and the concert element of Count 1. This construction does not place a subchapter-II-only enterprise within §846's distinct subchapter-I coverage. A distinct agreement, different offense or separate substantive predicate requires its own analysis; successive-prosecution questions remain separate. Congress did not authorize cumulative convictions and punishment under §§846 and 848 for the included agreement at issue. Concurrent imprisonment does not cure the unauthorized second conviction. The mandatory $50 assessment attached to the second felony conviction is actual additional punishment and may be considered in resolving the preserved challenge to the dual judgments. Vacatur must remove the selected conviction's assessment. The District Court must vacate either Count 1 or Count 2, its entire corresponding life sentence and its $50 assessment, choosing initially within lawful discretion. Retaining both convictions while vacating only one sentence, staying execution or applying a combined label is insufficient. An appellate court may, in an appropriate case, direct entry of judgment on a valid lesser included offense when reversal rests on a defect affecting only the greater offense. That existing power does not require two present convictions and does not make later reinstatement automatic. A valid conspiracy verdict may thus support appropriate lesser-offense relief after a CCE-specific failure. But a ground invalidating the agreement or otherwise tainting that verdict cannot be ignored. The precise limits, procedural vehicle and relief in a future contested application remain open. The Court orders no restoration now, adopts no automatic-revival or general finality exception, and decides no entitlement to retrial, compelled lesser judgment or harmlessness of a future error. Present vacatur for duplication is not an evidentiary acquittal. An earlier separate conspiracy prosecution, previously unknown CCE facts and a noncoterminous enterprise present questions this case does not decide. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Rutledge_v_United_States_merits_1996-03-27.md) |

IGRA's State-directed wording and detailed procedure do not exclude that route in this case. The remand permits only relief authorized by IGRA upon the actual statutory predicates. It neither resolves good faith or gaming scope nor disturbs the distinct merits judgment and appeal. The following conditions govern any relief through the recognized officer route. IGRA unmistakably authorizes a direct action naming the State. Its specified State-party action, State evidentiary burden, order to State and Tribe and successive State-directed steps satisfy the clear-statement requirement. Stone-Zsela, Stevens and the four dissenters actually adopt this statutory construction across their writings. | 1996-04-01 | O’Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers Corp., No. 95-354; 517 U.S. 308 | An ADEA plaintiff need not show replacement by a person under 40 to establish the initial inference of age discrimination. The replacement's membership in the protected group does not itself defeat that inference. The parties proceed under McDonnell Douglas, and the Court assumes its applicability here without deciding its wholesale application to every ADEA claim. Review likewise takes the case as a non-reduction-in-force matter; the Court does not settle every alternative prima facie formulation. Finnell was exactly 40, so he was protected, but that fact cannot defeat O'Connor's claim. Within the assumed framework, the prima facie evidence must adequately support an inference of age discrimination, and each required element must have a logical connection to that inquiry. A substantially younger replacement may support the inference even if at least 40; an insignificant age difference, standing alone, does not supply it. A substantially younger replacement is not indispensable where other evidence supplies the inference or no replacement can sensibly be identified. Conversely, neither every younger replacement nor protected status, qualification, discharge and continued need for the job necessarily suffices without circumstances supporting an age inference. Material differences in the circumstances may weaken or defeat the suggested comparison. The sixteen-year difference here cannot be excluded because Finnell was 40, but it does not establish every initial element, satisfactory performance or actual motive. Burdine keeps employer production distinct from employee persuasion. The employer remains free to articulate a lawful reason; the plaintiff retains the ultimate burden of proving that age caused the action. Hicks permits circumstantial proof without a special additional category of direct or independent evidence, but, after nondiscriminatory reasons are produced, rejection of those reasons does not compel liability. The Court decides neither pretext nor ultimate discrimination here. The reviewed ADEA merits affirmance is reversed, and the lower courts must reconsider the claim under the corrected replacement rule and ordinary proof and summary-judgment standards. This disposition neither invalidates every remaining ground nor requires trial or recovery; it leaves the unreviewed discovery and postjudgment rulings intact. As McKennon demonstrates, reversal of an ADEA categorical bar does not establish liability or relief. A genuinely sufficient remaining ground may still support summary judgment. The Court does not adjudicate the alternative reduction-in-force formulation, find all timely evidence sufficient, or reopen the diligence and likely-effect rulings concerning Dennis's later affidavit. That affidavit remains outside the timely record. No new discovery, compulsory hearing, willfulness finding, damages, backpay or reinstatement is ordered. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_OConnor_v_Consolidated_Coin_Caterers_Corp_merits_1996-04-01.md) |
| 1996-04-01 | Lonchar v. Thomas, No. 95-5015; 517 U.S. 314 | A first personal federal habeas petition satisfying the governing jurisdictional and pleading requirements may not be terminated solely for the reported delay and litigation purpose through an additional equitable sanction that dispenses with the conditions of the habeas statutes and Rules. Delay may support dismissal through Rule 9 or another lawful source only when that source's own predicates are satisfied. First-petition status does not exclude lawful independent consideration of the State's enforcement interest, unjustified delay or proved obstruction in deciding an execution stay. But the existence of that distinct discretion does not sustain this appellate order, whose stated premise was the supposed authority to dismiss through the sanction rejected in Part I. If execution would prevent completion of process actually required by the governing habeas statute and Rules, and lawful prompt disposition cannot finish in time, a court must provide the interim protection necessary to make that identified opportunity meaningful. Mere filing, first-petition status or a capital sentence establishes neither condition. The appellate stay-vacatur judgment cannot stand on its erroneous dismissal premise. Remand proceeds through the Eleventh Circuit for prompt district examination of the actual petition and proper State objections and redetermination of the need and terms of §2251 protection. Removing the appellate order restores the displaced district stay pending that decision, subject to lawful modification or dissolution. The full pre-AEDPA statutory qualifications, source-specific stay settings and conditions are preserved in the exact decision text below. | [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Lonchar_v_Thomas_merits_1996-04-01.md) |
