### Morse v. Republican Party of Virginia, No. 94-203; 517 U.S. 186 — March 27, 1996

**Stevens, concurring, joined throughout by Ginsburg.** They join the Court's limited application and both reversals but also adopt a broader functional explanation. Virginia recognizes the qualifying party's choice and certification as the means of obtaining preferential general-ballot access. That authority concerns an official stage of electoral choice; a monetary prerequisite to exercising it affects the effectiveness of voting under §§5 and 14. Allen, Sheffield and the White Primary Cases support coverage through delegated electoral authority, including the party-office/delegate route, without requiring that the nominee be virtually certain to win. The regulation's primary example is not exhaustive, and the statute itself supplies authority without administrative deference creating a missing power.

Their rule still requires an electoral function and a change affecting voting; it does not cover all party activity. They reject the asserted association obstacle to submission of this fee without approving every hypothetical application. Hurley preserves actual expressive choice, while the fee duty compels neither a message nor a candidate. They retain the pleading-versus-proof and nomination-method reservations and adopt the Court's Act-specific §10 ground without a poll-tax or refund finding.

They additionally conclude that the recurring fee practice, the Party's continued defense without disavowal and the unreturned payment preserve this controversy, including as capable of repetition yet evading review. That case-specific ground does not establish that every election dispute remains live or that every prospective request here is available. Their broader statutory and recurrence explanations are noncontrolling.

**Thomas, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Scalia throughout and Kennedy only in Part II.** He joins the Court's payment-based threshold discussion but would affirm both statutory dismissals. Part I first reads State or political subdivision as the covered governments and their organs, rather than every association whose conduct might count as constitutional state action. Sheffield's governmental-body holding does not erase that distinction; Congress used broader person/under-color-of-law language elsewhere. The regulation cannot extend the statute, and a litigant's legal concession about it cannot determine the meaning of the presented coverage question.

Alternatively, he finds Virginia's recognition, ballot benefits and limited requirements insufficient to establish the governmental delegation or effective substitution for an election that he regards as necessary. Smith and Terry retain their constitutional force, but do not make this private nomination a state election on these facts. He independently reads §14(c)(1)'s primary, special and general elections as excluding conventions: party-office and effective-vote language does not erase that list, and §2's later amendment did not amend these provisions. His actual Holder ballot-access position remains noncontrolling and is not substituted for the Court's §2 law.

His association/avoidance ground also incorporates Scalia's overbreadth, uncertainty, prior-restraint and avoidance objections. Party funding, membership and organization are substantial choices; denial of preclearance could require admission of those unwilling or unable to pay. The asserted financing justification remains advocacy. These grounds support his statutory construction, not a facial decree invalidating §5 or a final disposition of the separate constitutional counts. An appropriate challenge to a State's own discriminatory electoral practice remains distinct. No unverified Williams rationale supplies an independent holding.

Part II denies a private §10 action. In his view, the provision's declaration and express direction to the Attorney General lack the private statutory command found in Allen's §5 setting. General private-enforcement references in §§3, 12 and 14 and the 1975 amendment do not establish this additional action. Congressional intent, not usefulness, controls. Actual Central Bank preserves its confined received securities action; his contrary position there supplies no contrary Court holding. He would affirm without deciding whether the charge is an unlawful poll tax, awarding money or denying all constitutional voting remedies.

**Scalia, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined throughout by Thomas.** He joins Part I of the Court opinion and Thomas's entire separate opinion. His additional explanation treats candidate selection as central expressive association. Preclearance requires prior federal permission even for lawful changes, imposes the burden of establishing nondiscriminatory purpose and effect, and subjects convention timing and choices to governmental control. That is the concrete prior-restraint concern; it cannot be dismissed as mere regulation of customer identity under Hurley.

He also objects to overbreadth and chilling uncertainty. Even if this isolated fee could constitutionally require submission, the interpretation's reach across protected party activity must be addressed. Leaving the covered class indefinite can chill current conduct; reserving every difficult application for later supplies neither the limiting construction nor the overbreadth treatment he considers necessary. The substantial constitutional doubt favors the statute's express reference to States and political subdivisions rather than imposing this restraint on parties.

Congress could address some discriminatory practices through other provisions without extending §5 to every party procedure. References to party office elsewhere do not prove the distinct preclearance duty. Those statutory and avoidance grounds, together with Thomas's §10 analysis, support affirmance. The opinion declares neither facial invalidity of the Act or regulation nor immunity from constitutional law, and decides no fee merits or refund.

**Kennedy, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins Part I of the Court opinion and only Part II of Thomas's separate opinion. His independent §5 ground distinguishes a statutory covered government from every person whose conduct may be attributed to the State under constitutional doctrine. Congress named governments here while using broader private-person language elsewhere; ordinary ballot recognition and preserved party autonomy do not impose the asserted direct submission duty on the Party.

A State's own change making party practices legally operative or facilitating discriminatory nomination can remain subject to §5 as a state practice. That governmental-responsibility inquiry differs from requiring the Party to submit every procedure because its nominee receives ballot benefits. He does not decide whether these appellants would prevail under constitutional state-action principles, the full reach of Congress's Reconstruction Amendment powers or Thomas's separate convention-definition theory. Smith and Terry remain available for the constitutional claims in their existing posture.

He also identifies serious costs in placing party procedure under prior control of a politically accountable federal officer, without alleging misconduct. That concern would support avoidance if ambiguity existed; his statutory entity reading is an independent ground. His §10 objection is the specific congressional-intent analysis in Thomas's Part II, consistent with distinguishing development within an established action from creation of a new one. He would affirm both statutory dismissals without deciding fee legality or monetary relief.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Morse_v_Republican_Party_of_Virginia_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### Rutledge v. United States, No. 94-8769; 517 U.S. 292 — March 27, 1996

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs in part and dissents in part. He begins with Blockburger's element comparison and the offenses as charged and tried. Here the CCE verdict necessarily incorporated the same agreement and concerted conduct supporting conspiracy, so every element of the §846 count was necessarily established. His conclusion is confined to that elements-and-trial structure; it does not bar convictions for distinct conspiracies or offenses requiring an element not necessarily included in the CCE count.

Ball makes the second judgment consequential even though imprisonment runs concurrently. The separate assessment, stigma and other collateral effects prevent treating the included conviction as an empty entry. On that basis, the Double Jeopardy Clause requires removal of the included judgment. His partial joins adopt the corresponding case-specific application, second-conviction consequences and assessment correction; they do not adopt the Court's broader statutory construction, fuller congressional-intent analysis, preservation ruling or future appellate-entry proposition.

His remedial disagreement is concrete. Because conspiracy is the included offense established by this CCE verdict, he would direct vacatur of Count 2 and its special assessment and leave the CCE conviction and sentence undisturbed. He therefore agrees that the dual-conviction ruling must be reversed but dissents from allowing the District Court to vacate CCE instead. No other Justice joins his separate writing.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Rutledge_v_United_States_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, No. 94-12; 517 U.S. 44 — March 27, 1996

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins the officer holding and statutory limits and supports removal of Florida's dismissal direction, but would affirmatively sustain Congress's clearly enacted prospective direct-State action. Indian Commerce authority, the ongoing federal duty and unmistakable authorization support that route. Prospective compliance costs do not become accrued treasury compensation merely because payment is needed. Congress's express enforcement channel and the Tribe's continuing-duty claim warrant retaining a forum. Young independently reaches the connected officer, with the same statutory restraints. Neither route permits a preferred compact, bypassed mediation, enlarged duty or disguised retrospective damages; lawful relief should avoid double or inconsistent commands.

He expressly refuses to treat officer availability as sufficient reason to stop short of sustaining the State action. He retains Union Gas's actual damages judgment without adopting every broader abrogation rationale. He reserves materially new compensatory, punitive or restitutionary liability, compulsory state-court actions and different statutory schemes, while recognizing that already-decided Union Gas questions remain settled within its scope. He supplies no new waiver or Reconstruction ground.

**Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins Parts II–III and would sustain both routes. Outside the Eleventh Amendment's actual textual restriction, Hans immunity is judicial doctrine subject to displacement by valid congressional legislation. IGRA supplies the affirmative direction absent from Hans; Congress cannot amend the Constitution or exceed Article III. His rationale is not confined to prospective Indian Commerce litigation and does not require overruling Hans's actual result. He retains Union Gas's constitutional conclusion and leaves the textual issue concerning out-of-state or foreign-citizen plaintiffs open; the Tribe is not treated as such a plaintiff. His own remedial-intent analysis supports the constrained officer action, and he accepts lawful officer-only resolution as a narrower sufficient alternative without abandoning his affirmative State position.

He nevertheless retains serious doubt whether this intermediate judicial step, particularly if separate executive relief could make it dispensable, is fully judicial under Article III. That is a reservation, not a vote to dismiss independently. Wisconsin's partial-redress holding does not settle this different judicial-function issue. He does not formally join Souter's entire separate theory.

**Souter, joined by Ginsburg and Breyer, respecting the State claim in Part IV.** They prefer the established officer route and vacatur of Florida's immunity-dismissal direction without deciding abrogation. Intricate remedies and State wording alone do not clearly exclude received prospective equity; Congress may limit statutory enforcement, but they find no sufficient indication of exclusion here. This is distinct from inventing a personal damages action. They would address whether State adjudication is necessary in light of lawful officer relief while preserving lawful jurisdiction before State merits adjudication or a proper nonmerits resolution. The Tribe might forgo its State claim or adequate officer relief might support denying duplicative relief, but neither fact is found. They prescribe no automatic abandonment, mootness, dismissal or indefinite stay. Their additional sequence is not the Court's mandate.

If Young were rejected and Florida's still-live immunity claim adjudicated, they would recognize the direct-State clear statement and uphold congressional displacement of Hans immunity under valid Article I power. They regard that nontextual immunity as federal common law, retained by stare decisis absent deliberate legislative displacement, rather than constitutional immunity Congress can never alter. Constitutional text, limited prior holdings and legislative control of common law independently support that account; it is not a wholesale adoption of Brennan's Union Gas reasoning. Their view is not confined to prospective relief or commerce, but decides no damages or unrelated statute. Because Young succeeds here, these constitutional views remain conditional alternatives, not actual joins in a State-amenability holding.

**O'Connor, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** They join the judicial-character ruling and find unmistakable direct-State intent, but would affirm both dismissals. Their constitutional rule is broad: original Article I powers cannot overcome the constitutional immunity limiting federal judicial power over a nonconsenting State. Prospective relief does not cure the defect; neither Indian/interstate commerce nor proprietary/governmental distinctions justifies retaining Union Gas. They would expressly overrule its constitutional conclusion while leaving its statutory construction and Fitzpatrick's later Fourteenth Amendment authority intact.

They acknowledge Union Gas's five-vote constitutional conclusion rather than declaring it never precedent. In their view its conflict with the constitutional immunity structure, fractured rationale and deficient integration with prior immunity decisions supply the special justification for correction. They reject the opposing distinction between a common-law default and congressional displacement, without inventing zero reliance or proof that clear-statement rules are empirically unworkable. Their premise does not adjudicate every other statute or remedy, grant immunity to every public entity, foreclose United States enforcement or eliminate ordinary Young relief.

Independently, they read IGRA as selecting the State-party action, reciprocal State/Tribe order and limited subsequent progression. An ordinary officer injunction risks judicial coercion Congress withheld, but their objection is not limited to unlimited contempt: even an officer action copying the deadlines changes Congress's selected defendant and enforcement form. The sovereign-compacting arrangement reinforces that inference. They recognize that Congress can authorize constrained officer remedies; they conclude it did not do so here. They establish no universal detailed-scheme bar, no categorical affirmative-duty exception to Young, and no power to rewrite the Act merely because enforcement otherwise has a gap.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Seminole_Tribe_of_Florida_v_Florida_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### Shieh v. Kakita; Shieh v. United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit; Shieh v. Krieger, Nos. 95-7587, 95-7588 and 95-7589; 517 U.S. 343 — April 1, 1996

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs while joining the Court's opinion. Financial leave provides an opportunity for consideration, not endorsement of a petition or entitlement to certiorari. Each of these declarations and papers satisfies the conditions for that opportunity; neither one adequate affidavit nor one defective allegation can resolve the other motions.

He would apply a strong presumption against predictive personal exclusions and require demonstrated inadequacy of ordinary paper-specific controls before contemplating exceptional future restrictions. A history of unsuccessful submissions does not establish the contents of an unwritten petition, and a potentially cognizable future claim should not be excluded merely because of its author's identity. Past filings can justify close scrutiny; they do not supply a presumption that an unexamined paper is malicious or frivolous.

That stronger position goes beyond the Court's refusal of the unsupported condition here. He does not turn the prior filing decisions into a universal prohibition or claim that individual screening is costless. Targeted sanctions for proved misconduct, valid jurisdictional and finality rules, financial eligibility and ordinary filing requirements remain distinct. The three grants imply no underlying relief or disposition of certiorari. No other Justice joins this additional presumption.

### Bowersox v. Williams, application No. A-828; 517 U.S. 345 — April 9, 1996

**Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** I join Part I's reservation of final disposition and immediate record examination. Execution before the Court can identify the lower court's substantial grounds would make review irretrievable. Lack of an explanation calls for one; it does not establish that a successive habeas claim is substantial.

I would direct the lower court to supply its stay order, reasons, identified claims and relevant successive-petition findings within two hours after service of the order, with concise party responses within two further hours. I would also administratively stay execution until the full Court resolves the dissolution application or twelve hours after service, whichever occurs first, unless the Court expressly extends protection. The Court must review the matter before expiration, and the Clerk must confirm actual notice to the executing authorities. Those are my proposed terms, not additional relief entered by the Court.

The short administrative interval would preserve the ability to decide the actual application. It would neither dissolve nor adjudge valid the Eighth Circuit stay. Delo v. Blair's equal division supplies no controlling rationale; McFarland's preparation rule and Schlup's gateway retain their own predicates. I select no final grant or denial. The Court's different implementation and decision to issue no additional execution stay are not my proposed disposition.

**Justice John Paul Stevens.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The actual basis of the challenged stay must be examined before this application is decided. This procedural action decides neither the stay's ultimate propriety nor any habeas claim.

**Justice Sandra Day O'Connor.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The successive-petition standard remains governing; the certificate and the unexplained order do not themselves answer it. No new execution stay is granted.

**Justice Antonin Scalia.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The State is entitled to prompt consideration of its application on the actual grounds. The reservation confers no entitlement to further delay.

**Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order for the reasons in Parts I–III. Prompt consideration on the relevant papers protects the lawful interests of both parties. Any further judicial action must rest on its own basis.

**Justice David H. Souter.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. This permits examination of the actual appellate basis without treating the certificate or the petition's number as dispositive.

**Justice Clarence Thomas.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The actual claims and prior dispositions are necessary to apply the successive-petition rules. This order creates no additional habeas entitlement.

**Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The need for further process or protection must be established on the actual papers. Neither is found by this procedural action.

**Justice Stephen G. Breyer.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The application returns promptly for decision; no unknown claim, procedural exception or stay duration is resolved now.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Bowersox_v_Williams_interim_application_order_1996-04-09.md).

### Bowersox v. Williams — final application order — April 9, 1996

**Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, signed final Circuit Justice explanation and Opinion of the Court.** I grant the application for the reasons in Parts I–V. The identified cause, repeated-instruction, distinct second-degree and amendment grounds do not satisfy the substantial-grounds standard. The available noncapital options answer the Beck issue; the assumed state-rule inconsistency does not add the federal deprivation shown in Hicks. My explanation removes the challenged stay without deciding entitlement to the writ or directing execution.

**Justice Antonin Scalia.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice David H. Souter.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice Clarence Thomas.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice John Paul Stevens, dissenting.** I would deny the application. A State's creation of a particular jury opportunity is not made immaterial by a different lawful noncapital option. Schad controls the minimum Beck safeguard; the available second-degree claim raises the distinct Hicks question whether inconsistent withholding of the state-created option was arbitrary. The reported intent and kidnapping dispute gives that question potential consequence. It warrants appellate consideration without establishing a violation, a writ or an automatic successive-petition stay. I need not decide an independent equal-protection ground or the other claims.

**Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, dissenting.** I would deny the application. Genuine noncapital alternatives answer Beck but do not conclusively answer arbitrary deprivation of the separately available state-law opportunity under Hicks. On the assumed availability and inconsistent treatment, that due-process question is substantial enough for meaningful appellate examination. I find no proved violation or independent equal-protection ground and rely neither on the certificate alone nor on unknown papers. The existing stay would remain subject to lawful modification, without a new Supreme Court stay or guaranteed duration.

**Justice Stephen G. Breyer, dissenting.** I would deny the application. The available Hicks question could affect the conviction or sentence on the reported intent and kidnapping evidence. Absence of an all-or-nothing choice under Schad does not conclusively resolve the alleged arbitrary withholding of a further state-created jury opportunity. That concrete issue, rather than uncertainty or the certificate, supplies substantial grounds. Ultimate relief remains undecided; I require no new hearing, gateway or protection through every appellate step and need not decide the other claims.

**Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela, dissenting.** I would deny the application. The available second-degree claim presents a substantial question whether Missouri arbitrarily withheld a state-created jury opportunity when it refused an available instruction differently from materially similar cases. The reported dispute about intent and the kidnapping gives that question potential consequence. Hicks protects against arbitrary deprivation of a state-created opportunity. Schad establishes that genuine noncapital verdict options satisfy Beck's minimum safeguard; it does not conclusively resolve this distinct due-process issue. Availability alone does not establish a mandatory instruction duty, and the assumed inconsistency does not prove a constitutional violation. The question is substantial enough for the existing appeal, although ultimate relief remains undecided. Denial would leave the appellate stay governed by its own terms and subject to lawful modification. I would issue no new Supreme Court stay, guarantee no particular duration, and adopt no independent ground on the other claims.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Bowersox_v_Williams_final_application_disposition_1996-04-09.md).

## April 15 completed public authority — Miller

Exact public decision from [the authoritative Record](../records/Planned_Parenthood_Sioux_Falls_Clinic_v_Miller_merits_1996-04-15.md#public-projection). This effective decision supplements the earlier public state; its parental-notice application creates no general competency or jury-allocation rule.

## Event

Planned Parenthood, Sioux Falls Clinic v. Miller. Merits decision, April 15, 1996; October Term 1995. On review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Eighth Circuit's August 31, 1995 judgment, 63 F.3d 1452, in Nos. 94-3326SD and 94-3398SD. Those numbers identify the appeals below; no separate Supreme Court docket or oral-argument date is supplied.

The question is what facial-review standard governs and whether South Dakota may impose this compulsory parental-notification condition on unemancipated minors seeking previability abortions without a usable independent maturity or best-interests route. The clinic, Buck J. Williams, M.D., and Women's Medical Services, P.C., challenge the official-capacity administration of the law. The District Court resolved cross-motions for summary judgment, invalidating notice and separate penalty provisions while sustaining mandatory information and severability. The court of appeals affirmed. Only the minor-notice and facial-review component is before this Court.

Section 34-23A-7 ordinarily prohibits abortion until at least forty-eight hours after written parental notice. Personal delivery must be by the physician or an agent; certified mail requires return receipt and restricted delivery, with delivery deemed at noon on the next regular mail-delivery day after mailing. The period is not measured simply from mailing.

The exceptions require either a physician's good-faith clinical certification that immediate abortion is necessary to avert the minor's death or that delay will create a serious risk of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function, and that insufficient time exists to provide notice; written certification by the person entitled to notice that notification occurred; or the minor's declaration or information indicating statutory abuse or neglect, followed by the physician's required report. Recipient social-services, prosecutorial and law-enforcement authorities must protect the fact that an abortion was sought or obtained against parental disclosure. The abuse definition includes threatened substantial harm, an injurious environment and substantial emotional or mental impairment, as well as completed abuse. None of these provisions supplies an independent determination of maturity or best interests. The separate general information provision's twenty-four-hour period is not a new period imposed by the abuse exception.

## Participation

Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at consideration and decision. No case-specific nonparticipation is established. Nine participate and constitute a quorum.

## Public Action

The judgment is affirmed insofar as it invalidates the compulsory previability minor-notice condition, and the case is remanded to conform relief to the scope stated below, 6–3.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Supporting:** Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Opposing:** Justices Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, who would reverse the facial minor-notice invalidation and conform the decree to that disposition.

The injunction against the challenged compulsory previability minor-notice condition remains in force. On remand, declaratory and injunctive relief must protect providers and affected minors against enforcement of that condition and dependencies resting solely on its violation. The remand implements the decided constitutional and scope rulings; it orders no new merits trial. The separate lower rulings on mandatory information, criminal and civil penalties, and severability remain outside this review and undisturbed.

The adult-incapacity clause and unadjudicated postviability applications receive no merits determination. Decree language reaching them on the basis of this minor-notice adjudication must be confined to the violation decided here. This is neither an affirmative approval of those applications nor automatic revival of enforcement barred on an unreviewed ground. The Court does not enact a bypass, prescribe a tribunal or Pennsylvania's deadlines, or compel the State to retain notice in a revised form.

## Opinion Topology

Justice O'Connor delivers the Opinion of the Court, Parts I–IV, joined throughout by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. These six directly support every controlling proposition and its explanation below.

Justice Scalia dissents, joined throughout by Justice Thomas. Justice Kennedy files a separate dissent and does not join Scalia's constitutional ground. The three dissenters do not join any of the Court's four Parts; their agreement that the question and decree must remain bounded does not supply assent to the invalidation or its rationale. There is no judgment-only concurrence, partial majority join or fractured controlling rationale.

## Holdings

### I. The complete Casey standard governs the actual notice duty

**Holding and operative rule:** The complete six-step previability standard of Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey, as applied in Fargo Women's Health Organization v. Schafer, governs this notice challenge. Neither an independent no-valid-applications barrier nor a numerical facial threshold displaces its duty, causation, proof, substantive-protection and remedial requirements. The challengers must establish the triggering interference; a state justification burden does not arise merely because abortion is regulated.

**Authority:** Part I of Justice O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, with the six complete joins identified in Opinion Topology.

**Controlling explanation:** Casey requires identification of the enacted command and protected baseline, its function and purpose, the additional interference it causes, the applicable substantive protection, clinical and communication safeguards, and relief matching the violation. A baseline violation, proved obstructive purpose or substantial obstacle independently invalidates the requirement; no interest balancing rescues it. Remaining severe interference requires compelling justification and narrow tailoring. Remaining meaningful interference requires substantiated justification and fit, including a response to a concrete practicable less burdensome alternative. Below meaningful interference that heightened access inquiry ends without extinguishing independent constitutional protections.

Here the starting population is unemancipated minors seeking protected previability care who are subject to this notice condition. Compare their circumstances with the same system absent this duty and its interval, holding other law and relevant conditions constant. Within that population, examine supported circumstances of compelled disclosure and unusable exceptions before deciding injury. Neither all pregnant patients nor only successful constitutional claimants defines the population. The single-parent-household statistic answers an assumed safe second parent; it is not an injury rate.

The State may encourage useful parental advice, assistance and informed consideration. Legislative opposition to abortion alone proves no obstructive purpose, and this decision makes no such finding. But calling a command notice rather than consent does not end review of what it does. Fargo applies the full inquiry without an independent Salerno barrier. Correcting the court of appeals' abbreviated facial formulation requires that inquiry, not a remand for findings the supported record does not need.

**Precedent treatment:** Casey supplies the whole standard and proof allocation; Fargo applies them without a separate numerical or all-applications prerequisite. Salerno does not impose such a prerequisite in this setting; its operation elsewhere is not decided.

### II. The supported practical-control and obstruction applications are unconstitutional

**Holding and operative rule:** Compulsory notice is invalid where its demonstrated operation gives a parent practical control over the minor's protected decision or substantially obstructs timely care. The record establishes such applications of this notice condition, and the actual exceptions do not adequately protect them. A permissible parental-welfare interest cannot justify that established interference.

**Authority:** Part II of the same Opinion of the Court, joined by the same six Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Formal consent and notice differ, and minors' welfare permits a parental role not imposed on an adult spouse. Those differences do not erase demonstrated practical prevention. The summary-judgment submissions recounted below include an honor-student minor whose father, after learning she was at the clinic, assaulted staff and forced her to leave; other accounts describe parental obstruction, newly threatened abuse after disclosure, and reporting reluctance causing delay. They support additional interference attributable to compulsory disclosure. Private hostility alone is not the constitutional injury; the State's added condition exposes the protected decision to the demonstrated obstruction.

The abuse definition reaches threatened harm and is not limited to an earlier assault. Its confidentiality command also matters. Yet the reporting requirement does not furnish a route for every mature or best-interests minor, and supported reluctance to report an abusive parent limits its practical use. The court of appeals' account of access to juvenile records, testimony and the provider's identity supports confidentiality concerns without establishing that every official will breach the command or that a particular later disclosure occurred. Written parental acknowledgment proves notice, not independent authorization. An emergency exception conditioned on insufficient time does not resolve the nonemergency problem. Casey's practical-control protection therefore applies while preserving the distinct permissible interests in minors' welfare.

**Precedent treatment:** Casey's spousal-notice holding supplies the distinction between formal notice and effective control; its application here rests on this minor-specific record. Matheson, addressing an immature dependent minor without an established mature or best-interests claim, does not decide these applications. No categorical equivalence of every notice and consent law follows.

### III. The State also fails to justify the remaining meaningful interference

**Holding and operative rule:** Independently of the established obstacle applications, the condition imposes demonstrated remaining meaningful interference through additional delay, forced disclosure and coercive consequences, and the State has not substantiated its fit or adequately answered the concrete alternative of a usable confidential maturity or best-interests route. That failure supplies a separate sufficient basis for invalidating this compulsory structure at the scope addressed in Part IV.

**Authority:** Part III of the same Opinion of the Court, joined by the same six Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Meaningful interference triggers review; it is not by itself invalidity. Parental help can promote sound decisions, but general reliance on that benefit does not explain compelling disclosure where the supported circumstances make involvement harmful or inappropriate. The challenger must establish a concrete added burden, and the State may answer through reliable experience and reasonable predictions. Neither scientific certainty nor a new legislative study is required. Here the actual burdens and the missing independent route are established sufficiently to decide the question.

An effective maturity or best-interests procedure is a concrete alternative, illustrated by Casey's sustained consent structure and the independent-authorization authorities. It preserves justified parental involvement while addressing minors for whom compulsory disclosure frustrates the asserted welfare interest. The broad abuse route cannot substitute for a maturity inquiry and does not fully answer the supported best-interests, reporting and confidentiality gaps. The State offers no adequate showing of the alternative's unavailability, insufficiency or material countervailing consequences. This is not a demand to select the cheapest policy or disprove every imagined alternative.

Casey's severe-interference branch remains distinct: an established serious intrusion into protected confidentiality, health or clinical judgment requires its own compelling justification and narrow tailoring when the independent prohibitions have not already resolved the issue. The Court need not classify every remaining notice injury as severe; the supported obstacle ground and the separate failure of justification and fit suffice. Timely necessary care and genuine clinical judgment remain protected, without deciding an independent challenge to this emergency definition.

**Precedent treatment:** Casey and Fargo retain their full residual-interference inquiry. Bellotti's independent-authorization principle and Casey's sustained bypass establish a concrete alternative; they do not transplant every procedural feature of a consent statute into this notice law. Ohio v. Akron Center's approval of an available bypass did not itself decide its universal necessity.

### IV. Relief must remove the unconstitutional compulsory condition without deciding other applications

**Holding and operative rule:** The challenged previability minor-notice condition may be enjoined in its compulsory operation because the demonstrated defect is indivisible within that condition and the law supplies no usable independent maturity or best-interests route. Voluntary notice by other families does not cure that compulsion. Declaratory and injunctive relief must be conformed to the adjudicated minor violation, with independently lawful requirements and unreviewed rulings preserved.

**Authority:** Part IV of the same Opinion of the Court, joined by the same six Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** A nominal decree that mature minors are exempt would leave unanswered how a minor obtains that protection before disclosure and delay defeat it. The enacted condition supplies no independent route that a court can assume already exists. Retaining enforcement on that assumption would invent the missing safeguard. The broader protection of minors subject to this condition therefore rests on its indivisible compulsory structure, demonstrated interference and inadequate justification, not on one injured person or the premise that every family objects to consultation.

Casey permits relief against such a proved condition while preserving independent lawful operation. Dalton requires a decree corresponding to the violation, and does not impose a new facial formula or forbid adequate relief against an indivisible defect. Here its limit requires excluding an adjudication of adult incapacity and unreviewed postviability applications. It does not require leaving the established minor violation without an effective remedy.

The receiving courts must preserve the notice injunction at the stated scope, protect against dependencies resting solely on breach of that invalid condition, and conform any excessive declaratory or injunctive language. They must not reopen the separate information and penalty rulings or automatically revive enforcement those rulings independently prohibit. No new report-field or general scienter ruling is made. The State remains free to abandon the condition or pursue an adequate independent route through lawful means; the Court does not write that route into state law. Ordinary voluntary consultation remains possible. The remand implements these conclusions and requires no new merits trial or newly assigned proof burden.

**Precedent treatment:** Casey's tailored-relief qualification and Dalton's preservation of severable nonconflicting operation are applied together. Neither is narrowed, and no earlier precedent is overruled.

## Precedent Treatment

Casey, June 29, 1992, governs without alteration: protected choice, the complete six-step standard, practical-control protection, genuine necessary-care safeguards and matched relief all survive. Its particular consent scheme supplies a concrete alternative without establishing that every sustained deadline or institution is universally indispensable. Fargo, February 13, 1995, supplies the full current access and facial-review method; its separate emergency-vagueness ruling neither resolves this notice question nor approves every narrow health exception.

Matheson retains its limited immature-dependent-minor holding. Bellotti's mature and best-interests authorization principle informs the actual alternative; Hodgson's treatment of family circumstances and bypass operation is applied with its two-parent setting kept distinct. Ohio v. Akron Center retains its holding sustaining an available bypass and its reservation concerning necessity. Salerno supplies no independent facial barrier displacing the governing abortion standard here. Dalton, March 18, 1996, controls the bounded remedial inquiry without turning its Medicaid disposition into a parental-notice holding. No precedent is overruled or treated as authorizing a general prohibition on parental communication.

## Law After Decision

South Dakota may not enforce this compulsory previability minor-notice condition without an adequate independent route protecting the mature and best-interests circumstances identified in the decision. The governing Casey rule remains unchanged; this decision applies it to the supported compulsory structure and actual exceptions. Practical control or a substantial obstacle independently defeats the requirement, and the inadequately justified remaining meaningful interference supplies an additional sufficient ground.

The injunction protects the adjudicated minor operation and its solely dependent enforcement consequences. It creates no freestanding objection to all parental communication, categorical rule against every forty-eight-hour period, particular tribunal, mandatory legislative timetable or universal severe-confidentiality classification. The separate information, penalty and severability rulings remain undisturbed. Adult-incapacity and unreviewed postviability applications receive no merits decision or automatic enforcement approval. Six direct joins support the Court's complete rule; no aggregation of dissenting grounds or Marks analysis supplies authority.

## Separate Writings

**Justice Scalia, dissenting, joined by Justice Thomas.** They would reverse the facial invalidation of the minor-notice condition and conform relief accordingly, leaving the unrelated rulings untouched. They retain their constitutional objection to Casey's heightened abortion framework and regard the actual one-parent notice duty, finite interval and emergency and abuse accommodations as reasonable means of protecting minors and parental responsibility. The abuse definition reaches threatened harm, and its confidentiality duty is a real statutory protection. In their view, the Federal Constitution does not require the additional maturity or best-interests mechanism the Court demands.

They recognize the Court's practical-obstruction evidence but reject the constitutional premise that places these supported notice burdens within the majority's heightened sequence. Approval of Pennsylvania's available bypass establishes its permissibility, not a general duty to enact one elsewhere. Their disagreement is with the governing constitutional rule and its justification burden; it does not authorize lower courts to disregard Casey or depend on an independent numerical facial bar. They do not decide every hypothetical emergency or wrongful-enforcement claim.

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting.** He would reverse this facial minor-notice invalidation and conform the decree to that result. He retains protected choice and the prohibition on effective control expressed in Casey, but rejects the general residual lesser-burden allocation that requires the State to answer the Court's independent-authorization alternative here. A parent's responsibility for a minor differs from a spouse's control over another adult. The actual law requires notice rather than consent and contains emergency, threatened-harm and confidentiality protections with more reach than a completed-assault-only description suggests.

The honor-student episode and the reporting and disclosure concerns are material. In his assessment, the supplied incidents and predictions do not establish that this entire notice structure is an effective veto or that all mature minors must be exempted. He would preserve relief for a separately established unprotected instance of practical prevention or denial of necessary care, with an identified application and effective remedy. That reservation does not lead him to join the facial injunction. He does not treat Salerno as displacing the Court's controlling method, accept all parental obstruction, or join Scalia's rejection of the underlying constitutional protection.

## Procedure After Action

Supreme Court merits review of the assigned minor-notice question is complete. The case returns through the Eighth Circuit to the District Court for decree conformance within the limits stated above. The challenged compulsory previability minor-notice condition remains enjoined; no new merits hearing, enactment, replacement bypass or automatic enforcement of an unreviewed provision is ordered. Ordinary mandate procedures apply; no special issuance date or later Supreme Court event is prescribed.

## Rule 57 — December 1, 1995 effective source

The [Rule 57 source Record](../records/Rule_57_Federal_Rules_of_Criminal_Procedure_rule_amendment_1995-12-01.md) adds the fifth noncase-law source, effective December 1, 1995. Its local-form and actual-notice protections retain their exact limited subjects; pending-case application is qualified by justness and practicability. It changes no completed Court event, posture, national-rule deadline or automatic application to earlier conduct. This source insertion did not advance the Court-event chronology cursor.

## Event

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 57, amended April 27, 1995, effective December 1, 1995, subject to the specified pending-case transition.

## Participation

No case-specific judicial participation attaches to this general procedural rule.

## Public Action

The amended district-court practice rule takes effect. This source entry issues no Court action in a case.

## Judgment & Remedy

No judicial judgment or remedy is entered.

## Opinion Topology

There is no merits opinion or separate writing.

## Holdings

The rule amendment creates no judicial holding.

## Precedent Treatment

No case precedent is treated by this source admission.

## Law After Decision

Rule 57(a)(1) permits district local rulemaking after appropriate public notice and opportunity to comment, requires consistency with—but no duplication of—Acts of Congress and rules adopted under 28 U.S.C. §2072, and requires conformity with any prescribed uniform numbering system. Under (a)(2), a local form requirement may not be enforced to cause loss of rights because of a nonwillful failure to comply.

Under (b), a judge may regulate practice consistently with federal law, the criminal rules and district local rules. No sanction or other disadvantage may be imposed for noncompliance with a requirement outside federal law, federal rules and local district rules unless the alleged violator received actual notice of that requirement in the particular case. Subdivision (c) governs local-rule effectiveness, amendment or circuit-council abrogation, transmission and public availability.

Effective December 1, 1995, the amendment governs all proceedings in criminal cases thereafter commenced and, insofar as just and practicable, all proceedings in criminal cases then pending. That qualification does not establish automatic application to earlier conduct, excuse noncompliance with a national rule, or adjudicate a particular pending case.
