## May 20, 1996 completed public authority — Henderson

Exact public text from [the bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Henderson_v_United_States_merits_1996-05-20.md). This decision used the common May 13 entering-law baseline and does not supply intervening law for any May 20 peer.

## Event

Henderson v. United States, 517 U.S. 654, No. 95-232. Argued March 19, 1996; decided May 20, 1996; October Term 1995. On certiorari under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) to the Fifth Circuit, 51 F.3d 574, which affirmed dismissal without prejudice under the Suits in Admiralty Act's forthwith-service direction. The questions concern whether Rule 4 displaces that timetable and, alternatively, whether its statutory period may be extended.

Henderson filed April 8, 1993, after administrative disallowance, alleging injury on or about August 27, 1991 aboard the United States-owned DELMONTE. His negligence, unseaworthiness, maintenance, cure and damages claims remain unadjudicated. The Attorney General received the mailed papers May 25, day 47. The original 120-day period expired August 6. The district court signed a fifteen-day service extension August 31, filed September 1, and the United States Attorney was served September 3, day 148. The order contains no express finding of good cause, diligence or clerk fault. Counsel's account of problems with forms, seals and mail and the Government's challenge to his diligence remain opposed submissions.

The Government sought dismissal under §742, without a distinct Rule 4 dismissal ground, and described service as properly effected September 3. The district court ultimately dismissed under Rule 12(b)(1) in June 1994. The Fifth Circuit treated forthwith service as a jurisdictional consent condition applying to both recipients and held 148 days insufficient even assuming good cause and a reasonable-time construction. It did not decide whether day-47 receipt independently satisfied the statute. Dismissal without prejudice did not establish that a new suit would be timely.

## Participation

Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision. No Justice is recused or otherwise nonparticipating.

## Public Action

The Fifth Circuit's judgment affirming dismissal under §742's forthwith-service direction is reversed, and the case is remanded.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Judgment:** Reversed and remanded, 7–2. **Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. **Opposing:** O'Connor and Thomas would affirm dismissal under the surviving statutory service condition.

The action was timely commenced by filing. Neither the day-148 service nor day-47 receipt can sustain dismissal under the displaced statutory timetable. Further proceedings must apply the Federal Rules to any genuinely available service issue and to the injury claims. The Court does not decide that the existing extension was valid, compel a new good-cause hearing, create a new service objection, or direct immediate trial or relief on the merits.

## Opinion Topology

Justice Scalia delivers the Opinion of the Court, Parts I–III, joined throughout by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Those seven directly adopt each controlling proposition and explanation below. Justice Thomas dissents, joined throughout by Justice O'Connor. There is no partial join, judgment-only concurrence or fractured controlling rationale.

## Holdings

### I. The forthwith-service direction implements the existing waiver

**Controlling proposition:** Section 742's direction to serve the filed complaint forthwith regulates procedure in an already authorized Suits in Admiralty Act action; it does not independently condition this waiver or remove subject-matter jurisdiction. Congress can make a procedural requirement a jurisdictional condition of consent, but the placement, function and surrounding provisions establish that it did not do so with this timetable.

**Authority:** Part I of Scalia's Opinion of the Court; the seven Justices identified in Opinion Topology join.

**Controlling explanation:** Section 742 first authorizes the specified nonjury in-personam admiralty proceeding. Its later sentences direct delivery to the United States Attorney, registered mailing to the Attorney General and a sworn return. Those steps bring notice of the filed action to the designated recipients. Consent, venue, service and transfer have separate functions within the same section; proximity to the waiver does not make every direction jurisdictional.

Section 743's instruction to follow principles and practice applicable between private parties reinforces this procedural reading. It does not erase that section's separate prescriptions concerning costs, interest, admiralty review, in-rem principles or government security. Nor does the procedural subject alone settle the question: Congress remains free to attach jurisdictional consequences to procedure. The Court interprets the particular scheme, rather than announces a categorical immunity exception.

The Government's strongest argument is that §742 states the service command separately from §743's general practice provision and therefore specially conditions consent. That structure gives the service directions work without turning their timetable into a substantive waiver limit. Nordic Village requires clear consent to the particular monetary remedy and distinguishes consent from general jurisdiction; no new monetary remedy is supplied here. McNeil enforces an actual prefiling exhaustion sequence, and Keene a filing-time jurisdictional bar. Neither determines this postfiling direction's function. Carlisle likewise shows why a procedural restriction and subject-matter jurisdiction must be distinguished, without classifying every procedural provision alike.

The two-year commencement limit and substantive boundaries of consent remain intact. Whether this service timetable survives as a nonjurisdictional command is a separate question answered in Part II.

### II. The later Rule 4 scheme displaces the competing statutory timetable

**Controlling proposition:** In this timely commenced domestic SAA action, the applicable Rule 4 timing scheme, including its authorized enlargement, governs service; §742 cannot independently require dismissal for failure to serve sooner. Congress's direct enactment of former Rule 4(j) displaces the incompatible procedural timetable without enlarging substantive consent or dispensing with the designated-recipient requirements.

**Authority:** Part II of the same seven-Justice Opinion of the Court.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress enacted former Rule 4(j) in Pub. L. 97-462. It required dismissal without prejudice when service was not made within 120 days and good cause was not shown, on motion or on the court's initiative after notice; foreign service under former subdivision (i) was excepted. This extendable timing scheme governs the same postfiling service event as §742.

The Government argues that prompt service can satisfy both texts and that a general outer deadline does not repeal a special command. But physical compliance is not the whole inquiry. Retaining a separately fatal, shorter timetable would deny the very service allowance and authorized enlargement the later scheme supplies. Former Rule 4(a)'s prompt-service responsibility does not create that independent statutory dismissal condition; the holding nevertheless grants no permission deliberately to disregard service responsibilities.

Section 2072 authorizes procedural regulation, protects substantive rights and expresses the treatment of conflicting procedural laws. That framework supports this construction, but its clause concerning rules prescribed under the Act does not directly nullify earlier law through a rule Congress itself enacted. The operative route here is the later congressional enactment, construed with the specific conflict established above. The Court does not adopt a second independently sufficient Court-promulgation ground. Rule 82 is respected because neither substantive consent nor jurisdiction is enlarged.

Hanna and Mississippi Publishing Corp. v. Murphree support treating service mechanisms as procedure; they do not replace the conflict inquiry. Walker and Ragan preserve a state-created right's distinct state-law commencement condition: Rule 3's filing provision did not address that different limitations question. Here both rival provisions regulate the same service event. Section 743 reinforces the limited displacement without erasing other special SAA provisions.

The holding concerns timing, not every service statute, all government/private procedural differences or an unpresented registered-versus-certified-mail dispute. The 1993 amendment's qualified pending-case application remains governed by Part III.

### III. The remand removes the statutory dismissal without deciding a new service dispute

**Controlling proposition:** The statutory dismissal must be reversed as to both designated recipients, and ordinary further proceedings must apply the governing Federal Rules to any properly presented issue. The decision neither validates the existing extension nor orders a new service hearing; any necessary application of amended Rule 4 must honor its express pending-case qualification.

**Authority:** Part III of the same seven-Justice Opinion of the Court.

**Controlling explanation:** September 3 was outside the original 120 days but within the district court's fifteen-day direction. No distinct Rule 4 defect supplied the dismissal under review. The absence of express good-cause findings does not itself invalidate the order or require renewed factfinding. Any genuinely available later objection remains subject to its own authority, preservation and procedural conditions. Neither recipient's timing can sustain the displaced §742 ground; the Court need not decide whether either service was forthwith.

Former Rule 4(j) governed the April–September 1993 acts. The April 22, 1993 order made amended Rule 4 effective December 1 for new cases and, insofar as just and practicable, proceedings in then-pending cases. If a properly presented issue concerning the 1994 dismissal or further proceedings requires choosing the applicable Rule, that direction controls. The Court does not automatically relabel the 1993 order or hold that amended Rule 4(m) necessarily supplies relief.

Under Rule 4(m), after notice, the court must dismiss without prejudice or direct service within a specified time when service exceeds 120 days; good cause requires an appropriate extension. Without good cause, enlargement is permitted, not compelled. Foreign service under subdivisions (f) and (j)(1) is excepted. A limitations bar may support discretion but does not require relief. Pioneer preserves flexibility actually authorized by a governing rule, not an SAA tolling power. Landgraf requires attention to express temporal direction and does not automatically reopen completed acts.

The district-court Rule 12 waiver contention supplies no independently sufficient reversal ground: the transfer motion's legal effect and appellate preservation are not established. No new waiver ruling, negligence finding, maintenance or cure award, damages judgment, immediate trial entitlement or separate due-process decision follows. Section 745's two-year limit and its narrowly dated 1950 savings provision create no general new refiling opportunity.

## Precedent Treatment

- United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30: preserves clear consent to the actual monetary remedy and the distinction between consent and jurisdiction; its original §106(c) construction does not classify this service timetable.
- McNeil v. United States, 508 U.S. 106: distinguishes its prefiling administrative-exhaustion requirement; that statutory sequence and its express alternatives and exceptions remain unchanged.
- Keene Corp. v. United States, 508 U.S. 200: distinguishes the particular filing-time bar; later service in this action presents a different operative event.
- Carlisle v. United States, April 29, 1996: applies its distinction between procedural authority and subject-matter jurisdiction while preserving rule-consistent discretion, express transition limits and independently supported avenues of relief.
- Hanna v. Plumer, 380 U.S. 460: applies its recognition of federal service procedure; actual conflict and lawful authority remain necessary.
- Mississippi Publishing Corp. v. Murphree, 326 U.S. 438: applies the procedural character of service implementing an existing right without using procedure to enlarge substantive rights or jurisdiction.
- Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., 446 U.S. 740: distinguishes the state limitations/commencement issue from two provisions governing the same federal postfiling service event.
- Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co., 337 U.S. 530: preserves the state-law commencement condition for the state-created right; Rule 3 is not a universal displacement of such conditions.
- Pioneer Investment Services Co. v. Brunswick Associates Limited Partnership, 507 U.S. 380: preserves rule-specific enlargement authority and its limits; it supplies neither the former Rule 4 good-cause test nor a general extension of SAA conditions.
- Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244: applies respect for express temporal direction; neither a pending case nor procedural characterization automatically reopens completed acts.

No Supreme Court precedent is overruled. The Fifth Circuit's contrary premise that this forthwith-service timetable remains a jurisdictional condition enforceable independently of Rule 4 is rejected.

## Law After Decision

Effective May 20, 1996, §742's competing forthwith timetable cannot defeat service allowed by the governing Rule 4 scheme in a timely commenced domestic SAA action. This particular procedural direction does not define substantive consent. Congress retains power to impose jurisdictional procedural conditions, and only a lawful superseding source can displace an enacted command.

The designated-recipient requirements, §745's two-year commencement period, substantive waiver limits and the need to comply with the applicable Rules remain. The Court does not decide the extension's validity, every possible service issue, the Clarification Act/PVA classification, maritime liability or relief. It does not extend a surviving statutory deadline or create a general refiling period. Further use of amended Rule 4 remains subject to the express just-and-practicable transition and the distinction between permitted and mandatory enlargement.

## Separate Writings

Justice Thomas, joined by Justice O'Connor, would affirm. Congress may make a procedural requirement a condition of sovereign consent, and the dissent reads §742's particular service command separately from §743's general private-party practice instruction as doing so here. Sherwood, Block and Nordic Village require respect for the actual scope of consent; this is not a contention that every sentence in a waiver statute is jurisdictional. Meyer's broad agency clause and Carlisle's criminal procedural mechanism do not determine the SAA's differently structured waiver.

A judicial rule cannot enlarge that consent under §2072(b) and Rule 82. Congress itself enacted former Rule 4(j) and had power to change the waiver, but its general dismissal timetable does not sufficiently establish repeal of the retained special condition. Prompt service can satisfy both, and general authorized enlargement need not displace the special statute. The 1993 transition supplies no independent substantive enlargement.

Service on the United States Attorney after 148 days fails the surviving requirement even under a reasonable-dispatch reading and assuming good cause. The Rule 4 extension does not extend that separate condition. No universal number of days, adverse diligence finding or conclusion about day-47 Attorney General receipt is required. Pioneer and the American Pipe/McCormick analogy do not establish general authority to extend this consent condition. The dissent neither creates a new Rule 4 defect nor decides injury merits, separate due process or a right to timely refiling. The unestablished Rule 12 waiver route does not supply an alternative reversal of the jurisdictional condition. These propositions are noncontrolling.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns through the Fifth Circuit for ordinary further proceedings consistent with Parts I–III. The displaced statutory timetable cannot again sustain dismissal. Any genuine Rule 4 question must meet its own authority, preservation and procedural conditions, with the 1993 transition applied if material. No new good-cause hearing, favorable extension decision or immediate merits trial is ordered. Supreme Court merits review is complete, subject to ordinary mandate procedures; no later Supreme Court event is prescribed.

## Source Notes

The [filed petition, joint appendix and merits submissions in No. 95-232](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40385013_0641) supply the procedural record and competing arguments. Petition Appendix 1–9 reproduces the lower decisions; Joint Appendix page 15 supplies the fifteen-day order, without express good-cause findings. The complaint's injury date remains an allegation; inconsistent incidental recitations establish no different merits finding. The actual earlier venue-transfer motion and appellate preservation needed for a dispositive Rule 12 waiver ruling are not established here.

The enacted Suits in Admiralty Act, 41 Stat. 525, its 1960 amendment, 74 Stat. 912, and Pub. L. 97-462 supply the statutory language and Congress's direct adoption of former Rule 4(j). The [April 22, 1993 order and Rule text, 507 U.S. 1091, 1103–1110](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/507bv.pdf), supply the effective date and qualified application to pending proceedings; the 1993 subdivision (m) note distinguishes discretionary relief from good-cause enlargement. Section 745's amendment history preserves its dated 1950 savings provision; it is not a general extension for present refiling.


## May 20, 1996 completed public authority — Casarotto

Exact public text from [the bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Doctors_Associates_Inc_v_Casarotto_merits_1996-05-20.md). This decision used the common May 13 entering-law baseline and does not supply intervening law for any May 20 peer.

## Event

Doctor's Associates, Inc. v. Casarotto, 517 U.S. 681, No. 95-559. Argued April 16, 1996; decided May 20, 1996; October Term 1995. On certiorari under 28 U.S.C. §1257(a) to the Montana Supreme Court, 274 Mont. 3, 901 P.2d 596, reviewing its August 31, 1995 judgment sustaining a statutory notice bar to arbitration. The question presented is whether FAA §2 preempts the arbitration-specific first-page notice condition.

Paul Casarotto signed DAI's April 25, 1988 franchise agreement. Paragraph 10(c), on page nine, requires arbitration of controversies arising out of or relating to the contract or its breach under AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules in Bridgeport, Connecticut; commencement of arbitration is a condition precedent to legal action, and costs are shared equally. The agreement selects Connecticut law, provides severability and acknowledges reading, understanding and consent. Its integration clause preserves representations in the agreement, offering circular and franchisor advertising. The offering circular disclosed arbitration; the agreement has no first-page arbitration notice. Paul's affidavit describes a nonnegotiable contract, absent explanation and lack of understanding of the lost Montana forum. That affidavit and the signed acknowledgment are evidence, not findings of informed assent or ignorance.

The district court found actual interstate commerce, clause coverage of claims against DAI and its alleged agent Lombardi, and an arbitration demand. It stayed those claims June 2, 1993, invoking FAA §3, and later certified its order under state Rule 54(b). The Montana majority rejected the stay because §27-5-114(4) requires notice that a contract is subject to arbitration pursuant to the chapter, typed in underlined capital letters on its first page, with nonenforcement absent that notice. It selected Montana law under conflicts principles and relied on Volt, reasoning that informed consent advances arbitration. It announced no independently sufficient general contract-defense ruling.

The statutory dispute concerns subsection (4). Subsection (2) separately excludes personal-injury claims, contracts for an individual's acquisition of property, services, money or credit with total consideration of $5,000 or less, insurance or annuity agreements except contracts between insurance companies, and workers' compensation claims. Its express subsection (3) qualification concerns written agreements among trade or professional organization members to arbitrate future disputes among members. Those are not exceptions written into subsection (4), and their validity or application is not decided here.

## Participation

Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision. No Justice is recused or otherwise nonparticipating.

## Public Action

The Montana Supreme Court's judgment sustaining the arbitration-specific notice bar is reversed, and the case is remanded.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Judgment:** Reversed and remanded, 8–1. **Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. **Opposing:** Thomas would affirm because, in his view, the FAA does not command enforcement in state court.

The state courts must resolve the stay request without the preempted notice condition. Existing commerce, clause-scope and demand determinations remain undisturbed. If no genuinely available, properly preserved independent ground defeats the stay, the rejected notice objection cannot prevent its restoration. The Court does not unconditionally reinstate the stay, direct arbitration of all persons and claims, revive waived defenses or order a new hearing.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg | All nine adopt reviewability. |
| Opinion of the Court, Parts II–III | Breyer | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg | Eight adopt notice preemption, its contractual limits and reversal/remand. |
| Dissent from the merits judgment | Thomas | No other Justice | Joins Part I; rejects the state-court FAA premise and would affirm. |

## Holdings

### I. The finally decided federal notice bar is reviewable

**Controlling proposition:** Section 1257(a) permits review of Montana's finally resolved federal notice-preemption question despite continuing merits proceedings, because Southland/Cox finality applies and no independently sufficient lower contract-defense ground is established. State Rule 54(b) certification alone does not establish federal finality, and this conclusion creates no universal right to review interlocutory arbitration orders.

**Authority:** Part I of Breyer's Opinion of the Court; all nine participating Justices join.

**Controlling explanation:** Southland applied Cox Broadcasting to a state judgment finally rejecting arbitration despite further litigation below. Delaying review risks both losing later review if the arbitration proponent prevails on nonfederal grounds and eroding the claimed federal forum right through the very litigation arbitration would avoid. Here the State conclusively sustained the notice bar; reversal removes that adjudicated obstacle to the existing stay request.

Neither Rule 54(b) nor the existence of unadjudicated damages claims supplies the answer by itself. A genuinely sufficient independent ground defeating arbitration would require its own finality analysis, but no such lower ground is established. Possible defenses are not adjudicated defenses. Montana's conflicts ruling selects the notice rule whose federal validity is challenged; it does not independently sustain that rule against federal law. The Court therefore need not resolve a separate state-law conflicts challenge to reach preemption.

Southland's earlier appeal route under former §1257(2) is not the present jurisdictional provision. Its finality reasoning applies to this §1257(a) certiorari review. Thomas's disagreement about §2's substantive reach does not remove jurisdiction to decide that federal question.

### II. Section 2 forbids this arbitration-only notice condition

**Controlling proposition:** For this agreement covered by FAA §2, Montana may not deny arbitration because notice was not typed in underlined capital letters on the contract's first page as §27-5-114(4) requires; generally applicable formation and revocation rules remain available. Volt protects actual contractual selection of state arbitration procedure, not this imposed condition invalidating the clause, and no selection of Montana's condition is established.

**Authority:** Part II of Breyer's Opinion of the Court; the eight Justices identified for Parts II–III in Opinion Topology join.

**Controlling explanation:** Section 2 makes covered written arbitration agreements valid, irrevocable and enforceable, subject to grounds at law or equity for revoking any contract. Allied-Bruce retained Southland's application in state courts and actual-commerce coverage. The district's commerce finding stands; no new coverage hearing or outer constitutional ruling is needed. Retained statutory precedent governs despite the dissent's original-construction objection.

Perry preserves ordinary contract law while rejecting disabilities keyed specifically to arbitration. Montana's condition attaches its required typography, placement and nonenforcement consequence because the contract selects arbitration. Allowing enforcement after compliance does not make that additional condition a ground for revoking any contract.

Respondents invoke informed consent, adhesion, reasonable expectations and Restatement §211. Those concerns can support genuinely applicable contract doctrines; they do not transform this categorical special condition into general law. Modest compliance cost, physical compatibility with federal law and a consent-protective purpose do not answer §2's saving-clause limit. No subjective hostility finding is required.

Volt enforced an actual selection of state arbitration procedure. This agreement selects Connecticut law and AAA arbitration in Bridgeport, not Montana's first-page condition. Mastrobuono requires attention to the integrated agreement and genuine contractual restrictions. Neither decision shields an imposed invalidity rule or requires deciding every Connecticut-law or conflicts question. The lower dissent's construction of the statute's “pursuant to this chapter” language is not an independent ground adopted here.

The Montana majority announced no independently sufficient reasonable-expectations, fraud or unconscionability holding. A properly available general defense survives; arbitration's uniqueness cannot itself become an unconscionability rule under another label. Respondents' asserted Chor actual-knowledge exception is not established: its majority addressed a common-law defense on its evidence, not an express exception to this statute. Paul's affidavit and acknowledgment supply no new finding of knowledge, ignorance or invalidity. No general conspicuousness requirement or broader disclosure rule is adjudicated. The conclusion follows the enacted equal-footing command, not a free-standing preference for arbitration.

### III. Ordinary remand preserves actual contractual and party limits

**Controlling proposition:** The stay request must be resolved without the notice bar, subject to genuinely available, properly preserved independent grounds and the actual parties' contractual rights. This reversal leaves existing commerce, clause-scope and demand determinations intact and requires neither unconditional compulsion nor a new evidentiary proceeding.

**Authority:** Part III of the same eight-Justice Opinion of the Court.

**Controlling explanation:** Petitioners request immediate reinstatement of the stay, but invalidating the notice condition does not decide every distinct enforcement predicate. Paul signed; the record does not resolve Pamela's entire position. Lombardi's alleged agency is not an actual agency finding, and his contested nonsignatory enforcement right is not independently decided. Existing scope findings are preserved without expansion into every enforcement theory. Claims against the Hudson defendants and D&D Subway remain outside this stay and appeal.

First Options requires courts independently to determine whether a party agreed to arbitrate arbitrability. Only clear and unmistakable delegation established under ordinary contract law permits arbitrators to decide the underlying arbitrability question; one party's assent supplies no other person's assent to that delegation. The broad clause and AAA reference establish no adjudicated delegation here, and independent nonsignatory theories remain unresolved. Ordinary appellate review of legal questions and factual findings remains independent and for clear error, respectively. No new conditional award-review holding is made.

The lower majority relied on the notice statute. The parties dispute whether an ordinary adhesion defense remains preserved; neither abandonment nor a successful defense is found. General formation, fraud, duress, unconscionability, lack of assent and other evenhanded defenses retain their own requirements. The remand creates no defense, revives none already waived and orders no hearing simply because a defense is conceivable.

The district's invocation of §3 does not import §§3–4 wholesale into state courts. Section 3 addresses courts of the United States and requires a written agreement, a referable issue, the court's satisfaction, a party's application, arbitration according to the agreement and no applicant default in proceeding. Those conditions remain distinct if invoked; no default or mandatory default inquiry is established. The state courts must implement §2 through lawful procedure.

The agreement's forum, cost, severability and integration terms are not rewritten or independently upheld against every defense. No liability, damages, actual arbitral expenses, award or constitutional jury-waiver rule is decided. Absent an available preserved independent ground, the notice objection cannot prevent restoration of the existing stay.

## Precedent Treatment

- Southland Corp. v. Keating, 465 U.S. 1: applies its finality reasoning at pages 6–8 and its retained substantive state-court §2 rule; its former appellate subsection is not the current review channel.
- Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cohn, 420 U.S. 469: applies the finality doctrine for this conclusively resolved federal obstacle despite further merits proceedings; no general interlocutory-review rule follows.
- Perry v. Thomas, 482 U.S. 483: applies equal enforcement while preserving grounds applicable to contracts generally; an arbitration-specific disability is not saved by a general consent label.
- Allied-Bruce Terminix Cos. v. Dobson, January 18, 1995: applies retained state-court coverage and actual commerce, preserving ordinary defenses, assent, scope and the reservation of wholesale §§3–4 incorporation.
- Volt Information Sciences, Inc. v. Board of Trustees, 489 U.S. 468: preserves actual contractual selection of state arbitration procedure; distinguishes invalidation by an unselected forum notice rule.
- Mastrobuono v. Shearson Lehman Hutton, Inc., March 6, 1995: applies attention to the actual integrated agreement and genuine contractual restrictions, without resolving every conflicts question.
- First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan, May 22, 1995: preserves antecedent assent, actual clear-and-unmistakable delegation, ordinary legal/factual review and unresolved nonsignatory theories. Its conditional review rule remains governing in its own setting; no delegation or new award-review question is decided here.

No precedent is overruled. Thomas's proposed rejection of Southland's state-court construction does not alter its controlling force.

## Law After Decision

Effective May 20, 1996, Montana's §27-5-114(4) cannot defeat an FAA-covered arbitration agreement for lack of the prescribed first-page notice. The decision applies §2's state-court command and adds its application to this special formality; it does not invalidate all of §27-5-114 or decide its separate exclusions.

Facially neutral, generally applicable contract law remains effective; merely affecting arbitration does not displace it. Ordinary formation, scope, fraud, duress, unconscionability, lack of assent and other defenses retain their genuine evenhanded operation and preservation requirements. Arbitration's special character cannot itself supply a disguised invalidity rule. Existing actual-commerce coverage stands, while the outer Commerce Clause boundary and wholesale state incorporation of §§3–4 remain unaddressed. The decision creates no unconditional enforcement entitlement against every person or claim.

## Separate Writings

Justice Thomas joins Part I and dissents from the merits judgment. He reads the FAA's structure and its federal-court judicial directions as failing to create §2's substantive command to state tribunals. He would overrule Southland to that extent and affirm the Montana judgment on federal nonapplication, maintaining the ground stated in his Allied-Bruce dissent. Statutory stare decisis and reliance do not, in his view, cure that original construction error.

His participation in federal arbitration cases concerning assent or other statutes does not adopt Southland's state-court rule. The dissent does not conditionally uphold the notice law under a state-applicable §2, find a successful general contract defense, decide commerce coverage, announce an independently sufficient §§3–4 specific-performance rule or restrict Congress's constitutional power to enact a different command. It supplies no liability, damages or party-wide arbitration judgment. These proposed changes are noncontrolling.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns to the Montana courts for further proceedings consistent with Parts II–III. The notice condition cannot again sustain denial of the existing stay. Its restoration remains subject to genuinely available, preserved independent grounds and actual contractual rights; no new commerce inquiry, mandatory defense hearing, reopened waiver or arbitration of all claims and parties is ordered. Supreme Court merits review is complete, subject to ordinary mandate procedures; no later Supreme Court event is prescribed.

## Source Notes

The [filed papers in No. 95-559](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40385013_0656) supply the petition, joint appendix and opposing merits submissions. Petition Appendix 1a–46a reproduces the state decisions; 49a–50a gives the June 2 stay; 51a reproduces the contemporaneous Montana statute. Joint Appendix 64–78 supplies the agreement and 86–87 Paul's affidavit. The complete amended complaint and appellate papers needed to settle every party-status and preservation question are not established here. The lower court accepted misconduct allegations for review of the stay, not as liability findings; general cost concerns establish no actual arbitration expenses.

## May 21, 1996 completed public authority — Pinder

Exact public text from the [bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Pinder_v_Johnson_merits_1996-05-21.md). Entering law is the full completed May 20 group, preserving each earlier source’s qualifications and all earlier open matters.

## Event

Pinder v. Johnson. Decided May 21, 1996; October Term 1995. On certiorari under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) to the Fourth Circuit in No. 93-2125, reviewing its May 30, 1995 en banc judgment, 54 F.3d 1169. The question is Officer Johnson's individual qualified immunity on the substantive-due-process claim arising from his alleged conduct and assurances before Pittman's attack.

On March 10, 1989, Johnson responded after Pittman broke into Pinder's home, assaulted her, threw objects and threatened her and her children. Johnson was told of prior threats and an earlier attempt to burn the house. After arresting Pittman, Johnson assured Pinder that Pittman would remain detained overnight. Pinder alleges that this induced her to return to work instead of staying with or arranging protection for her children. Johnson charged trespass and malicious destruction of property under $300. Commissioner Ames released Pittman that evening; Pittman returned, set the house on fire and killed Pinder's three children. No warning of release is alleged.

The district court denied dismissal and immunity. A divided panel affirmed, but its opinion was vacated on rehearing. The en banc court granted immunity, 9–4 in judgment. Its principal opinion classified this account as nonprotection and found inadequate notice while recognizing a different affirmative-danger paradigm; the supporting judges did not all adopt the same reasoning. The competing view treated the assurance-induced withdrawal of private protection as affirmative causation. The review concerns those legal characterizations on proper favorable assumptions, not a finding that Pinder proved the alleged causal chain.

## Participation

Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate in the decision. No Justice is recused or otherwise nonparticipating.

## Public Action

The Fourth Circuit's judgment granting Johnson individual qualified immunity on the reviewed substantive-due-process claim is affirmed.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Judgment:** Affirmed, 5–4. **Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. **Opposing:** Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer would vacate the reviewed immunity disposition and remand on a bounded affirmative-danger theory.

Johnson receives judgment on the individual damages claim within this immunity issue. The Court does not decide that the assumed affirmative conduct was constitutional or that custody is indispensable to every possible affirmative-deprivation claim. Other defendants and distinct preserved claims retain their proper disposition. No new merits or damages proceeding on this reviewed claim, liability finding or compensation award is ordered.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I–II | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | All nine adopt legal-review authority and the common constitutional and notice limits. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Five adopt the sufficient notice-only ground and affirmance. |
| Dissent from the judgment | Ginsburg | Stevens, Souter, Breyer | Joins Parts I–II; supports a bounded affirmative-deprivation and preconduct-notice conclusion requiring vacatur/remand. |

## Holdings

### I. Review reaches the legal immunity issue on favorable assumptions

**Controlling proposition:** The §1254(1) review and underlying §1291 legal-immunity appeal permit determination of the separable legal question on the properly assumed favorable account. They do not permit deciding factual sufficiency, selecting disputed intent or causation, or adjudicating the separate excluded claims.

**Authority:** Part I of O'Connor's Opinion of the Court; all nine Justices join.

**Controlling explanation:** Mitchell permits appeal of the separable legal immunity issue. Johnson v. Jones and Kimberlin distinguish that question from whether the plaintiff can prove the facts. Doe and Behrens preserve the same boundary: an official may obtain the legal consequences of the favorable account, but cannot obtain appellate findings that the alleged warnings, contribution or causal effect did not occur.

The district court expressly used Rule 12(b)(6); the appellate opinions describe summary judgment. Neither description authorizes an adverse factual determination here. The asserted assurance-induced withdrawal of private protection can be assumed for legal review without deciding credibility, knowing falsity or whether that withdrawal actually caused the deaths. No second pretrial immunity appeal is established, and no ruling on successive-appeal conditions is necessary.

Official-capacity or municipal claims, equal protection, §1985 and state tort counts do not enter this appeal merely because they concern the same events. Behrens preserves their distinct posture. No new procedural-due-process claim is supplied. The lawful legal question can therefore be decided without resolving the record's factual disputes or extending review to every claim.

### II. Private nonprotection, affirmative deprivation and historical notice remain distinct

**Controlling proposition:** Knowledge of danger, promises of protection and custody of Pittman create no custodial special relationship with Pinder or her children; the alleged affirmative loss of otherwise available private protection must be considered separately from a failure to supply public protection. Individual immunity requires particularized objective notice from all relevant preconduct law, without an identical-case requirement, and neither judicial disagreement nor the official's subjective belief in legality independently decides that inquiry.

**Authority:** Part II of the same unanimous Opinion of the Court.

**Controlling explanation:** DeShaney generally rejects a due-process duty to protect against private violence. Its custodial rule arises from state restraint of the injured person's ability to act, not knowledge, assistance or a promise. It also emphasized that the State had neither created the danger nor increased Joshua's vulnerability; it did not announce a complete test for every affirmative-danger claim. Johnson's alleged alteration of available private protection therefore cannot be discarded simply by identifying Pittman as the assailant.

That distinction does not establish liability. Section 1983 supplies a remedy for an attributable federal deprivation, not a general constitutional duty to perform state protective functions. Daniels excludes merely negligent injury. Culpability must concern the deprivation, not merely the intentional utterance of an assurance; its reservation concerning recklessness and gross negligence cannot be converted into a holding that any nonnegligent reassurance is unconstitutional.

Anderson requires unlawfulness sufficiently apparent in pre-existing law at the appropriate level of specificity. The exact act need not already have been held unlawful. Elder requires the entire relevant preconduct landscape, including adverse decisions and their limits. A subjective element of the underlying claim differs from the official's belief about legality; Kimberlin permits competent circumstantial proof without inventing a substantive mental-state requirement.

March 10, 1989 fixes notice. Collins, Doe, Hodge, Love and Sheets inform present analysis but cannot supply notice retroactively. Love permits a dispositive notice inquiry without mandating either merits-first or immunity-first sequencing. The common principles here do not decide whether the affirmative-danger theory succeeds on its constitutional merits or whether its particular wrong was sufficiently established then.

### III. The contemporaneous law did not sufficiently establish this particular obligation

**Controlling proposition:** Even accepting the alleged assurance-induced withdrawal of private protection for legal review, the pre-March 10, 1989 authorities did not make sufficiently apparent that this noncoercive undertaking, ensuing release and uncorrected exposure constituted Johnson's own constitutional deprivation. He therefore has individual qualified immunity on the reviewed claim; the Court reserves the distinct affirmative-danger merits.

**Authority:** Part III of O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas; five direct joins control.

**Controlling explanation:** The alleged loss of private protection is consequential and more specific than a general failure to prevent crime. The question is nevertheless whether existing law sufficiently identified that combination of assurances, charging decisions, third-party release and reliance as this officer's constitutional wrong. DeShaney had rejected knowledge-and-promise protective duties sixteen days earlier, while leaving affirmative increases in danger incompletely defined.

Bowers distinguished an active state tortfeasor but rejected liability for releasing a dangerous person. Archie discussed increased risk and interference with private aid, yet found neither culpable deprivation nor state creation of danger or hindrance of aid. Its discussion of intentional deprivation and extreme indifference to known mortal risk cannot be detached from those limits. Jensen's distinct danger discussion remains relevant, but its broader knowledge-and-promise relationship ground cannot survive DeShaney. Those cases' adverse outcomes do not erase their reasoning; neither does their general recognition of affirmative injury settle this noncoercive reliance mechanism.

The contrary argument identifies the qualifying wrong as culpable displacement of otherwise available protection against a known immediate mortal danger. Even on that favorable legal account, the extension from earlier affirmative-injury and private-aid principles to this undertaking was not sufficiently apparent. This is uncertainty over constitutional attribution, not a requirement that an earlier case reproduce every fact or award a plaintiff relief. Disagreement among judges is not itself the test.

As Hodge and Doe's Caplinger holding illustrate in their own settings, an individual notice judgment can leave constitutional sufficiency unresolved. Those later decisions provide no retrospective notice here. The conclusion rests neither on finding negligence nor on rejecting alleged reliance. Greater charges are not established to have ensured detention, and unlawful preventive confinement is not the prescribed solution. No freestanding warning entitlement, endorsement of affirmative injury, general custody prerequisite or new actual-reliance immunity defense is adopted.

## Precedent Treatment

- Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511: applies the separable legal-immunity collateral-order channel; it does not bring factual sufficiency or all related claims into review.
- Johnson v. Jones and Kimberlin v. Quinlan, June 12, 1995: apply the legal/factual appellate boundary; Kimberlin preserves circumstantial proof subject to actual constitutional elements and ordinary burdens.
- DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189: applies the limits on private-protection and custodial duties while preserving the distinction concerning state-created or increased vulnerability. Its foster-care, culpability, individual-immunity and municipal-responsibility reservations are not resolved.
- Daniels v. Williams, 474 U.S. 327: applies the exclusion of mere negligence; its reservation concerning recklessness and gross negligence remains open.
- Anderson v. Creighton, 483 U.S. 635: applies particularized apparent unlawfulness without requiring an identical prior case.
- Elder v. Holloway, February 23, 1994: applies independent review of all relevant preconduct authority on the preserved question; it supplies no retrospective notice or mandatory merits-first sequence.
- Collins v. Harker Heights, February 26, 1992: preserves the distinction between a federal deprivation and state duties or municipal attribution; its reservation of a different affirmative-danger claim remains.
- Doe v. Taylor Independent School District, October 16, 1995: applies its review boundary and preserves its distinct personal-causation and Caplinger notice holdings; official-authority abuse is not treated as the same as this private attack.
- Hodge v. Jones, October 23, 1995: applies the method of individualized notice adjudication with constitutional merits reserved; its confidential-record claim is not made a danger-creation rule.
- Love v. Pepersack, December 11, 1995: preserves lawful sequencing and the distinction between state illegality and a federal wrong; no mandatory order of decision or general merits test is inferred.
- Behrens v. Pelletier, February 21, 1996: applies favorable legal-review assumptions and separate-claim limits; no second-appeal premise is supplied.
- Sheets v. Salt Lake County, April 29, 1996: preserves its confined affirmative-disclosure rule; it neither defines this danger theory nor supplies March 1989 notice.

Bowers v. DeVito, Archie v. City of Racine and Jensen v. Conrad are considered as preconduct circuit authority with their adverse outcomes and limited affirmative-danger discussions intact. They are neither treated as Supreme Court holdings nor overruled. No Supreme Court precedent is overruled; Albright's separate positions are not converted into a general bodily-integrity bar or state-tort cure.

## Law After Decision

Effective May 21, 1996, Johnson is individually immune on the reviewed due-process claim because the particular constitutional attribution was insufficiently established on March 10, 1989. The ruling applies existing objective notice law; it creates no identical-facts prerequisite and does not adopt a defense requiring actual reliance on authoritative law.

The Court leaves the outer substantive boundary of affirmative state-created danger unresolved. A private assailant does not categorically exclude an attributable affirmative official deprivation, but neither promises, serious injury nor intentionally speaking establishes one. No minimum culpability standard for every lesser account, general warning duty, mandatory detention rule or expanded remedial entitlement is announced. Constitutional merits, personal causation, historical notice and appellate authority retain their separate functions.

## Separate Writings

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Breyer, joins Parts I–II but would vacate the reviewed immunity disposition and remand. Injured-party custody is not indispensable where an official's own sufficiently culpable conduct actually removes otherwise available protection and thereby exposes the victims to a known immediate mortal danger. The dissent concludes now that the qualifying form of this alleged deprivation was sufficiently identified by pre-March 10, 1989 law to defeat immunity disposing of the entire theory at this stage.

Bowers's active-tortfeasor distinction, Archie's private-aid reasoning and Jensen's distinct danger discussion, read with DeShaney's no-increased-vulnerability limit, supply that particular principle. Their adverse outcomes and culpability restrictions remain material. Purposefully giving reassurance alone is insufficient; culpability must attach to the deprivation, and actual causal displacement must be shown. The dissent does not restore a knowledge-and-promise special relationship or infer notice from the deaths' severity. It disagrees with the en banc application to this account, not with an invented universal custody rule.

The favorable pleading possibility includes intentional or conscience-shocking deprivation without establishing that mental state. The dissent selects no minimum standard for every lesser account, finds no knowing falsity or favoritism, and does not assume greater charges would have prevented release. A later factual finding cannot create historical legal notice. Materially different or less culpable conduct retains its own constitutional and immunity analysis.

The requested remand would proceed through the Court of Appeals under ordinary preservation, pleading and proof rules, addressing culpability, actual causal predicates and genuinely available defenses only as needed. It would not unconditionally restore the entire district order or vacated panel opinion, mandate discovery, a hearing or trial, award damages, or adjudicate excluded counts. This bounded merits-and-notice position is noncontrolling.

## Procedure After Action

The individual immunity judgment stands on the reviewed substantive-due-process claim. The receiving courts must give effect to Johnson's judgment within that issue; the decision orders no new merits or damages proceeding on it. Official-capacity or municipal liability, equal protection, §1985, Maryland wrongful-death and survival counts, and other legally distinct preserved claims remain outside this disposition. No unpresented procedural claim is added. Supreme Court merits review is complete, subject to ordinary mandate procedures; no formal mandate date or additional Supreme Court event is prescribed.

## May 28, 1996 completed public authority — Ornelas

Exact public text from the [bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Ornelas_v_United_States_merits_1996-05-28.md). Entering law is the complete public state through May 21.

## Event

Ornelas v. United States, 517 U.S. 690, No. 95-5257. Decided May 28, 1996; October Term 1995. On certiorari under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1), following federal appeals under §1291, reviewing the Seventh Circuit's decisions at 16 F.3d 714 and 52 F.3d 328 (table). The question concerns appellate review of ultimate reasonable suspicion for a stop and probable cause for a nonwarrant search, preserved through conditional guilty pleas.

On December 11, 1992, detectives investigated an older two-door General Motors car with California plates, motel and travel circumstances, and two NADDIS entries thought related to the men. The entries were not established to identify petitioners. Detectives approached as petitioners entered the car, obtained identification and consent, and eventually removed a vent cover and panel, recovering approximately two kilograms of cocaine. The officer's gun was not visible. The Government conceded petitioners could challenge the search and that a reasonable person would not have felt free to leave. It did not contend that the stop or consent independently authorized dismantling.

The first appellate opinion accepted reasonable suspicion under clear-error review, held inevitable discovery waived and remanded the loose-panel credibility question. On the stipulated existing record, the magistrate credited the loose-panel testimony, retained the adverse assessment of testimony about rust indicating recent removal, and found the scratches inconclusive. He recommended suppression. The district judge accepted the loose-panel credibility finding but found probable cause; the second appellate order affirmed for want of clear error. The remaining disagreement is not an unresolved conflict over that credited observation.

Both petitioners and the United States seek independent ultimate review and appellate remand, while disagreeing about suppression. Amici defend deferential review. The separate database-discovery claim and initial determination by this Court of the stop/search merits are outside the question presented.

## Participation

Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate in the decision. No Justice is recused or otherwise nonparticipating.

## Public Action

Both reviewed Court of Appeals judgments, 16 F.3d 714 and 52 F.3d 328, are vacated, and the case is remanded to that court for independent review of both ultimate constitutional determinations.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Judgment:** Vacated and remanded, 8–1. **Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. **Opposing:** Scalia would affirm the reviewed allocation under deferential ultimate review.

The Court of Appeals must independently decide reasonable suspicion and probable cause while reviewing historical findings for clear error and giving genuine due weight to grounded contextual inferences. The Court orders no suppression, acquittal, release, new trial, new evidentiary hearing or automatic plea withdrawal. It does not decide whether the existing suppression result ultimately changes.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joins | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | All nine adopt review authority and the preserved question's scope. |
| Opinion of the Court, Parts II–III | O'Connor | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Eight adopt independent ultimate review, factual protection, genuine due weight and vacatur of both appellate judgments. |
| Dissent from the judgment | Scalia | No other Justice | Joins Part I; favors deferential ultimate application with independent correction of legal errors. |

## Holdings

### I. Review includes both preserved ultimate thresholds

**Controlling proposition:** Sections 1291 and 1254(1), following the supported conditional pleas, permit review of the appellate standard for both ultimate reasonable suspicion and probable cause. The parties' agreement does not determine that standard, and neither the separate database-discovery claim nor initial Supreme Court resolution of suppression's merits enters this review.

**Authority:** Part I of O'Connor's Opinion of the Court; all nine participating Justices join.

**Controlling explanation:** The first appellate decision applied clear-error review to reasonable suspicion; the second sustained probable cause under the same formulation after the limited remand. The independent-review contention remained preserved in both appeals. Considering only the final probable-cause discussion would leave the earlier preserved threshold governed by the contested allocation.

Rule 11(a)(2) permits a conditional plea with court approval and Government consent, reserving in writing review of a specified adverse pretrial determination. The selected orders and docket entries establish the suppression reservation here; incomplete copies of the full agreements create neither an additional reservation nor a finding of noncompliance. The Government's concession concerning petitioners' ability to challenge this search resolves no other issue by implication.

Although the parties agree on independent review, suppression remains contested and legal classification is the Court's responsibility. The Court decides the review standard and returns its application to the Court of Appeals. No database-disclosure ruling, new waiver or ultimate Fourth Amendment result follows from accepting this channel.

### II. Ultimate constitutional sufficiency is independently reviewed, with factual protection and genuine due weight

**Controlling proposition:** Appellate courts independently decide whether established circumstances, objectively considered in their totality, supply reasonable suspicion for the stop and probable cause for the nonwarrant search; no finding of clear error in the ultimate conclusion is required. Historical facts, credibility and genuinely factual subsidiary findings or inferences receive clear-error review, while grounded contextual inferences of resident judges and experienced local officers receive genuine due weight without controlling the ultimate constitutional judgment.

**Authority:** Part II of O'Connor's Opinion of the Court; the eight Justices identified for Parts II–III in Opinion Topology join.

**Controlling explanation:** Reasonable suspicion and probable cause demand different degrees of justification, but both require applying a national constitutional boundary to established circumstances. Brinegar, Gates, Sokolow and White preserve practical, objective totality analysis rather than mechanical formulas. That practical character does not answer who independently determines constitutional sufficiency.

Miller's functional approach and Thompson's treatment of ultimate custody distinguish historical findings from constitutional application without making every mixed question independently reviewable. First Options likewise preserves ordinary legal/factual review but does not itself classify these questions. Applications give constitutional standards practical content; appellate comparison supplies guidance and error correction even when a particular combination yields little general precedent. Ultimate deference could permit materially similar established conduct to receive different constitutional treatment merely because different trial conclusions survived review.

The competing argument properly emphasizes trial experience, local conditions and fact-specific probabilities. Those advantages remain protected. Courts review what happened, physical conditions and credibility for clear error. They also give genuine due weight to grounded inferences from resident judges' local knowledge and officers' experience, including supported trial assessments of credibility and inferential reasonableness. This is real contextual deference, not a direction merely to notice and disregard the assessment. But experience cannot establish an unproved observation or create a presumption that a search was lawful. Ultimate constitutional sufficiency remains independently decided.

Gates's substantial-basis review of an issuing magistrate's warrant decision serves the preference for advance judicial authorization. That institutional relationship differs from appellate review of a suppression decision after a nonwarrant search; its deference is not transplanted here. Pierce and Cooter & Gell demonstrate that other tasks can justify ultimate deference, not that all concrete applications share one allocation. Salve Regina's appellate advantages likewise require issue-specific analysis. The Court adopts no numerical weight, police-credibility preference, new evidentiary burden or intermediate standard insulating the ultimate conclusion.

### III. Both appellate judgments require reconsideration under that allocation

**Controlling proposition:** Both reviewed appellate judgments are vacated so the Court of Appeals can apply independent review to reasonable suspicion and probable cause on the established record, with the qualifications in Part II. This remand neither changes accepted historical findings nor supplies an alternative search justification, additional evidentiary proceeding or immediate plea-withdrawal entitlement.

**Authority:** Part III of the same eight-Justice Opinion of the Court.

**Controlling explanation:** Whether the panel was loose is a historical finding; its significance to an experienced officer deserves due weight; whether that fact and the remaining established circumstances satisfy the constitutional threshold is independently decided. The district judge accepted the remand credibility finding. No new hearing is needed to resolve an invented conflict about it, and neither the rejected rust testimony nor inconclusive scratches becomes additional support by invoking experience. Nor does due weight establish that the NADDIS entries identified petitioners.

Section 636(b)(1)(B) governs a magistrate's suppression recommendation, followed by the district judge's de novo determination of specifically objected-to portions. The judge may accept, reject or modify, receive evidence or recommit. Raddatz distinguishes that determination from an invariably required fresh hearing and reserves the serious question of rejecting dispositive credibility findings without hearing witnesses. Acceptance of the credited loose-panel finding does not present that reserved question. The nondispositive review provision in §636(b)(1)(A) supplies no different final suppression standard, and neither provision fixes appellate review.

For this decision the Court assumes the circuit's limitation on the consent given; it announces no universal consent rule. The existing consent supplies no ground for dismantling, and inevitable discovery was waived. Neither may be revived as an alternative affirmance ground. The database-discovery issue remains excluded.

Rule 11(a)(2) permits withdrawal when a defendant ultimately prevails on the preserved issue. Obtaining a new appellate standard and remand alone does not establish that condition. The Court orders no suppression, release, acquittal, new trial, inspection or additional evidentiary hearing. Proper challenges to historical findings remain governed by ordinary clear-error review and preservation, not new disputes created by this mandate.

## Precedent Treatment

- Miller v. Fenton, 474 U.S. 104: applies functional allocation between historical findings and ultimate constitutional application; its own statutory setting is not transplanted.
- Thompson v. Keohane, November 29, 1995: applies its issue-specific method, not a universal mixed-question rule or its §2254(d) factual presumption and burden.
- First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan, May 22, 1995: preserves ordinary independent legal and clear-error factual review; its arbitration holding does not itself classify suspicion or probable cause.
- Illinois v. Gates, 462 U.S. 213: preserves practical totality analysis and warrant-issuance substantial-basis review; distinguishes that reviewing relationship from this nonwarrant appellate inquiry.
- Brinegar v. United States, 338 U.S. 160: preserves the practical-probability character of probable cause without treating it as conclusive on appellate allocation.
- United States v. Sokolow, 490 U.S. 1: preserves objective totality assessment of reasonable suspicion; its substantive application supplies no previously settled answer to this review question.
- Alabama v. White, 496 U.S. 325: preserves the distinction between reasonable suspicion and the more demanding probable-cause showing without requiring different appellate standards.
- Pierce v. Underwood, 487 U.S. 552: distinguishes its EAJA substantial-justification task; comparative advantage and limited generalizability remain relevant functional considerations.
- Cooter & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp., 496 U.S. 384: distinguishes its litigation-management allocation while preserving correction of erroneous law and clearly erroneous factual assessment.
- Salve Regina College v. Russell, 499 U.S. 225: applies attention to appellate legal responsibility without converting every mixed question into an independently reviewed one.
- United States v. Raddatz, 447 U.S. 667: preserves the district determination/fresh-hearing distinction and its credibility-rejection reservation; accepted credibility findings do not trigger that reservation here.

Stansbury's objective custody rule remains within its substantive Miranda setting. Markman's trial-allocation holding leaves appellate subsidiary findings open; Sheets and Pinder do not authorize factual redetermination or transfer civil pleading assumptions into these suppression proceedings. No precedent is overruled.

## Law After Decision

Effective May 28, 1996, ultimate reasonable suspicion and probable cause in this nonwarrant appellate setting receive independent review, while historical findings receive clear-error review and grounded contextual inferences receive genuine due weight. The lower court called its ultimate review clear error. Abuse of discretion more precisely describes that rejected deferential mixed-question alternative; clear error remains the factual-review term. Neither label creates an intermediate rule replacing independent ultimate judgment.

The allocation governs otherwise authorized Government suppression appeals as well, without expanding their availability. Section 3731 retains its bar on appeals from suppression orders made after the defendant has been put in jeopardy and before verdict or finding, the United States attorney's certifications of no delay purpose and substantial proof of a material fact, thirty-day filing and diligent prosecution. Its distinct dismissal/new-trial and release provisions, double-jeopardy bar and inapplicable pre-January 2, 1971 savings provision remain unchanged. The present case proceeds through defendants' appeals, not that Government channel.

No habeas factual presumption, clear-and-convincing burden or civil Rule 52 command governs this direct criminal appeal. The ruling does not decide suppression's merits, create facts, restore waived inevitable discovery, enlarge consent or alter Rule 11(a)(2)'s condition for plea withdrawal.

## Separate Writings

Justice Scalia joins Part I but would affirm the reviewed allocation. Courts should independently correct legal definitions and legal-rule errors while deferring to the district court's concrete reasonable-suspicion and probable-cause applications under the circuit's clear-error formulation. Practical probabilities depend heavily on interacting circumstances and trial experience; many applications offer little reusable guidance. Pierce and Cooter & Gell demonstrate why that institutional comparison can favor ultimate deference even when a legal standard is applied.

Thompson's custody question and Salve Regina's state-law exposition do not require the same allocation for every mixed issue. Gates's practical observations remain relevant even though its warrant-issuance test does not directly govern this appeal. Magistrate referral does not eliminate the district judge's institutional responsibility or power to supplement the record.

Scalia regards the majority's combination of independent ultimate review and deference to contextual inferences as unstable: its factual and evaluative parts are often difficult to separate. He would preserve correction of legal errors and clear factual mistakes without independently repeating each final probability estimate. Deference would run to the district court, not a presumption that officers were correct. His response to the majority's warrant-incentive rationale also invokes Leon's distinct treatment of searches under warrants; it supplies no alternative good-faith holding on this search.

His proposed ultimate deference is noncontrolling. He does not decide suppression in the first instance, reopen inevitable discovery, resolve database disclosure or supply an immunity-style reasonable-error defense.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns to the Seventh Circuit for independent review of both preserved ultimate thresholds under Parts II–III. Accepted factual and credibility findings retain clear-error protection, and supported contextual inferences receive genuine due weight. The appellate court must apply the allocation first; the Court prescribes no suppression outcome or new evidentiary hearing. Any later Rule 11(a)(2) withdrawal consequence depends on ultimately prevailing on the preserved issue. Supreme Court merits review is complete, subject to ordinary mandate procedures; no further Supreme Court event is prescribed.
