## June 10, 1996 completed public authority — Degen

Exact public text from the [bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Degen_v_United_States_merits_1996-06-10.md). All 4 decisions used the common June 3 entering-law baseline; no decision supplies intervening law for a same-date peer.

## Event

*Degen v. United States*, 517 U.S. 820, No. 95-173. October Term 1995; argued April 22, 1996; decided June 10, 1996. On certiorari under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) to review the Ninth Circuit's judgment, 47 F.3d 1511, sustaining the District of Nevada's exclusion of Brian Degen's claims and defenses in civil forfeiture. The district ruling is reported at 755 F. Supp. 308. The question is the existence and permissible scope of the court's asserted inherent or supervisory authority to impose that bar because Brian has not returned for a related criminal prosecution.

Brian is a dual United States and Swiss citizen who left before indictment. He disputes an intent to evade prosecution at departure; the Government and lower court rely on his later knowing refusal to return. The extradition treaty does not require a party to surrender its own nationals. The Government seeks forfeiture of real and personal property in California, Nevada and Hawaii as alleged drug proceeds or facilitating property. The court controls that property and can enforce its eventual judgment. Brian timely filed verified claims and answers through counsel, denying substantive forfeiture allegations and raising defenses including limitations, retroactivity and probable cause. Neither indictment nor absence establishes guilt or the merits of the property dispute.

The District Court struck Brian's claim in December 1990. The Ninth Circuit approved the bar, identifying but treating as waived his objection to the District Court's mistaken view that disentitlement was mandatory rather than discretionary. That subsidiary preservation ruling is distinct from the preserved challenge to the asserted power. Karyn Degen's claims initially survived; her later failure to oppose a supported renewed summary-judgment motion, after extensions and reopened discovery, produced a separate judgment and affirmance. She did not seek this review.

Swiss authorities arrested Brian in November 1992. The Ninth Circuit refused supplementation with Justice Department correspondence and rejected the inadequately developed contention that Swiss custody ended fugitivity. Here the Government acknowledges the correspondence's authenticity and its request for Swiss prosecution principally concerning the same conduct, correcting its misleading descriptions below. The parties dispute preservation, the consequences of custody, unclean hands and responsibility for the deficient record. These admitted developments establish neither present freedom nor impossibility of return.

The governing forfeiture provisions retain separate coverage and conditions:

- Section 881(a)(6) covers money, negotiable instruments, securities or other things of value furnished or intended for a prohibited controlled-substance exchange, traceable proceeds, and money, negotiable instruments and securities used or intended to facilitate a covered violation. Its facilitating-property clause is not extended to all property.
- Section 881(a)(7) covers real-property interests, including leaseholds, in the whole lot or tract and its appurtenances or improvements, used or intended, in any manner or part, to commit or facilitate a covered offense punishable by more than one year's imprisonment.
- Each paragraph protects the extent of an owner's interest for an act or omission that the owner establishes occurred without that owner's knowledge or consent. The Court determines no claimant's satisfaction of those qualifications.
- Section 881(d) incorporates customs forfeiture procedures insofar as applicable and consistent. Under the incorporated §1615 burden rule, the Government must first show probable cause for instituting the action, to be judged by the court, before the claimant bears the statutory burden. No new probable-cause or property-liability finding follows from this decision.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision. No case-specific nonparticipation is established.

## Public Action

The Court reverses the Ninth Circuit's judgment insofar as it sustains Brian's categorical civil-defense bar and remands for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Judgment:** Reversed and remanded, 9–0, on the reviewed defense-bar issue.

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer.

Brian must receive a lawful opportunity to contest forfeiture without the rejected categorical exclusion. The dependent forfeiture result cannot rest on that exclusion. The Court decides no merits defense or separate sufficient ground outside this review and leaves Karyn's judgment and the criminal and Swiss proceedings undisturbed. No immediate property return, payment, damages, compensation, release, criminal dismissal or stay is ordered.

## Opinion Topology

Justice Scalia delivers the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine join its inherent-power ground, conditional-management limits and reversal/remand. No separate opinion is filed.

## Holdings

**Common authority:** Scalia's unanimous Opinion of the Court supplies nine direct joins for Holdings I–III, their explanations and qualifications. No constitutional alternative holding, partial join or combination of separate rationales is involved.

### I. The asserted inherent power does not support this complete defense bar

**Operative rule:** When the court controls the forfeiture property and can enforce its eventual judgment, a claimant's failure to return for a related criminal prosecution alone does not justify striking his timely civil-forfeiture claims and defenses. Inherent authority must respond reasonably to the actual need provoking its exercise; this complete exclusion lacks the necessary connection and justification in the forfeiture proceeding.

**Controlling explanation:** The existence of inherent authority does not establish the permissible extent of a particular sanction. *Chambers v. NASCO* recognizes power to protect judicial proceedings while requiring restraint. *Ortega-Rodriguez v. United States* requires a sufficient connection to appellate proceedings in its preappeal-flight setting. That connection principle informs this case without transferring its particular appellate rule wholesale to civil forfeiture.

The court controls the property and can enforce its judgment. Brian filed timely verified claims and answers through counsel. His physical absence does not create the enforcement difficulty that can support disentitlement in a criminal appeal. Denying affirmative appellate assistance also differs from foreclosing a defense to the Government's requested property deprivation.

The Government identifies genuine concerns: civil discovery could circumvent criminal restrictions, absence could impede litigation, and selective submission to judicial authority can undermine deterrence and judicial dignity. But anticipated misuse is not an established discovery violation or inevitable inability to adjudicate. Those interests do not justify this excessively blunt and arbitrary exclusion. Refusal to return supplies neither drug guilt nor forfeiture liability. Courts retain the conditional tools discussed below to address supported litigation problems.

*McVeigh*, *Hovey*, *Hammond Packing* and *Societe Internationale* distinguish an opportunity to defend from punitive exclusion and properly grounded litigation sanctions or evidentiary consequences. *United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property* separately protects process in its real-property seizure setting. These considerations reinforce restraint, but the sufficient ground here is the scope of the inherent power asserted. The Court does not decide Congress's constitutional ability to authorize a different disentitlement rule or whether enforcing a rule supplied under proper authority would violate due process. No present statute authorizes this categorical sanction. Conversely, the decision does not require a fresh express enactment for every inherited judicial power or abolish criminal-appellate disentitlement within its actual scope.

**Precedent treatment:** *Chambers*' restrained sanction authority survives; *Ortega-Rodriguez* supplies the proceeding-connection analogy. The hearing and sanction precedents retain their distinctions without a new independent constitutional holding.

### II. Lawful management and properly supported sanctions remain available

**Operative rule:** The District Court may address a supported litigation problem through applicable statutes, Rules and bounded inherent authority, subject to each source's predicates, process and justified scope. This decision neither establishes those predicates nor orders a stay, protective order, proof restriction or sanction, and it imposes no universal exhaustion, mandatory sequencing or least-restrictive-means requirement.

**Controlling explanation:** Under 21 U.S.C. §881(i), filing an indictment or information alleging a violation of the federal drug provisions in subchapter I or II—or a state or local violation chargeable under those provisions—shall stay a related §881 civil-forfeiture proceeding upon a United States motion and good cause shown. The qualifying charge, relationship, Government motion and good cause are separate conditions. None is found satisfied here; an indefinite stay pending a prosecution that cannot begin is not presumed adequate.

Rule 26(c) permits supported discovery protection. Courts may also control the form of proof and, in an extreme justified case, permissible theories to prevent improper exploitation of the civil/criminal asymmetry. Those possibilities do not authorize eliminating an identified defense now. If absence produces noncompliance with a legitimate pleading, discovery or evidence order, ordinary sanctions remain possible, including dismissal when appropriate under Rules 37 or 41(b), or properly bounded inherent authority. The actual source, predicate, notice and process, and scope must support the response. Perjury, discovery refusal, contempt, fraudulent transfer or other established misconduct gains no immunity from a lawfully tailored sanction.

*Carlisle v. United States* preserves inherent power while rejecting its use to supply relief that specific Rules foreclose. *Kokkonen v. Guardian Life* likewise connects authority to its function; this court, unlike the postdismissal court there, already has jurisdiction. *Quackenbush v. Allstate* requires authority for the remedy actually used without treating the availability of a different conditional remedy as sufficient. These decisions do not create a default or compel one management sequence here. The available tools explain why categorical exclusion is unjustified without guaranteeing that every future difficulty has an easy solution or requiring courts to await completed abuse before taking justified preventive action.

**Precedent treatment:** *Carlisle*, *Kokkonen* and *Quackenbush* retain their distinct source-and-function limits; none is converted into either a general denial of inherent power or an automatic forfeiture sanction.

### III. Reversal restores an opportunity to defend, not entitlement to the property

**Operative rule:** The Ninth Circuit's judgment is reversed insofar as it sustains striking Brian's claims and defenses on the asserted disentitlement ground, and the case is remanded for lawful further proceedings. The dependent forfeiture result cannot stand on that bar; no merits defense, independent sufficient ground outside this review, ownership right or entitlement to return is adjudicated.

**Controlling explanation:** The legal defect is the categorical exclusion from defending this civil action. Reversal removes that exclusion rather than deciding whether Brian succeeds on limitations, retroactivity, innocent ownership, probable cause or another defense. Section 881's separate forfeiture categories and owner protections remain operative. Through §881(d)'s qualified incorporation, §1615 requires the Government's antecedent probable-cause showing before placing the statutory burden on the claimant. The Court neither newly finds probable cause nor declares an otherwise established showing absent.

The preserved power question can be resolved even assuming the Government's fugitive characterization for this inquiry. The Court need not determine Brian's status in every disputed sense, his present ability to return from Switzerland, unclean hands or responsibility for the disputed record deficiencies. Nor does the Court overturn the Ninth Circuit's adverse preservation treatment of the separate objection to calling disentitlement mandatory.

Karyn's separate judgment is outside this review. Her failure to oppose the renewed summary-judgment motion directed to her claims is not Brian's misconduct. The criminal prosecution and Swiss proceedings remain undisturbed. *Republic National Bank v. United States* preserves lawful effectual relief and a conditional return/payment route upon a sufficient judgment; procedural success here supplies no immediate property return or payment. No damages, compensation, criminal dismissal, release, stay, new evidentiary hearing or full retrial is ordered. The District Court must proceed under existing lawful forfeiture procedure, without the rejected bar and without any promise that Brian will prevail.

**Precedent treatment:** *Republic National Bank* retains its conditional jurisdiction and return/payment rules; *Good* supplies no automatic dismissal, title transfer or compensation remedy.

## Precedent Treatment

- *Chambers v. NASCO, Inc.*, 501 U.S. 32, retains genuine, restrained litigation-sanction authority. Recognition of that power does not establish the scope or necessity of this bar.
- *Ortega-Rodriguez v. United States*, 507 U.S. 234, supplies by analogy the required connection between a sanction and the proceeding it protects. Its preappeal-flight rule, actual-disruption qualifications and absence of a least-restrictive-sanction requirement remain intact. Criminal-appellate disentitlement is not abolished.
- *McVeigh v. United States*, *Hovey v. Elliott*, *Hammond Packing Co. v. Arkansas* and *Societe Internationale v. Rogers* retain their distinctions between opportunity to defend, punitive exclusion and justified litigation sanctions or evidentiary consequences. They inform the limit on inherent power without supplying an independent constitutional disposition here.
- *United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property*, 510 U.S. 43, retains its meaningful prior-process rule for civil seizure of real property, its justified-exigency qualification and its separate refusal to infer an unstated dismissal sanction from administrative timing duties. Its exigency inquiry does not become a universal sanction test.
- *Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America*, 511 U.S. 375, retains the need for an actual jurisdictional basis to enforce a separate settlement after dismissal. This pending forfeiture already lies within the court's jurisdiction; the analogy concerns function and extent, not absence of jurisdiction.
- *Carlisle v. United States*, April 29, 1996, preserves inherent powers while barring circumvention of the specific Rules controlling the same relief. No identical Rule 29 conflict is found here, and its dissent's distinct retained pre-sentence duty supplies no civil-defense sanction.
- *Quackenbush v. Allstate Insurance Co.*, June 3, 1996, preserves its source-specific abstention/remedy boundary. An otherwise available conditional remedy neither validates the act actually ordered nor proves the alternative's predicates.
- *Republic National Bank of Miami v. United States*, 506 U.S. 80, preserves jurisdiction when lawful effectual relief remains possible and its conditional statutory return/payment route; it supplies no immediate return or money judgment upon this procedural reversal.

## Law After Decision

Effective June 10, 1996, the court's asserted inherent power does not authorize this complete forfeiture-defense bar solely because Brian has not returned for the related criminal prosecution, where property control and judgment enforcement are secure. The holding adds that civil-forfeiture limit without changing the statutory forfeiture categories, owner protections, burdens or properly supported litigation sanctions.

Statutes and Rules may constrain or override inherent powers; the Court does not require fresh express legislation for every inherited power. It reserves both Congress's constitutional ability to authorize a different disentitlement rule and the due-process validity of enforcing a rule supplied under proper authority. No later statute supplies present authority. The judgment establishes no universal constitutional invalidity of disentitlement, new fugitive definition, general appellate-review standard, or mandatory sequence of lesser measures.

The Swiss status and preservation disputes, merits of the property defenses, and the separate mandatory-versus-discretionary preservation ruling are not resolved anew. The Court's rejection of this categorical bar does not immunize actual misconduct or withdraw otherwise lawful preventive management supported by a real litigation problem.

## Separate Writings

No separate writing is filed.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns through the Ninth Circuit for lawful further forfeiture proceedings concerning Brian without the rejected defense bar. Properly available requests for discovery protection, a statutory stay or a supported sanction remain subject to their own legal conditions; no request is presumed made or meritorious and no new default is found. The Court prescribes no evidentiary hearing, full retrial or particular resolution of a defense.

Karyn's separate judgment and Brian's criminal and Swiss proceedings remain undisturbed. Eventual return of property or proceeds requires a legally sufficient entitlement and applicable return or payment authority; this reversal supplies neither. Supreme Court merits review of the power issue is complete, subject to ordinary mandate procedures.

## June 10, 1996 completed public authority — Exxon

Exact public text from the [bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Exxon_Co_USA_v_Sofec_Inc_merits_1996-06-10.md). All 4 decisions used the common June 3 entering-law baseline; no decision supplies intervening law for a same-date peer.

## Event

*Exxon Co., U.S.A. v. Sofec, Inc.*, No. 95-129, 517 U.S. 830. Argued March 19, 1996; decided June 10, 1996. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, 54 F.3d 570, which affirmed a Rule 54(b) judgment against Exxon for stranding-related damages after the first phase of a maritime bench trial.

The submitted questions concern whether comparative maritime fault abolished superseding cause and whether Exxon may recover the stranding loss under the asserted contractual warranties. A separate challenge to this particular bifurcation as an abuse of discretion or denial of due process is outside the questions presented. Claims concerning oil spilled when the vessel broke from its mooring remain pending.

The tanker broke free during severe conditions. A connected hose continued to cause concern, but the district court found that by 6:30 p.m. the vessel had reached a safe position from which it could continue backing out. The master failed for an extended period to plot position fixes, failed to use available personnel, and began the final shoreward turn without knowing the vessel's position. Both lower courts characterized that navigation as extraordinary, independent and unforeseeable, and as the superseding and sole proximate cause of the stranding. Exxon contests the legal consequences and argues that grounding remained within the original risk.

For phase one, Exxon was relieved of proving defendants' fault or strict liability for the breakout, which was assumed to contribute in fact to the sequence. That collective premise did not establish each respondent's negligence, breach, corporate obligation or share of responsibility.

The safe-berth undertaking promised a berth to which vessels could proceed or depart and where they could always lie safely afloat; an amendment included single point mooring. Its express exclusion denied any warranty of the safety of public channels, fairways, their approaches, anchorages and other publicly maintained areas inside or outside the port. No finding places the grounding within that exclusion. The lower court quoted the agreement in relevant part, without establishing every term of the complete executed agreement.

Joint Trial Exhibit 92 is a separate General Instructions, Discharging/Loading Orders and Indemnification instrument. Its service-personnel provisions treat the supplied mooring master, tug and launch operators and crews, and vessels as servants of the vessel and owners while rendering services, and provide indemnity for resulting liabilities, losses, claims or damages whether or not arising from the stated personnel's or indemnitees' fault. The master's legal responsibilities and final decisions remain expressly his. The lower court qualified imputation where the same conduct breached the safe-berth undertaking; the complete interaction of the two instruments is not decided here.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participated at argument and decision.

## Public Action

The judgment of the Court of Appeals is affirmed.

## Judgment & Remedy

| Judgment component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Remedy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tort and comparative-fault claim for stranding damages | Affirmed, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Judgment against Exxon remains in force; no apportionment or remand. |
| Submitted safe-berth and workmanlike-service warranty claim for the same loss | Affirmed, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Judgment against Exxon remains in force on the distinct contractual causation ground; no contract-construction proceeding is ordered. |

No damages award, contribution order, allocation percentage, new hearing or individual corporate-liability determination is entered. The untried breakout oil-spill claims are not disposed of.

## Opinion Topology

Justice Stevens delivers the opinion of the unanimous Court. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join Parts I–V in full. The same coalition supplies authority for every holding below. No separate opinion is filed.

## Holdings

### I. Review of the legal rule and the concurrent causation findings

**Holding and operative rule.** The Court independently reviews the governing legal rule while protecting historical findings under Rule 52. Application of proximate and superseding cause to the found circumstances ordinarily rests with the factfinder subject to limited review; under *Graver Tank*, concurrent lower-court findings are not disturbed without a very obvious and exceptional showing of error, which Exxon has not made here.

**Authority.** Part I of Justice Stevens's opinion, joined by the full Court.

**Controlling explanation.** *Graver Tank & Manufacturing Co. v. Linde Air Products Co.* supplies the restrained treatment of concurrent findings. It does not immunize a mistaken legal definition, require acceptance of unsupported new facts, or establish a universal standard for every mixed question of law and fact. *Ornelas v. United States* assigns independent ultimate review in its particular Fourth Amendment setting and expressly supplies no contrary universal rule.

The distinction matters here. Exxon identifies tension between the continuing hose concern and the finding that safety had been restored. The Court acknowledges that tension and its relevance to the claimed continuation of the original peril. The safe-position finding, available time and personnel, missing fixes and final turn remain findings made below. The lower courts nevertheless agreed that the navigation was independent and unforeseeable. The required exceptional showing for disturbing their causal conclusion has not been made. Leaving that conclusion undisturbed does not necessarily ratify their particular application of the doctrine.

The Court does not independently recalculate the navigational sequence or add an alternative holding that fresh appellate review would produce the same causal result. Nor does it adopt HIRI's asserted abandonment of a factual challenge as a separate waiver ground.

### II. Comparative fault does not abolish legal causation

**Holding and operative rule.** Comparative maritime fault apportions a loss among actors who legally caused it; a later independent and unforeseeable cause may supersede an earlier factual contribution. A plaintiff whose conduct is the superseding and sole proximate cause cannot recover part of that loss merely because others' blameworthy conduct helped produce the sequence in fact.

**Authority.** Part II, joined by the full Court.

**Controlling explanation.** *United States v. Reliable Transfer Co.* replaced automatic equal division of maritime collision or stranding damages with proportional allocation when multiple parties' fault contributes legally to the loss. Equal division remains when fault is equal or cannot fairly be measured. The decision changed allocation; it did not eliminate the antecedent requirement of legal causation.

Its rejection of the major-minor doctrine remains important. A court cannot excuse one legally contributing actor merely because another was much more negligent. Severity of fault alone therefore does not establish supersession. The later conduct must have the independence and unforeseeability necessary to break the legal causal connection. Ordinary foreseeable efforts to escape the first actor's danger do not automatically have that effect, and the Court does not hold that grounding can never be a foreseeable consequence of a mooring failure.

*McDermott, Inc. v. AmClyde* and *Boca Grande Club, Inc. v. Florida Power & Light Co.* require reliable allocation for their settlement-credit and contribution rules after legal responsibility is established. They do not make every factual contributor liable. *City of Milwaukee v. Cement Division, National Gypsum Co.* concerns prejudgment interest on a compensable loss and likewise presupposes liability.

The Court retains the term comparative fault without deciding whether allocation should reflect comparative culpability alone or also relative causal contribution, assuming a meaningful distinction exists. No settlement-credit, contribution-protection or prejudgment-interest rule changes.

### III. Consequence of the undisturbed tort-causation determination

**Holding and operative rule.** The undisturbed finding that Exxon's navigation was the superseding and sole proximate cause defeats tort recovery for the stranding loss. No comparative allocation is required because the accepted determination leaves no other legally operative cause of that injury.

**Authority.** Part III, joined by the full Court.

**Controlling explanation.** The mooring failure explains the initial emergency and remains an assumed factual contributor. The lower courts relied on the later safe position, available opportunity to depart and assistance, and the master's final navigation as separating the stranding from that original peril. Their analysis thus purported to identify an independent causal intervention rather than merely compare degrees of negligence or count elapsed time.

Exxon's strongest contrary argument, supported by its invocation of Restatement §442B and *Kinsman*, is that the later navigation and grounding remained within the risk created by the breakout. That objection prevents a categorical rule treating every negligent emergency response as superseding. The continuing hose concern makes the application contestable; the Court does not declare that concern nonexistent or independently find complete freedom from danger. Under Part I's limited review, however, the lower courts' concurrent ultimate conclusion remains undisturbed.

The legally permissible distinction between factual contribution and legal responsibility therefore sustains this tort judgment. Phase one's assumed fault or strict liability does not become a finding that respondents were blameless, that every respondent breached a duty, or that an already established comparative share has been extinguished. No present percentage or fresh finding about each respondent is needed.

### IV. Contractual warranties require their own causal connection to recoverable loss

**Holding and operative rule.** Contractual duties may exceed negligence duties, but recovery under the submitted safe-berth and workmanlike-service warranties still requires legal causation of the claimed loss. Assuming the stricter undertaking and relevant breach, the undisturbed determination that Exxon's navigation alone proximately caused the stranding defeats recovery of that loss without deciding strict warranty versus due diligence.

**Authority.** Part IV, joined by the full Court.

**Controlling explanation.** *Italia Societa per Azioni di Navigazione v. Oregon Stevedoring Co.* recognizes breach of workmanlike service through nonnegligently supplied defective equipment. It does not remove the causal limitation on warranty damages. *East River Steamship Corp. v. Transamerica Delaval Inc.* and contract foreseeability principles distinguish promised performance from the losses recoverable for its breach. Contractual causation can be more restrictive in some circumstances; the Court does not hold that it is always stricter than, or categorically identical to, tort causation.

The asserted strict promise is assumed, not replaced with a duty of reasonable care. The district court chose due diligence before finding no post-breakout breach. Exxon's concession that diligence was satisfied does not concede performance of a stricter promise; the Court of Appeals expressly reserved that choice. The safe-departure and available-assistance findings retain causal significance independently of the disputed duty standard. Under the undisturbed sole-proximate-cause determination, an assumed breach contributing only in fact does not establish the causal connection required for these warranty damages.

The duty continued after breakout: an earlier superseding force cannot by itself excuse a later breach. That later-breach theory is subject to the contractual causal requirement rather than erased through the diligence concession. Neither the clause's public-area exclusion nor blanket imputation or indemnity under Exhibit 92 supplies an alternative holding. Their complete interaction and individual corporate responsibility remain reserved. No unquoted promise insuring every later navigational loss is inferred, nor is an unquoted exclusion invented.

HIRI's avoidable-consequences contention need not be decided as an independently sufficient ground that every stranding-loss item was wholly avoidable. The holding creates neither automatic forfeiture for ordinary promisee negligence nor a rule that mitigation must always be proportional. A materially different express allocation of later losses would require consideration of its own supported terms and preserved theory.

### V. The limited bifurcation issue and the stranding-only judgment

**Holding and operative rule.** Comparative fault does not invariably require assessment of every party's relative fault before a court can determine a genuinely superseding cause. The phase-one assumptions permit that antecedent inquiry here; the separate claim that this particular bifurcation was an abuse of discretion or denied due process is not decided.

**Authority.** Part V, joined by the full Court.

**Controlling explanation.** Legal responsibility precedes apportionment. Because phase one assumed factual contribution and relieved Exxon of proving defendants' fault or strict liability for the breakout, the submitted legal-causation questions could be decided on that basis. This rejects a categorical legal bar to separate consideration, not every objection to the management of this trial.

Supreme Court Rules 14.1(a) and 24.1(a) preserve the question limits. *Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. v. Calhoun* addresses issues within a certified interlocutory order, and *Quackenbush v. Allstate Insurance Co.* addresses appealability and abstention; neither enlarges the questions submitted here. The exclusion of a free-standing bifurcation challenge does not erase Exxon's argument that the available evidence was insufficient to resolve the submitted issues. That argument has been considered within their actual scope.

The affirmed Rule 54(b) judgment concerns stranding damages alone. No further contract-construction proceeding, allocation, hearing or damages determination is required by this decision. The breakout oil-spill proceedings retain their existing posture and undecided liability and damages issues.

## Precedent Treatment

- *Reliable Transfer* is applied as a comparative-allocation rule that preserves legal causation, its equal-fault and unmeasurable-fault exception, and its rejection of the major-minor shortcut.
- *Graver Tank* supplies limited review of concurrent lower-court findings; the Court does not convert that practice into immunity from review for legal error.
- *Italia Societa* retains warranty responsibility beyond negligence but does not eliminate legal causation of contract damages.
- *East River* supports the distinct treatment of contractual responsibility and recoverable loss; no universal equivalence between contractual and tort causation is adopted.
- *McDermott* and *Boca Grande* retain their settlement-credit and contribution-protection rules, including the need for reliable allocation where those rules operate.
- *City of Milwaukee* retains its rule governing compensatory prejudgment interest on otherwise recoverable loss; no compensable principal is created here.
- *Ornelas* remains confined to its stated review setting, without establishing universal independent review of mixed questions.
- *Yamaha* retains its certified-order review rule and reservations concerning causation and liability standards; it supplies no broader certiorari scope.
- *Quackenbush* retains its appealability and abstention holdings; the obligation to adjudicate a contract claim does not guarantee recovery or expand these questions.

## Law After Decision

Comparative maritime fault and superseding cause remain complementary. Courts identify legal responsibility before allocating loss, and relative severity of negligence alone cannot remove an otherwise operative legal cause. The accepted sole-proximate-cause determination therefore leaves no stranding loss to apportion among these defendants.

The submitted warranty claims fail on their separately examined contractual causation requirement, even assuming the stricter duty and breach. The decision does not adopt due diligence as the meaning of the safe-berth promise, adjudicate wholesale avoidability, comprehensively construe Exhibit 92, excuse later breaches through an earlier superseding event, or determine any related corporation's individual obligation. The particular causal application remains undisturbed under limited review without necessarily being ratified in every respect.

## Separate Writings

No separate opinion is filed.

## Procedure After Action

The Ninth Circuit's judgment sustaining the stranding-related Rule 54(b) judgment is affirmed. Ordinary mandate procedures apply; no special mandate date, remand, new hearing, apportionment or further Supreme Court event is ordered. The pending breakout oil-spill claims and their unadjudicated liability and damages issues remain for the proceedings below.

The judgment relies on the supported submitted undertakings, assumed stricter duty and preserved causal findings; it does not decide a theory requiring an additional unprovided risk-allocation term.

Richards, Whren, Degen and Exxon completed the chunk 7 Court actions scheduled for June 10. Those four decisions and the subsequently entered IBM and Spink decisions all use the complete June 3 entering-law baseline; none supplies precedent to a same-date peer. All nine admitted sources retain their actual dates, conditions and unresolved applications. No unrecorded Court or lower-court action is inferred.

All twelve chunk 7 events are complete. IBM and Spink are now also completed June 10 events, as projected below. The preserved pre-June10 projection and public chronology clarification remain their common entering-law sources. The clarification preserves Smiley’s qualified antecedent-transaction holding without changing the OCC rule’s April 1 effectiveness; the source qualifications and public procedural limits remain in force.

## Utah H.B. 206 — April 29 source insertion

Utah H.B. 206, effective April 29, 1996, enacts the specified postviability procedure restrictions in section 76-7-310.5, with individualized viability and the exception when all other available procedures risk life or health; it separately amends sections 314 and 315 and confines its viability method to section 310.5. Its effect on the earlier sections 307–308 and pending litigation remains contested. Admission supplies no judicial construction, injunction change or enforcement authorization.

[Controlling source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Utah_HB206_admitted_source_1996-04-29.md).

## Event

Utah H.B. 206, Chapter 267, Laws of Utah 1996. Enacted noncase law reported effective April 29, 1996; the enrolled text accompanies the March 27 supplemental filing in Leavitt v. Jane L., No. 95-1242. The Act adds section 76-7-310.5, amends sections 76-7-314 and 76-7-315, and states a separate legislative-intent limit.

## Participation

This is a legislative source, not a judicial vote.

## Public Action

No action of the Court is entered by the enactment's inclusion in the pending case materials.

## Judgment & Remedy

No judicial judgment, injunction modification or remedy follows from source admission.

## Opinion Topology

No judicial opinion accompanies this legislative source.

## Holdings

The Act creates no holding of the Court. Its text prohibits knowing performance of the defined procedures after viability is determined under section 310.5, unless all other available abortion procedures would risk the woman's life or health. The section uses a physician's best clinical judgment based on the known particular pregnancy facts and reasonably available medical technology and information, assessing a realistic possibility of life outside the womb with or without temporary artificial support. Its definition of dilation and extraction excludes dismemberment before removal, suction curettage and suction aspiration. Its own third-degree-felony clause requires intentional, knowing and willful violation.

Amended section 314 separately retains intentional unauthorized-abortion liability, the pregnant woman's exemption from criminal liability for her own abortion, willful-violation penalties for the listed sections including sections 307, 308 and new 310.5, and misdemeanor treatment of other violations. Amended section 315 makes sections 302, 304(2), 305(2) and 310.5 inapplicable when a serious medical emergency leaves no time to comply. Section 4 confines the new viability method to section 310.5 and its purposes and disclaims effects on other statutory provisions and their litigation.

## Precedent Treatment

No judicial precedent is changed by admission of the enactment.

## Law After Decision

The new text is relevant noncase law within its specified scope. Its constitutional validity, relation to existing injunctions, and alleged implied repeal of other provisions remain undecided.

## Separate Writings

No judicial separate writing is associated with this source.

## Procedure After Action

The pending Leavitt petition remains pending. The statute neither supplies a grant of review nor adjudicates mootness, the scope of the petition questions, or the legality of enforcement.

## Source Notes

The complete enrolled text is reproduced in the [March 27 supplemental brief, appendix 1b–3b](https://archive.org/download/micro_IA40385013_0692/micro_IA40385013_0692%205.%20Supplemental%20Brief.pdf). The brief reports passage on February 28, signature on March 18 and effectiveness on April 29, 1996. Its arguments about repeal and mootness are distinct from the enrolled language and from an adjudicated legal consequence.

## Event

**United States v. International Business Machines Corp., 517 U.S. 843, No. 95-591 — June 10, 1996.** Argued March 18, 1996, on certiorari to the Federal Circuit. The question is whether the Export Clause permits application of the general foreign-insurance premium tax in 26 U.S.C. §4371 to insurance of goods in export transit.

For 1975–1984, IBM paid assessments concerning foreign policies covering its exported products and sought refunds. The Federal Circuit, 59 F.3d 1234, affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' ruling that this application was unconstitutional. The policies attach to identified shipments; their premiums reflect both cargo value and shipment-specific risks. Section 4371 is not confined to exports.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate. Justice Stevens takes no part in consideration or decision.

## Public Action

The Federal Circuit's judgment is affirmed.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Affirmed, 6–2.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Breyer.

**Opposing:** Kennedy, Ginsburg.

The judgment requiring refund of the challenged unconstitutional assessments stands within the claim and amount properly preserved. The Court neither determines a new refund amount nor invalidates section 4371 in all its applications.

## Opinion Topology

Justice Thomas delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Souter and Breyer. Justice Kennedy dissents, joined by Justice Ginsburg.

## Holdings

**Authority:** Thomas's opinion, with the six direct joins identified above, controls the rule, application and limits below.

### The general tax cannot reach this export-transit insurance

**Operative rule:** A federal tax on goods in export transit does not escape the Export Clause merely because it applies without discrimination to other transactions. Thames & Mersey remains controlling for premiums on insurance of goods during that transit, so section 4371 cannot be applied to the insurance at issue here; the rule does not exempt every activity or expense that indirectly affects exporting.

**Controlling explanation:** The Constitution expressly forbids federal taxes or duties on articles exported from a State. Fairbank protects export bills of lading, and Hvoslef protects charter arrangements for export carriage; those cases prevent taxation of the protected export transaction through its integral documents. Thames & Mersey directly applies that protection to insurance of goods during the export voyage.

The Government's contrary argument rests on nondiscrimination and changes in other tax doctrines. Those doctrines answer different constitutional questions. Michelin concerns the States' Import-Export restriction and goods no longer in transit. Washington Stevedoring concerns a service tax and reserves direct taxation of goods in transit. Neither converts the federal Export Clause into a prohibition only of discriminatory taxes. Itel preserves the direct-export question while sustaining a distinct local container transaction; Jefferson Lines concerns a local retail sale under the Commerce Clause. Fulton requires comparison of actual taxable events within that Clause, rather than transferring its standard to different constitutional text.

The insurance here covers the identified outward shipments. Risk as well as cargo value affects the premium, but that does not distinguish the export-insurance category already decided in Thames & Mersey. The Government's asserted interclause developments do not justify overruling that directly applicable precedent. Its decision to press nondiscrimination, while declining to advance a separate goods-versus-services challenge, also counsels against undertaking a comprehensive reconsideration of that boundary here. An included legal argument may be considered; the Court is not required to decide it.

The Court retains the distinction between taxing exports and imposing ordinary burdens before exportation or on genuinely distinct or tangential activities. It leaves fuller classification of other services open. Applying the existing insurance rule is sufficient to preserve this refund judgment.

## Precedent Treatment

- **Thames & Mersey Marine Insurance Co. v. United States, 237 U.S. 19:** Retained and applied to export-transit insurance; its directly governing rule is not displaced by nondiscrimination alone.
- **Fairbank v. United States, 181 U.S. 283:** Applied as the export-document precedent supporting the Clause's protection of the export transaction.
- **United States v. Hvoslef, 237 U.S. 1:** Applied as the export-carriage precedent supporting the Clause's protection of the export transaction.
- **Michelin Tire Corp. v. Wages, 423 U.S. 276:** Distinguished by its state-tax setting and goods outside export transit; it does not replace the federal Clause's rule.
- **Department of Revenue v. Association of Washington Stevedoring Cos., 435 U.S. 734:** Distinguished as a service-tax decision reserving direct goods-in-transit taxation.
- **Itel Containers International Corp. v. Huddleston:** Distinguished by the separate local container transaction and its reserved direct-export question.
- **Oklahoma Tax Commission v. Jefferson Lines, Inc.:** Its transaction-specific Commerce Clause rule remains effective in its own setting and supplies no federal Export Clause transformation.
- **Fulton Corp. v. Faulkner:** Its transaction-specific Commerce Clause rule remains effective in its own setting and supplies no federal Export Clause transformation.
- **Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp.:** Its permission to consider an included argument remains discretionary. The Court announces no new review-scope restriction.

## Law After Decision

The Export Clause continues to protect the export-insurance application governed by Thames & Mersey even under a generally applicable, nondiscriminatory federal tax. No comprehensive immunity for export-related services or incidental exporter costs is adopted. No earlier decision is overruled.

## Separate Writings

**Kennedy, joined by Ginsburg, dissenting.** The dissent would reach the narrower argument that the tax falls on a purchased indemnity service rather than the exported articles. Itel and Jefferson Lines illustrate the need to identify the actual taxable transaction. The stipulated premium reflects shipment risks as well as cargo value; that relationship does not make the service identical to the goods. The dissent would expressly overrule Thames & Mersey to the extent its commercial-integration rationale treats this genuine insurance-premium tax as a tax on exports.

The dissent regards the narrower issue as fairly included in the question presented and sufficiently supported by the stipulated record despite the Government's emphasis on nondiscrimination. It would reverse and remand without validating all export-associated taxes, creating a nondiscrimination safe harbor for an actual goods tax, or determining a new assessment amount. Its service classification does not command a majority.

## Procedure After Action

The refund judgment remains in force subject to ordinary mandate procedures. No new trial, tax computation or further Supreme Court proceeding is ordered.

## Source Notes

The record and litigation positions are supported by the [Federal Circuit opinion](https://static.case.law/f3d/59/cases/1234-01.json) and the [petition and party briefs](https://archive.org/details/micro_IA40385013_0659). The applicable insurance-tax terms are those governing the 1975–1984 assessments; later statutory exemptions are not substituted. Reported argument statements establish the described presentation limits without resolving any unpresented exemption or computation question.

## Event

**Lockheed Corp. v. Spink, 517 U.S. 882, No. 95-809 — June 10, 1996.** Argued April 22, 1996, on certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 60 F.3d 616. The questions concern fiduciary status and prohibited transactions under an amended pension plan offering enhanced retirement benefits for employment-related releases, and OBRA's application to earlier uncredited service.

Spink returned to Lockheed in 1979 at age 61 and was then lawfully excluded from its plan. He entered on December 25, 1988, the first day of the relevant plan year. He declined a 1990 enhanced-retirement offer because he would not release his claims. The complaint distinguishes sponsor adoption from Retirement Committee implementation; its allegations are accepted at the dismissal stage, not found after trial. The Ninth Circuit reinstated Counts I–III while leaving independent loyalty and anti-inurement grounds unaddressed and awarding appellate fees.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision.

## Public Action

The reviewed adverse portions of the judgment are reversed and the case is remanded. The appellate fee award is vacated for reconsideration.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Reversed and remanded, 9–0 overall.** All nine named participants support that disposition, with the following component differences.

| Component | Disposition and support |
|---|---|
| Fiduciary liability based solely on sponsor design/adoption | Rejected, 9–0: all nine. The theory resting solely on amendment is dismissed. |
| Section 406(a)(1)(D) release-payment classification | The reviewed per se theory is rejected by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg, seven. Souter and Breyer oppose deciding that question now and would remand it without a merits answer. |
| Counts I–II, asserted OBRA credit for the earlier lawful nonparticipation period | Reinstatement reversed and dismissal restored, 9–0. Stone-Zsela agrees with the disposition without adding a ground. |
| Preserved independent Count III alternatives | Returned for consideration under their own elements, consistently with the decided holdings; all nine. No unconditional dismissal of Count III or finding of breach follows. |
| Appellate fees | Award vacated for reconsideration, 9–0. Stone-Zsela agrees with the disposition without adding a ground. No amount is fixed. |

Count V's dismissal and refusal of offensive collateral estoppel remain undisturbed. Withdrawn Count IV is not revived.

## Opinion Topology

Justice Ginsburg delivers the Court's opinion. Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas join throughout.

| Portion | Additional joins and controlling support |
|---|---|
| I — Fiduciary prerequisite and sponsor capacity | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Breyer; all nine. |
| II — Release-conditioned benefit payments | Stone-Zsela; seven. Souter and Breyer do not join. |
| III — OBRA | Souter, Breyer; eight. Stone-Zsela agrees with the judgment only. |
| IV-A — Independent claims and remand | Stone-Zsela, Souter, Breyer; all nine. |
| IV-B — Appellate fee consequences | Souter, Breyer; eight. Stone-Zsela agrees with the judgment only. |

Breyer concurs in part and dissents in part, joined by Souter, explaining their reservation of Part II. Stone-Zsela's disposition-only agreement on OBRA and fees adds no ground on those components.

## Holdings

### I. Plan design and plan administration are different functions

**Authority:** Part I, joined by all nine.

**Operative rule:** An employer acts as a plan sponsor, rather than an ERISA fiduciary, when designing and adopting the pension-plan amendments at issue. Subject to section 408's statutory exceptions, section 406(a)(1) requires a fiduciary to cause a transaction that the fiduciary knows or should know is of a prohibited kind; employer party-in-interest status alone does not satisfy that requirement, and actual implementation must be examined as a separate function.

**Controlling explanation:** Curtiss-Wright recognizes the sponsor's plan-amendment role. Section 3(21) attaches fiduciary status to the functions performed, not to every employer act affecting future expenditures. Pension funding and vesting requirements do not transform design itself into fiduciary administration. Varity requires a separate inquiry when the employer actually performs an administrative function; John Hancock likewise separates assets, control and fiduciary duties. Thus sponsor status cannot dispose of the distinct allegation that the Committee controlled plan distributions. The asset-disposition branch does not acquire an extra discretion requirement. The holding leaves amendment procedures and ERISA's other substantive commands in force, and does not establish authorized adoption or lawful implementation merely from amendment power.

### II. Employer benefit from the release does not alone prohibit the payment

**Authority:** Part II, joined by the seven identified in Opinion Topology.

**Operative rule:** Payment of the described genuine enhanced retirement benefits under an otherwise lawful plan is not the transaction prohibited by section 406(a)(1)(D) merely because the required employment-related releases benefit the employer. This rule assumes fiduciary implementation for the legal inquiry and does not immunize a sham asset transfer, kickback, independently unlawful plan or unenforceable release.

**Controlling explanation:** The prohibited-transaction provision addresses dealings with parties in interest of a different character from these plan benefits. Employers obtain recruitment, retention and retirement advantages from ordinary benefit programs; that advantage alone cannot turn payment to participants into prohibited diversion. The release has value, but Keystone's exchange of property to discharge an enforceable funding obligation is a distinct transaction. Surplus does not become employer property, and the Court creates no section 408 exemption or general net-benefit defense.

The rule rejects the asserted per se section 406 theory on the accepted allegations. Independent participation, funding, vesting, loyalty and anti-inurement requirements remain. Section 406(b)'s different prohibitions are not merged into the presented question. Whether a particular waiver is enforceable under the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act or other law is undecided. No sham or kickback is alleged in the issue decided; no finding of loss, deception or hidden diversion is made.

### III. OBRA does not require the claimed credit for earlier lawful exclusion

**Authority:** Part III, joined by the eight Associate Justices. The Chief Justice agrees with the disposition only.

**Operative rule:** OBRA sections 9201 and 9202 do not require pension credit for Spink's service during his earlier lawful exclusion from participation. Section 9204(a)(1)'s express direction applies their new accrual protections to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 1988 and employees with an hour of service in a covered year; a smaller total benefit from earlier uncredited service is not itself a reduced accrual rate during a covered year.

**Controlling explanation:** Landgraf requires the Court first to apply Congress's enacted temporal direction. That direction resolves this claim. Applying the new protection to a participant in a covered plan year does not convert all prior lawful nonparticipation into credited service. The later date of benefit calculation and the statute's general antidiscrimination purpose supply no contrary command.

Section 9204(b) separately applies section 9203's participation amendments to covered plan years and service performed on or after January 1, 1988. Its additional service-date language is not inserted into subsection (a). The provisions perform distinct work. The plan year began on December 25, 1988; this ruling establishes no independent violation during the preceding part of that calendar year.

For a plan maintained under one or more collective-bargaining agreements between employee representatives and employers ratified before March 1, 1986, section 9204(a)(2) applies subsection (a)(1) to benefits pursuant to, and individuals covered by, those agreements using a substituted date: the commencement of the first plan year beginning on or after the earlier of January 1, 1990 or the later of January 1, 1988 and termination of the last qualifying agreement, disregarding extensions after February 28, 1986. No allegation invokes that transition. Section 9204(c) permits delayed formal amendment until the first plan year beginning on or after January 1, 1989 only if interim operation complies and the amendment covers that interval retroactively. A pension plan is not treated as failing to provide definitely determinable benefits or contributions, or to operate according to its provisions, merely because it operates under that subsection. This does not postpone substantive compliance. No general rule forbidding every use of a past fact, or new default presumption of temporal reach, is adopted.

### IV. Independent claims and fees follow their own grounds

**Authority:** Part IV-A has nine joins; Part IV-B has eight Associate joins and the Chief Justice's agreement in the disposition.

**Operative directions and explanation:** The sponsor-capacity holding forecloses section 404 liability resting solely on design or adoption. Actually preserved independent fiduciary implementation and section 403(c)(1) anti-inurement grounds remain for ordinary lower-court consideration; no new allegation or claim is supplied. Varity, Mertens and Peacock preserve the distinct statutory predicate and remedy requirements rather than guaranteeing relief. The appellate fee award is vacated because its stated grounds included the substantive conclusions rejected here; reconsideration must rest on the remaining litigation and applicable fee law.

## Precedent Treatment

- **Curtiss-Wright Corp. v. Schoonejongen:** Applied to sponsor amendment of a pension plan; its amendment-procedure requirements remain separate from actual authorized adoption.
- **Varity Corp. v. Howe:** Applied to distinguish sponsorship from administration and preserve its qualified equitable-remedy rule. No general immunity for misleading or disloyal fiduciary conduct follows.
- **John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Harris Trust & Savings Bank:** Applied to keep asset status, fiduciary function, breach and remedy distinct.
- **Commissioner v. Keystone Consolidated Industries, Inc.:** Distinguished by its property-for-funding-obligation exchange; valuable consideration alone does not equate that transaction with these participant benefits.
- **Mertens v. Hewitt Associates:** Its remedial-category requirements remain in force on any properly preserved claim.
- **Peacock v. Thomas:** Its predicate requirements remain in force on any properly preserved claim.
- **Landgraf v. USI Film Products:** Its enacted-direction-first inquiry is applied. The Court does not reach a new default temporal rule.
- **Rivers v. Roadway Express, Inc.:** Its enacted-direction-first inquiry is applied. The Court does not reach a new default temporal rule.

## Law After Decision

Sponsor amendment alone is not fiduciary conduct. Genuine release-conditioned benefits do not become prohibited section 406(a)(1)(D) transfers merely through employer advantage. Separate administration, anti-inurement and release-validity requirements survive. OBRA's distinct effective-date provisions foreclose the claimed credit for this earlier lawful exclusion without deciding a different covered-period discrimination claim.

## Separate Writings

**Breyer, joined by Souter, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** They agree with the sponsor-capacity and OBRA rulings and with reversal and remand, but would not decide the implementation-based prohibited-transaction question. Whether the release-conditioned distribution falls within section 406 is a difficult technical issue that would benefit from further lower-court consideration and informed submissions. Assuming a fiduciary function and preserving independent statutory duties does not eliminate their objection to deciding that classification now. They would return it without holding either that the payment is prohibited or that every benefit payment is immune.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns through the Ninth Circuit for proceedings consistent with the component rulings and reconsideration of appellate fees. The Court orders no damages amount, benefit payment, invalidation of a particular release or finding of an independent breach.

## Source Notes

The complaint posture, mixed decree and preserved alternatives appear in the [Ninth Circuit opinion](https://static.case.law/f3d/60/cases/0616-01.json). The controlling text is ERISA's separate fiduciary, duty and transaction provisions and [OBRA section 9204, 100 Stat.1979–1980](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-100/pdf/STATUTE-100-Pg1874.pdf). No unreported release term, actual loss or fee amount is established by this decision.


<!-- chunk8-projection: United_States_v_Myers_merits_1996-06-11.md -->

## Event

**United States v. Myers — June 11, 1996.** On review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Seventh Circuit's judgment, 46 F.3d 668, in No. 94-1912. The questions are whether the targeted thermal examination of Myers's home was a Fourth Amendment search and what follows for his preserved suppression claim.

Police used an Agema 210 on March 12, 1992, to record comparative heat from the residence. The passive instrument emitted no rays and did not penetrate the viewed object; the reported pattern indicated concealed high-intensity cultivation lights. Police used the scan and other evidence to obtain the April 22 entry warrant. After suppression was denied, Myers entered a conditional guilty plea under §841(a)(1), preserving review of that denial, including his contention that the later warrant rested on the unlawful scan. The Seventh Circuit affirmed on the ground that the scan was not a search.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate.

## Public Action

The affected judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded.

## Judgment & Remedy

**Vacated in the stated part and remanded, 7–2.**

**Supporting:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg.

**Opposing:** Kennedy, Breyer.

The Court vacates the Seventh Circuit's judgment insofar as it sustains denial of Myers's preserved suppression claim and the dependent conviction affirmance on the no-search premise. The lower courts must dispose of that claim under Pinson and the preservation and remedy limits below. The Court orders neither final suppression nor final admission of the evidence, and does not order acquittal, release, retrial, a replacement sentence or immediate withdrawal of the conditional plea.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg | Vacatur and remand | Parts I–III in full |
| Opinion of the Court, partial join | Scalia | Stone-Zsela | Vacatur and remand | Parts I and III; not Part II |
| Dissent | Kennedy | Breyer | Would affirm | In full |

## Holdings

**Authority:** Parts I and III of Scalia's opinion control with seven direct joins: the six-Justice whole-opinion coalition identified above and Stone-Zsela. Part II controls with the six whole-opinion joins. No dissenting or judgment-only position is needed to establish any holding.

### I. This targeted acquisition of concealed domestic information is a search

**Operative rule:** A targeted technological examination of a closed home's heat patterns is a search when it reveals otherwise unobservable information about concealed domestic operation. External reception, passive equipment and the absence of a recognizable interior image do not defeat that protection; equipment use or investigative purpose alone does not establish a search.

**Controlling explanation:** Pinson supplies the precise rule for this acquisition. Its application of Katz protects concealed domestic information, and Karo establishes that technology can obtain protected information about a home without a physical entry. The Agema 210's heat pattern disclosed the operation of indoor cultivation lights that ordinary outside observation did not reveal. The Court need not find that the instrument identified a person, produced an intimate silhouette or penetrated a wall.

The contrary argument confuses the physical location of heat with the information acquired. Roof vents and failure to conceal emissions do not establish that Myers exposed the operation of his home to this examination. Greenwood concerns garbage delivered for collection; the underlying domestic information here was not similarly discarded. Place concerns detection confined to contraband; thermal patterns can reveal lawful domestic activity as well. The absence of curbside garbage supplied an investigative inference, not exposure of the scanned activity. No different record involving unaided observation of visible smoke is before the Court.

Pinson therefore forecloses the lower court's no-search ground. This application adopts no general rule for all instruments, emissions or uses of technology, and no new test based on market availability or predicted future capabilities.

### II. The later entry warrant did not authorize the earlier scan

**Operative rule:** This search required a warrant unless a recognized exception applied. No such exception is established on this record, and the April 22 entry warrant could not retroactively authorize the March 12 scan.

**Controlling explanation:** Pinson's warrant holding applies to the same protected acquisition. Investigation supported by other suspicious circumstances does not itself establish an exception to the warrant requirement. Whren's requirement of authority for the particular intrusion reinforces that distinction; its rule for an objectively justified ordinary traffic stop supplies no authorization to examine a home thermally. The Court finds no established exception here, while reserving the distinct admissibility of evidence obtained under the later warrant.

### III. The preserved suppression claim returns for a separate remedy determination

**Operative rule:** When rejection of a preserved suppression claim rests on this erroneous no-search ground, the affected judgment must be vacated and the claim decided under the correct search rule. Remand permits consideration of the actual preserved derivative-warrant contention and independently supported, procedurally available alternatives; it neither presumes exclusion nor establishes a new defense or revives a waived claim.

**Controlling explanation:** Pinson separates a search violation from the remedy. Karo permits a distinct inquiry into whether untainted information supports a later warrant. Unlike Pinson's litigant, Myers expressly challenged the warrant's dependence on the scan and preserved suppression review. That reservation does not preserve every newly formulated objection.

The published record does not establish the full affidavit's independent sufficiency, objective reliance, independent source or inevitable discovery. Other investigative information and the fact that a warrant issued cannot substitute for those determinations. Leon is available only if independently supported and procedurally open. It does not protect knowing or reckless deception of the magistrate, abandonment of judicial neutrality, reliance on an affidavit so lacking probable-cause indicia that reliance is wholly unreasonable, or reliance on a facially deficient warrant precluding reasonable reliance. Its inquiry includes officers obtaining or supplying information and assumes execution within the warrant's scope. Evans concerns qualifying non-law-enforcement court-employee clerical error and objectively reasonable reliance; it creates no exception for this deliberate police scan.

The mandate requires no new hearing, discovery or automatic affidavit-excision proceeding. It decides no absent factual predicate. A genuinely forfeited additional issue would remain subject to Olano's requirements of error, plainness and an effect on substantial rights, ordinarily outcome prejudice, followed by the separate discretionary requirement of serious effect on fairness, integrity or public reputation. Intentional waiver extinguishes the relinquished error. Those requirements are not imposed on the claim Myers preserved. Rule 11(a)(2) permits withdrawal of a conditional plea if the defendant prevails on appeal; this limited correction, leaving the suppression outcome unresolved, does not itself order withdrawal. Ordinary proceedings must resolve the available grounds before any final admission or exclusion determination.

## Precedent Treatment

- **United States v. Pinson, May 8, 1995:** Applied to the demonstrated thermal acquisition, its warrant requirement and its separate remedy inquiry. Its individual affidavit nonchallenge is distinguished from Myers's preserved derivative contention; its rules remain intact.
- **Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347:** Applied through Pinson to protection of concealed domestic information; physical penetration is not indispensable.
- **United States v. Karo, 468 U.S. 705:** Applied to technological acquisition of protected home information and retained for the distinct possibility that untainted information sustains a later warrant.
- **California v. Greenwood, 486 U.S. 35:** Distinguished because deliberate disposal of garbage does not establish exposure of concealed domestic operation through heat emissions.
- **United States v. Place, 462 U.S. 696:** Distinguished because this examination can reveal lawful domestic activity and is not confined to contraband.
- **Whren v. United States, June 10, 1996:** Its particular-intrusion requirement is retained; objectively justified traffic enforcement supplies no home-scan exception.
- **United States v. Leon, 468 U.S. 897:** Retained with its factual, procedural and reliance limits. No qualifying reliance finding or new police-technology exception is made.
- **Arizona v. Evans, March 1, 1995:** Confined to its qualifying court-clerical-error setting; it does not excuse the deliberate thermal examination.
- **United States v. Olano:** Retained for genuinely forfeited additional issues and distinguished from the suppression claim actually preserved here; intentional waiver remains distinct from forfeiture.
- **Ornelas v. United States, May 28, 1996:** Its legal and factual review allocation remains intact. It neither shields a categorical legal error nor orders a new hearing or displaces the distinct review of an issuing magistrate's warrant determination.

## Law After Decision

Pinson continues to govern targeted thermal examinations that reveal otherwise unobservable concealed domestic operation. Neither passive external reception nor the lack of a recognizable interior image removes this examination from the Fourth Amendment. Its warrant and exclusionary inquiries remain distinct. Myers's actual reservation preserves the derivative-warrant contention without enlarging it to every possible objection. No earlier decision is overruled, and no final rule admitting or excluding the later seized evidence is adopted.

## Separate Writings

**Kennedy, joined by Breyer, dissenting.** The dissent maintains the content-specific position it took in Pinson: a comparative measurement of exterior warmth, followed by an inference about its cause, does not itself acquire the concealed interior fact protected in Karo. Katz requires attention to the information actually obtained; neither concern about more revealing future equipment nor the fact that police used a device resolves that question. The dissent would reject Pinson's application to this kind of exterior measurement and affirm. It does not claim that a lower court may disregard existing precedent or that all externally received information is unprotected.

The dissent does not adopt a general rule that heat is abandoned property, treat the scanner as confined to contraband, or sustain admission on an unproved reliance or warrant-sufficiency ground. If the Court retains Pinson, the distinction between violation and remedy and the actual preservation limits still apply. That conditional agreement supplies no vote for the Court's vacatur or for its search holding.

## Procedure After Action

The case returns to the lower courts for lawful disposition of the preserved suppression claim and the judgment dependent on it, subject to ordinary mandate procedures. The search determination binds those proceedings. Available remedial grounds remain for decision within their actual factual and procedural predicates; the Court schedules no further event.

## Source Notes

The [Seventh Circuit opinion](https://static.case.law/f3d/46/cases/0668-01.json), cross-checked in [OpenJurist](https://openjurist.org/46/f3d/668), supports the investigative facts, device description, conditional plea and preserved derivative-warrant claim. It does not supply the full affidavit or resolve the alternative exclusionary grounds; this does not establish that the underlying materials are absent from the litigation record. The reported docket is the appellate docket, and no separate Supreme Court docket or argument date is reported.


<!-- chunk8-projection: Vera_and_consolidated_merits_1996-06-13.md -->

## Event

**Bush v. Vera; Lawson v. Vera; United States v. Vera, Nos. 94-805, 94-806 and 94-988 — June 13, 1996.** These direct appeals under 28 U.S.C. §1253 arise from the three-judge Southern District of Texas court's declaration and injunction concerning congressional Districts 18, 29 and 30. The Court decides the residents' standing and whether the racial design of those shared constituencies establishes the asserted equal-protection violation under Shaw and Miller.

Blum and Powers reside in District 18, Thomas and Vera in District 29, Orcutt in District 30, and Chen in District 25. The five residents challenge their own race-based assignments; Chen alleges no personal connection to the assignments in the three districts. No plaintiff asserts dilution, exclusion, unequal participation or another personal injury supporting this decree. The court below invalidated these districts and rejected challenges to 21 others. The state defendants, Lawson and the private defendant-intervenors, and the United States as defendant-intervenor appeal, respectively; no plaintiff appeal is before the Court.

The August 17, 1994 opinion was followed by a September 2 relief order and September 20 amended injunction. The lower court found racial predominance and subordination of ordinary districting considerations amid disputed incumbent, political and community explanations. The Court assumes the strongest predominance premise for deciding the legal sufficiency of the claims; it makes no conclusive determination of the disputed Dallas purpose findings. No argument date is reported for this event.

## Participation

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate in all three appeals.

## Public Action

The Court recognizes the five residents' standing, holds that Chen supplies no independent basis for the three-district relief, and reverses the challenged judgment on the merits in each appeal. The cases are remanded to enter judgment for defendants on the sole presented design-only claims and terminate relief dependent on that theory.

## Judgment & Remedy

| Component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standing in all three appeals | Five residents have standing; Chen supplies no independent basis, 9–0 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | — | The Court reaches the merits. |
| No. 94-805, state defendants | Reverse and remand, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Enter judgment for defendants on the sole design-only claims; remove the dependent declaration, injunction and compulsory-redraw relief. |
| No. 94-806, Lawson and private intervenors | Reverse and remand, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | The same disposition of the common decree; no independent intervenor liability or order is created. |
| No. 94-988, United States | Reverse and remand, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | The same disposition of the common decree; federal preclearance is neither vacated nor collaterally reviewed. |

The September 20 injunction against conducting the 1996 congressional elections, including candidate qualifying, under the specified Plan C657 districts must be dissolved. The compulsory-redraw direction and dependent remedial proceedings based solely on this constitutional theory terminate. The fee-application direction establishes no surviving entitlement from the reversed judgment; no fee award or amount is before the Court. The 21 unappealed district rulings remain undisturbed, and dismissed counts remain dismissed.

## Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court on standing and direct review | Thomas | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Supports the threshold disposition | In full; no merits disposition in this opinion |
